title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: package estimates Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) related quantities experimental observational data using meta-learners, propensity scoring, matching, uplift trees, policy learning, instrumental variables.

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: Three core modules align EconML’s API concepts: R/DMLearner.R — Double Machine Learning (DML): Chernozhukov et al.–style DML cross-fitting; outcome treatment fitted flexible ML (ranger, glmnet, xgb, lm), final stage (linear, sparse linear, kernel, nonparametric, causal forest) estimates CATE residuals. Includes LinearDML, SparseLinearDML, KernelDML, NonParamDML, CausalForestDML, plus native R DynamicDMLearner (panel/sequential treatments) OrthoIVLearner / DMLIVLearner / NonParamDMLIVLearner DML instrumental variables. predict.DMLearner robust near-degenerate OLS final stages (aliased lm coefficients replaced zero) guarantees finite output callers including explain_cate() / kernelshap. DoubleML, mlr3, mlr3learners, mlr3measures installed, -style DML Δy=y1−y0\Delta y = y_1 - y_0 available via doubleml_did_linear, doubleml_did_rf, doubleml_did_xgboost, optional nuisance metrics doubleml_did_eval_* doubleml_did_eval_preds; doubleml_plr, doubleml_plr_fit_data (pre-built DoubleMLData + mlr3 learners, including pipelines / ensembles), doubleml_plr_tune_data (mlr3tuning), doubleml_pliv fit partially linear regression PLIV DoubleML R package; doubleml_data_from_data_frame / doubleml_data_from_matrix build DoubleMLData; doubleml_make_plr_CCDDHNR2018, doubleml_make_pliv_CHS2015, doubleml_fetch_401k, doubleml_fetch_bonus provide example / simulated data aligned DoubleML. R/cate_interpreter.R — CATE interpreters: Single-tree interpretation CATE policy model. SingleTreeCateInterpreter fits regression tree predicted CATE summarize effect heterogeneity covariates; SingleTreePolicyInterpreter fits classification tree predicts optimal treatment (treat) covariates. API matches EconML’s econml.cate_interpreter. R/policy_learner.R — Policy learning: Learns treatment assignment policy maximize expected outcome (welfare). policy_learner implements Athey & Wager (2018) doubly robust weighted classification; DRPolicyTree DRPolicyForest provide cross-fitted outcome + policy tree/forest (EconML-style). Supports fit, predict, predict_proba, (tree/forest) feature_importances predict_value. R/automated_ml.R — Automated ML: Automate model selection nuisance models (Y, T) causal estimators. EconAutoMLConfig configures constraints (linear-, sample-weights required) task (regression/classification). AutomatedMLModel selects learner via cross-validation whitelist (lm, glmnet, ranger, rpart), fits exposes fit, predict, predict_proba. Use add_automated_ml pass configs meta-learners. Local AutoML (Azure); API aligned EconML’s econml.automated_ml.

code: install_missing <- function(pkgs, repos = getOption("repos")) {   pkgs <- unique(pkgs)   pkgs <- pkgs[nzchar(pkgs)]   pkgs <- setdiff(pkgs, rownames(installed.packages()))   if (length(pkgs)) install.packages(pkgs, repos = repos)   invisible(TRUE) }  desc <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION")[1, , drop = FALSE] fields <- intersect(c("Depends", "Imports", "Suggests"), colnames(desc)) deps_raw <- paste(desc[1, fields], collapse = ",")  # remove version constraints like "(>= 1.2)" and split deps_raw <- gsub("\\s*\\([^\\)]+\\)", "", deps_raw) deps <- trimws(unlist(strsplit(deps_raw, ","))) deps <- setdiff(deps, c("R"))  install_missing(c("remotes"))  # used below (lightweight) install_missing(deps)  remotes::install_local(".", dependencies = FALSE, upgrade = "never")

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: Build archive package root (writes RCausalML_0.3.0.tar.gz next DESCRIPTION): Ubuntu: Windows (PowerShell / R console): Package name: RCausalML (version 0.2.0). Load library(RCausalML). Dependencies: glmnet, ranger, rpart, R6, expm, igraph, htetree. Optional: grf, MatchIt, xgboost, reticulate, devtools (load_all standalone test scripts). DoubleML helpers R/DMLearner.R (PLR, PLIV, , DoubleMLData wrappers, simulators / fetch): install DoubleML, mlr3, mlr3learners, mlr3measures. NOTEARS (R/causalDeepNet.R): expm, igraph; torch nonlinear NOTEARS (MLP/Sobolev). DAG-GNN GraN-DAG (R/causalDeepNet.R): torch, R6, expm; ranger progress optional GraN-DAG PNS progress bars. causalStructureML (R/causalStructureML.R): NOTEARS / DAG-GNN / GraN-DAG depending method. SHAP / shapviz (see ): kernelshap, shapviz. causalDeepNet (R/causalDeepNet.R): torch (>= 0.10) (CEVAE, DragonNet, TARNet, CFRNet, GANITE, CausalGAN, DSCM, CausalDiscrepancyVAE, neural Granger models cMLP, cLSTM, EconomySRU, NRI via neural_granger_ml(), SCM Deep Components: deep_scm, deci_model, dynotears); nnet / ranger placeholders applicable. SCM graph utilities (plot_scm_dag): reshape2 (optional, falls back base graphics). tabular DCEVAE (optional, exported build): R package reticulate Python environment torch, numpy, tqdm (code inst/dcevae/DCEVAE_ours/).

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: RCausalML integrates causaldata R package (Huntington-Klein & Barrett), provides example datasets causal inference textbooks (Effect, Causal Inference: Mixtape, Causal Inference: ). Use load_causaldata(name) load dataset RCausalML-ready form (covariates X, treatment w, outcome y, optionally instrument Z), list_causaldata_datasets() see supported names variable roles. Install data package: install.packages("causaldata"). publishing reporting results use datasets, cite causaldata original source given citation component list returned load_causaldata(). See ?explain_cate arguments (n_samples, bg_X, use_permshap, options passed kernelshap/permshap).
code: library(RCausalML) list_causaldata_datasets()   # nsw_mixtape, cps_mixtape, abortion, close_college, ... d <- load_causaldata("nsw_mixtape") sl <- SLearner(learner = "ranger") sl <- fit(sl, d$X, d$w, d$y) estimate_ate(sl, d$X, d$w, d$y) # Always cite the data source (returned in d$citation) and the causaldata package: citation("causaldata") library(RCausalML) library(kernelshap) library(shapviz)  d <- synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 500, p = 5, sigma = 1) sl <- SLearner(learner = "ranger") sl <- fit(sl, d$X, d$w, d$y)  # SHAP for CATE; then all shapviz plots ks <- explain_cate(sl, d$X[1:100, ], bg_X = d$X, use_permshap = TRUE) shp <- shapviz(ks) sv_importance(shp) sv_dependence(shp, "X1") sv_waterfall(shp, 1) sv_force(shp, 1)

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: run faster multi-core machines (Unix/macOS), use n_cores argument supported: Meta-learners (fit_predict, estimate_ate return_ci=TRUE bootstrap_ci=TRUE): bootstrap runs parallel, e.g. fit_predict(sl, X, w, y, return_ci = TRUE, n_cores = 4) estimate_ate(sl, X, w, y, bootstrap_ci = TRUE, n_cores = 4). DR-Learner: n_cores bootstrap fit_predict.DRLearner estimate_ate.DRLearner. Uplift forests (uplift_rf_kl, uplift_rf_ed, uplift_rf_chi, uplift_rf_cts, uplift_randomForest): tree building runs parallel, e.g. uplift_randomForest(X, w, y, n_estimators = 100, n_cores = 4). Parallelization uses parallel::mclapply (multi-core lapply). Windows, n_cores > 1 ignored runs remain sequential.

text: Run quickstart example (see inst/examples/quickstart.R): Example output:
code: library(RCausalML)  # Synthetic data (Nie & Wager 2018 style) set.seed(42) d <- synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 1000, p = 5, sigma = 1) y <- d$y X <- d$X w <- d$w          # treatment (0/1) e <- d$e          # propensity (for X-Learner, R-Learner, TMLE)  # S-Learner (LRSRegressor = SLearner(learner = "lm")) lr <- LRSRegressor() lr <- fit(lr, X, w, y) ate_lr <- estimate_ate(lr, X, w, y, return_ci = TRUE)  # S-Learner with ranger sl <- SLearner(learner = "ranger") sl <- fit(sl, X, w, y) ate_sl <- estimate_ate(sl, X, w, y, return_ci = TRUE)  # T-Learner tl <- TLearner(learner = "ranger") tl <- fit(tl, X, w, y) ate_tl <- estimate_ate(tl, X, w, y, return_ci = TRUE)  # X-Learner (with propensity) xl <- XLearner(learner = "ranger") xl <- fit(xl, X, w, y, p = e) ate_xl <- estimate_ate(xl, X, w, y, p = e, return_ci = TRUE)  # R-Learner rl <- RLearner(learner = "ranger", n_fold = 5) rl <- fit(rl, X, w, y, p = e) ate_rl <- estimate_ate(rl, X, w, y, p = e, return_ci = TRUE)  # TMLE tmle <- TMLELearner(learner = "ranger") tmle <- fit(tmle, X, w, y, p = e) ate_tmle <- estimate_ate(tmle, X, w, y, p = e, return_ci = TRUE)  # Propensity and CATE ps <- propensity_glmnet(X, w, n_fold = 5) cate_s <- predict(lr, X, verbose = FALSE) cate_t <- predict(tl, X) ATE (S-Learner / LRSRegressor): 0.60 (0.46, 0.75) ATE (S-Learner ranger): 0.48 (0.41, 0.55) ATE (T-Learner ranger): 0.56 (0.49, 0.64) ATE (X-Learner ranger): 0.49 (0.42, 0.55) ATE (R-Learner ranger): 0.52 (0.37, 0.68) ATE (TMLE ranger): 0.44 (0.34, 0.54) Propensity scores (first 5): 0.8517243 0.5155485 0.6182359 0.7123617 0.6122691 Mean CATE (S-Learner): 0.6048919   Mean CATE (T-Learner): 0.5633381

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
code: # Policy learner (Athey & Wager: who to treat) — doubly robust + classifier d <- synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 800, p = 6, sigma = 1) pl <- policy_learner(outcome_learner = "ranger", treatment_learner = "glmnet", policy_learner = "rpart") pl <- fit(pl, d$X, d$w, d$y, control = rpart::rpart.control(maxdepth = 2)) policy_pred <- predict(pl, d$X)   # 0 = control, 1 = treat prob_treat <- predict_proba(pl, d$X)  # DR Policy Tree (EconML-style): cross-fitted outcome + single policy tree pt <- DRPolicyTree(model_regression = "ranger", cv = 2L, random_state = 42) pt <- fit(pt, d$X, d$w, d$y) pred_pt <- predict(pt, d$X) proba_pt <- predict_proba(pt, d$X) imp_pt <- feature_importances(pt)  # DR Policy Forest: ensemble of policy trees (majority vote) pf <- DRPolicyForest(n_estimators = 50L, cv = 2L, max_samples = 0.6, random_state = 123) pf <- fit(pf, d$X, d$w, d$y) pred_pf <- predict(pf, d$X)  # CATE interpreter: single tree over CATE (interpret heterogeneity) sl <- SLearner(learner = "ranger"); sl <- fit(sl, d$X, d$w, d$y) interp_cate <- SingleTreeCateInterpreter(max_depth = 3L, min_samples_leaf = 10L) interp_cate <- interpret(interp_cate, sl, d$X) cate_tree <- predict(interp_cate, d$X)   # tree-predicted CATE  # Policy interpreter: single tree over optimal treatment (who to treat) pol_interp <- SingleTreePolicyInterpreter(max_depth = 3L, min_samples_leaf = 10L) pol_interp <- interpret(pol_interp, sl, d$X) trt_rec <- treat(pol_interp, d$X)         # recommended treatment (0/1)

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: Use EconAutoMLConfig AutomatedMLModel auto-select nuisance models (e.g. outcome treatment) constraints (linear-, sample-weights). Assign result fit() fitted model stored.
code: # AutoML config: only models that support sample weights (e.g. for DR) cfg <- EconAutoMLConfig(sample_weights_required = TRUE, task = "regression", show_output = TRUE) m <- AutomatedMLModel(cfg) m <- fit(m, X, y)           # CV selects best of lm, glmnet, ranger, rpart; refit on full data pred <- predict(m, X)  # Classification (propensity): fit and predict_proba cfg_cls <- EconAutoMLConfig(task = "classification", show_output = FALSE, n_folds = 3) m_cls <- AutomatedMLModel(cfg_cls) m_cls <- fit(m_cls, X, treatment) prob <- predict_proba(m_cls, X)  # Replace configs with models in a list (e.g. for passing to meta-learners) args <- add_automated_ml(list(learner = cfg), workspace = NULL) # Counterfactual value estimator # cve <- counterfactual_value_estimator(treatment, control_name, treatment_names, #   y_proba = matrix(...), value = 1, conversion_cost = 0, impression_cost = 0) # best_idx <- predict_best_treatment(cve)

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
code: set.seed(123) n <- 1000 p_x <- 5 X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p_x), n, p_x) colnames(X) <- paste0("X", 1:p_x) W <- matrix(rnorm(n * 5), n, 5)  # Propensity: Pr[T=1 | X, W] propensity <- 1 / (1 + exp(-X[, 1] - 0.5 * W[, 1])) T_bin <- rbinom(n, 1, propensity)  # True CATE: non-linear in X1 true_cate <- 1 + 0.5 * X[, 1] + 0.3 * (X[, 1]^2) Y <- as.vector(2 + 0.3 * (W[, 1:3] %*% c(1, -0.5, 0.5)) + true_cate * T_bin + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5))  x_cols <- paste0("X", 1:p_x) data <- data.frame(   Y = Y, T = factor(T_bin), T_num = T_bin,   as.data.frame(X), W1 = W[, 1], W2 = W[, 2], W3 = W[, 3], true_cate = true_cate ) X_mat <- as.matrix(data[, x_cols]) treatment <- as.integer(data$T_num) y <- as.numeric(data$Y)

text: tests/test-neural.R runs neural network–based algorithms RCausalML. sets RCAUSALML_SOURCE_ROOT DCEVAE can find inst/python inst/dcevae script source()s R/causalDeepNet.R without installing package. Available models: CEVAE — Counterfactual Variational Autoencoder; generative model latent confounders (uses torch available). Ref: Louizos et al. (2017). DragonNet — Shared representation plus three heads targeted regularization (uses torch available). TARNet — Shared representation plus two heads (treatment-agnostic). CFRNet — TARNet MMD balancing. GANITE — Causal inference GANs: Generator, Discriminator, Inference net (uses torch available). test passes iterations (epochs) control training length. CausalGAN — Structural equation GAN (X,T,Y)(X, T, Y) node-wise generators interventional sampling (uses torch available). test path can run small epochs quick validation. DSCM — Deep Structural Causal Model latent abduction abduction-action-prediction counterfactual inference (uses torch available). CausalDiscrepancyVAE — Discrepancy-regularized VAE latent MMD balancing treatment-specific outcome heads (uses torch available). Neural Granger models — neural_granger_ml() wrapper cMLP, cLSTM, EconomySRU, NRI multivariate time series (uses torch available). DCEVAE — Tabular deep counterfactual equivariant VAE (Python implementation inst/dcevae/DCEVAE_ours/, called via reticulate). Skipped reticulate installed Python lacks torch / numpy / tqdm.
code: # Quick run (fewer epochs / iterations) QUICK=1 Rscript tests/test-neural.R  # Full run Rscript tests/test-neural.R

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: R/causalDeepNet.R exposes three attention-based causal models multivariate time series (v0.2.0, 03_attention_transforner_causalML.ipynb): TCDFNet (tcdf_model) — stacked causal dilated convolutions + attention head; inspired Nauta et al. (2019). CausalTransformer (causal_transformer_model) — Transformer encoder autoregressive mask + inter-variable cross-attention. TFT (tft_model) — Temporal Fusion Transformer (Lim et al., 2021): variable-selection networks, LSTM encoder, multi-head temporal attention. three also available unified wrapper attn_causal_model(). Causal graphs (variable--variable influence matrices) extracted causal_matrix_attn(). Requires torch.
code: library(RCausalML) library(torch)  set.seed(42) d <- 5L; T_len <- 300L A <- matrix(0, d, d) for (i in seq_len(d)) { A[i,i] <- 0.45; if (i > 1) A[i, i-1] <- 0.25 } x <- matrix(0, T_len, d) x[1, ] <- rnorm(d) for (t in 2:T_len) x[t, ] <- x[t-1, ] %*% t(A) + 0.15 * rnorm(d) colnames(x) <- paste0("V", seq_len(d))  # Fit all three models jointly fit <- attn_causal_model(x, lag = 10L,                          models = c("tcdf", "causal_transformer", "tft"),                          epochs = 20L, d_model = 64L, hidden = 48L, verbose = TRUE)  # Validation MSE per model print(fit$val_mse)  # Causal matrices (variable-to-variable influence) print(round(causal_matrix_attn(fit, "tcdf"), 3)) print(round(causal_matrix_attn(fit, "causal_transformer"), 3)) print(round(causal_matrix_attn(fit, "tft"), 3))  # One-step-ahead predictions ds   <- RCausalML:::.deepnet_attn_build_dataset(x, lag = 10L) preds <- predict(fit, model = "causal_transformer", newdata = ds$X[1:5, , ])  # Convenience single-model wrappers fit_tcdf <- tcdf_model(x, lag = 10L, epochs = 20L) fit_ctrf <- causal_transformer_model(x, lag = 10L, epochs = 20L, d_model = 64L) fit_tft  <- tft_model(x, lag = 10L, epochs = 20L, d_model = 64L)

title: RCausalML: Causal Inference with ML
text: R/causalDeepNet.R exposes three RNN/LSTM-based causal models multivariate time series (v0.2.0, 04_rnn_lstm_causalML.ipynb): CausalLSTM (causal_lstm_model) — per-variable LSTM learnable sparse causal-adjacency mask G∈[0,1]d×dG \[0,1]^{d \times d}; mask regularised L1 sparsity penalty true predictors survive. RETAIN (retain_model) — REverse Time AttentIoN (Choi et al., 2016): two-channel GRU reverse time — temporal attention α\alpha (step matters) + variable attention β\beta (variable step) — produces per-step attribution matrix interpretability. Intervention-Aware RNN (intervention_rnn_model) — GRU regime detector infers latent system states; learned regime embeddings explicit binary/continuous intervention-indicator channel concatenated input LSTM forecaster; exposes regime-conditioned causal effect matrices. three available unified wrapper rnn_causal_model(). Causal graphs extracted causal_matrix_rnn(). Requires torch.
code: library(RCausalML) library(torch)  set.seed(42) d <- 5L; T_len <- 300L A <- matrix(0, d, d) for (i in seq_len(d)) { A[i,i] <- 0.45; if (i > 1) A[i, i-1] <- 0.25 } x <- matrix(0, T_len, d) x[1, ] <- rnorm(d) for (t in 2:T_len) x[t, ] <- x[t-1, ] %*% t(A) + 0.15 * rnorm(d) colnames(x) <- paste0("V", seq_len(d))  # Intervention vector (e.g., volatility-spike proxy, top 25% quantile) interv <- as.numeric(apply(x, 1, function(r) sum(r^2)) >                      quantile(apply(x, 1, function(r) sum(r^2)), 0.75))  # Fit all three models jointly fit <- rnn_causal_model(x, lag = 10L,                         models = c("causal_lstm", "retain", "intervention_rnn"),                         intervention = interv,                         epochs = 30L, hidden = 32L, verbose = TRUE)  # Validation MSE per model print(fit$val_mse)  # Causal matrices (variable-to-variable influence) print(round(causal_matrix_rnn(fit, "causal_lstm"), 3)) print(round(causal_matrix_rnn(fit, "retain"), 3)) print(round(causal_matrix_rnn(fit, "intervention_rnn"), 3))  # One-step-ahead predictions ds    <- RCausalML:::.deepnet_rnn_build_dataset(x, lag = 10L, intervention = interv) preds <- predict(fit, model = "causal_lstm", newdata = ds$X[1:5, , ])  # Convenience single-model wrappers fit_lstm   <- causal_lstm_model(x, lag = 10L, epochs = 30L) fit_retain <- retain_model(x, lag = 10L, epochs = 30L) fit_irnn   <- intervention_rnn_model(x, lag = 10L, epochs = 30L,                                      intervention = interv)

text: Impute missing values X using per-column medians. Cross-fit nuisances (parallelised, n_folds folds): \(\hat m(X) = E[Y \mid X]\) \(\hat e(X) = E[W \mid X]\) \(\hat p(X) = E[Z \mid X]\) Residualise: \(\tilde Y = Y - \hat m(X)\),     \(\tilde W = W - \hat e(X)\), \(\tilde Z = Z - \hat p(X)\). Fit grf::instrumental_forest     \((\tilde Y, \tilde W, \tilde Z, X)\).

what: DMLearner: Double machine learning (EconML econml.dml.DML family) — DMLearner
title: DMLearner: Double machine learning (EconML econml.dml.DML family) — DMLearner
text: Special case R-learner style two-stage procedure: cross-fit nuisances \(\hat{q}(X) \approx E[Y \mid X]\) \(\hat{f}(X) \approx E[T \mid X]\), form residuals \(\tilde{Y} = Y - \hat{q}(X)\), \(\tilde{T} = T - \hat{f}(X)\), fit CATE model solving (linear parametric case) \(\hat{\theta} = \arg\min E_n[(\tilde{Y} - \Theta(\phi(X)) \cdot \tilde{T})^2]\) .e. OLS cross-product design \(\tilde{T} \otimes \phi(X)\) (EconML cross_product; Python _FinalWrapper._combine). Discrete treatment uses classification-style \(\hat{f}\) (probabilities / residualized binary \(T\)); continuous \(T\) uses regression \(\hat{f}\).

what: NOTEARS: Causal DAG structure learning via continuous optimization — NOTEARS
title: NOTEARS: Causal DAG structure learning via continuous optimization — NOTEARS
text: RCausalML package implements NOTEARS (TEARS) causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure learning observational data. NOTEARS treats discrete acyclicity constraint continuous constraint \(h(W) = 0\) using trace matrix exponential (\(h(W) = \mathrm{tr}(e^{W \odot W}) - d\)), problem solved continuous optimization (e.g. augmented Lagrangian L-BFGS-B linear, Adam + L-BFGS nonlinear). Linear NOTEARS (pure R): learns weighted adjacency matrix \(W\) minimizing loss (e.g. least squares, logistic, Poisson) plus L1 penalty, subject \(h(W) = 0\). Uses expm L-BFGS-B. Nonlinear NOTEARS (R + torch): uses MLP Sobolev basis models capture nonlinear relationships; acyclicity enforced via differentiable \(h(W)\). Requires torch package. Main functions: notears_linear — Linear NOTEARS: L2/logistic/Poisson loss + L1, augmented Lagrangian. notears_nonlinear — Nonlinear NOTEARS MLP Sobolev model (Adam L-BFGS). NotearsMLP — Torch module: MLP nonlinear SEM (torch installed). NotearsSobolev — Torch module: Sobolev basis nonlinear SEM (torch installed). Utilities simulation: is_dag — Check weighted adjacency matrix DAG. simulate_dag — Simulate random DAG (Erdős–Rényi scale-free). simulate_parameter — Draw edge weights DAG. simulate_linear_sem — Generate data linear SEM (Gaussian, exponential, uniform noise). simulate_nonlinear_sem — Generate data nonlinear SEM (MLP MIM). count_accuracy — Compare estimated graph ground truth (FDR, TPR, FPR, SHD, nnz). set_random_seed — Set R torch seeds reproducibility. Demos: demo_linear — Linear NOTEARS synthetic data. demo_nonlinear_mlp — Nonlinear NOTEARS (MLP) synthetic data. demo_nonlinear_sobolev — Nonlinear NOTEARS (Sobolev) random data.

title: NOTEARS: Causal DAG structure learning via continuous optimization — NOTEARS
text: Zheng, X., Aragam, B., Ravikumar, P., & Xing, E. P. (2018). DAGs TEARS: Continuous optimization structure learning. NeurIPS. https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.01422.

title: Precision in Estimation of Heterogeneous Effects (PEHE) — PEHE
text: Root mean squared error true estimated individual treatment effects: \(\sqrt{E[(\tau(x) - \hat\tau(x))^2]}\). Accepts two calling conventions: Matrix form (original): PEHE(y, y_hat)     arguments n x 2 matrices columns [Y(0), Y(1)].     Returns MSE ITE: \(E[((Y(1)-Y(0)) - (\hat Y(1)-\hat Y(0)))^2]\). Vector form (new): PEHE(tau_true = ..., tau_hat = ...)     arguments length-n numeric vectors individual treatment     effects. Returns RMSE: \(\sqrt{E[(\tau - \hat\tau)^2]}\).

Architecture follows [causalml dragonnet.py](https://github.com/uber/causalml/blob/master/causalml/inference/tf/dragonnet.py): 3 shared layers (ELU), propensity head (sigmoid), two outcome branches (2 hidden layers , output).

title: Compute SHAP values for any RCausalML CATE model — explain_cate
text: Works RCausalML models predict(object, newdata) returning CATE (list predictions), including: Meta-learners: SLearner, TLearner, XLearner, RLearner, DRLearner DML: LinearDML, SparseLinearDML, KernelDML, NonParamDML, CausalForestDML, DynamicDMLearner, OrthoIVLearner, DMLIVLearner, NonParamDMLIVLearner Trees/forests: causal_forest, uplift_rf_*, uplift_tree_*, interaction_tree, causal_inference_tree Policy: policy_learner, DRPolicyTree, DRPolicyForest Interpreters: SingleTreeCateInterpreter, SingleTreePolicyInterpreter Neural: cevae, dragonnet, tarnet, cfrnet, ganite : AutomatedMLModel, driv_learner

title: Compute SHAP values for any RCausalML CATE model — explain_cate
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(RCausalML) library(kernelshap) library(shapviz)  # Fit any CATE model set.seed(42) d <- synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 500, p = 5, sigma = 1) sl <- SLearner(learner = "ranger") sl <- fit(sl, d$X, d$w, d$y)  # Compute SHAP for CATE predictions X_explain <- d$X[1:100, ]   # optional: subset for speed ks <- explain_cate(sl, X_explain, bg_X = d$X, use_permshap = TRUE)  # Build shapviz object and use all shapviz functions shp <- shapviz(ks) sv_importance(shp) sv_dependence(shp, "X1") sv_waterfall(shp, 1) sv_force(shp, 1) } # }

Leaf estimation solves vector effects \(\boldsymbol{\tau}(x)\) (one effect per arm). \[   \hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}(x) = \left( \sum \tilde{\mathbf{D}}_i \tilde{\mathbf{D}}_i^T \right)^{-1} \left( \sum \tilde{\mathbf{D}}_i \tilde{Y}_i \right)   \] Use Case: Dose-response studies, choosing multiple marketing strategies.

Scenario: One Treatment, Multiple Outcomes (Revenue Retention Satisfaction). Treatment (\(W\)): Binary Categorical. Outcome (\(Y\)): Vector \(\mathbf{Y} \\mathbb{R}^M\). Estimates vector effects \(\boldsymbol{\tau}(x)\) (one effect per outcome). Uses outcome covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) weight loss function (exploiting correlations outcomes reduce variance). Requires Multiple Testing Correction (e.g., Bonferroni) confidence intervals. Use Case: Holistic health metrics, comprehensive business KPIs.

Scenario: Treatment affects time event (Death, Churn, Machine Failure). Treatment (\(W\)): Binary Categorical. Outcome (\(Y\)): Tuple \((T_i, \delta_i)\). \(T_i\): Time observed. \(\delta_i\): Censoring indicator (\(1\) event observed, \(0\) censored/lost follow-). Challenge: use standard squared error censored data (\(\delta=0\)) reveal true outcome \(Y\). Math Adaptation: IPCW Weighting: Outcomes weighted Inverse Probability Censoring Weighting correct bias. \[ \tilde{Y}_i^{\text{surv}} = \frac{\delta_i \cdot Y_i}{\hat{G}(T_i \mid X_i)} \] (\(\hat{G}\) probability censored). Use Case: Clinical trials (time death), Customer Churn (time cancellation), Reliability Engineering.
code: 2.  **Leaf Estimation:** Instead of minimizing squared error, leaves often minimize a **Cox Partial Likelihood** or estimate the difference in survival probability at a specific horizon $t$. $$ \hat{\tau}(x) = \text{Effect on Hazard Ratio or Survival Probability } S(t \mid x, W=1) - S(t \mid x, W=0) $$

text: Scenario: Multiple Treatments Multiple Time--Event Outcomes (e.g., Time Death Time Relapse). Treatment (\(W\)): Categorical \(\{0, \dots, K\}\). Outcome (\(Y\)): Vector Survival Tuples \(\mathbf{Y} \\{(T, \delta)\}^M\). parameter Matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Tau}(x)\) size \(K \times M\). Entry \(\Tau_{km}\) = Effect Arm \(k\) Survival Outcome \(m\). Leaf estimation uses Multivariate Survival Regression IPCW weighting. Use Case: Complex clinical trials (multiple drugs, multiple competing risks).

set.seed(42) dat <- synthetic_data(mode = 2, n = 2000, p = 12, sigma = 2) # Extract components y_sim   <- dat$y X_sim   <- dat$X w_sim   <- dat$w tau_sim <- dat$tau   # true CATE (for evaluation) feature_names <- paste0("X", seq_len(ncol(X_sim))) df_sim <- as.data.frame(X_sim) colnames(df_sim) <- feature_names df_sim$outcome   <- y_sim df_sim$treatment <- w_sim df_sim$tau_true  <- tau_sim cat("Simulated data:", nrow(df_sim), "rows,", ncol(X_sim), "covariates
") Simulated data: 2000 rows, 12 covariates summary(df_sim$tau_true) Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.  -1.9100  0.1490  0.7760  0.8633  1.4589  7.3492 table(df_sim$treatment) 0    1  1006  994 train_prop <- 0.8 n_sim <- nrow(df_sim) train_idx_sim <- sample(1:n_sim, size = round(train_prop * n_sim)) df_train <- df_sim[train_idx_sim, ] df_test  <- df_sim[-train_idx_sim, ] cat("Train:", nrow(df_train), "| Test:", nrow(df_test), "
") Train: 1600 | Test: 400 if (!exists("na.causalTree")) na.causalTree <- function(object, ...) object  covar_names_sim <- setdiff(colnames(df_train), c("outcome", "treatment", "tau_true")) formula_sim <- as.formula(paste("outcome ~", paste(covar_names_sim, collapse = " + ")))  # Honest split: half for tree structure, half for leaf estimation n_obs <- nrow(df_train) n_tree <- max(1L, floor(n_obs / 2)) tree_idx <- sample(seq_len(n_obs), size = n_tree, replace = FALSE) est_idx_sim <- setdiff(seq_len(n_obs), tree_idx)  ct_sim <- causal_tree(   formula   = formula_sim,   data      = df_train,   treatment = as.vector(df_train$treatment),   honest    = TRUE,   est_idx   = est_idx_sim,   split.Rule   = "CT",   cv.option    = "CT",   split.Bucket = FALSE,   minsize   = 20L,   cp        = 0,   xval      = 10L,   maxdepth  = 5 )  # Prune by minimum CV error cpt_sim <- ct_sim$cptable opcp_sim <- if (nrow(cpt_sim) > 1) cpt_sim[, 1][which.min(cpt_sim[, 4])] else 0.01 ct_sim <- prune(ct_sim, cp = max(opcp_sim, 0.005)) summary(ct_sim) Call: causal_tree(formula = formula_sim, data = df_train, treatment = as.vector(df_train$treatment),      honest = TRUE, est_idx = est_idx_sim, split.Rule = "CT",      cv.option = "CT", minsize = 20, split.Bucket = FALSE, xval = 10,      cp = 0, maxdepth = 5)   n= 800        CP nsplit rel error xerror         xstd 1 0.005      0         1      1 1.716693e-05  Node number 1: 800 observations   causal effect=1.317211, error=63448.09 # Predict CATE on test set (same covariate columns as training) df_test$cate_pred <- predict(ct_sim, newdata = df_test, type = "vector") # True CATE is in tau_true df_test$tau_true <- df_sim$tau_true[-train_idx_sim]  # Summary of predictions vs truth cat("Test set CATE summary:
") Test set CATE summary: cat("  Predicted CATE: mean =", round(mean(df_test$cate_pred, na.rm = TRUE), 4),     ", sd =", round(sd(df_test$cate_pred, na.rm = TRUE), 4), "
") Predicted CATE: mean = 1.3172 , sd = 0 cat("  True CATE:      mean =", round(mean(df_test$tau_true, na.rm = TRUE), 4),     ", sd =", round(sd(df_test$tau_true, na.rm = TRUE), 4), "
") True CATE:      mean = 0.8807 , sd = 1.0853 # Correlation (on complete cases) valid <- complete.cases(df_test$cate_pred, df_test$tau_true) if (sum(valid) > 1) {   cat("  Correlation (pred vs true):", round(cor(df_test$cate_pred[valid], df_test$tau_true[valid]), 4), "
") } Correlation (pred vs true): NA

Risky behavior proxied incidence gonorrhea (sexually transmitted infection) among 15–19 year olds. idea access abortion might influence sexual decision-making risk-taking behavior age group. important columns (based package documentation): fip — State FIPS code (numeric identifier U.S. state) age — Age years (focused 15–19 year olds) race — Race: 1 = white, 2 = black (similar coding) year — Calendar year t — rescaled time variable (often centered around policy change ) sex — Sex: 1 = male, 2 = female totpop — Total population (state-level) ir — Incarcerated males per 100,000 (proxy criminal justice environment) crack — Crack cocaine index (proxy drug epidemic intensity) alcohol — Alcohol consumption per capita income — Real income per capita ur — State unemployment rate poverty — Poverty rate repeal — Treatment indicator: 1 = state early repeal abortion prohibition (treatment group), 0 = otherwise (control group). main policy/treatment variable. pi — Parental involvement law effect (another policy control) bf15 — Indicator: black female 15–19 age group (useful subgroup analysis) outcome variable typically lnr (logged gonorrhea rate per 100,000 population among 15–19 year olds), measures logged incidence gonorrhea proxy risky sexual behavior.  80% training, 20% test.

what: 1.2 Causal Forest (CF) for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation
text: tutorial provides overview Causal Forests (CF) within Generalized Random Forests (GRF) framework, focusing estimating heterogeneous treatment effects observational experimental data. includes step--step guide implementing Causal Forests using grf package R, practical examples explanations tailored abortion dataset causaldata package. Causal Forest machine learning method within Generalized Random Forests (GRF) framework, designed estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (HTE) — specifically Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) — across individuals observational experimental studies. adapts classic random forest algorithm causal inference, asking “happen?” “effect treatment type person?” Treatment Effect measures difference outcomes treated untreated individual: \[\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\] \(Y(1)\) outcome treated, \(Y(0)\) untreated, \(X\) represents covariates (age, sex, income, etc.), \(\tau(x)\) CATE — expected treatment effect individual covariates \(X = x\). Heterogeneity core motivation: treatment effects aren’t uniform. drug may work better older patients; intervention may help high-income households low-income ones. Causal forests find much effects vary. Random Forest Foundation: Like standard random forests, causal forests use ensemble decision trees — trees grown maximize heterogeneity treatment effects, prediction accuracy. 1. Data Requirements — need three things: outcome \(Y\) (e.g. survival time, test score), treatment indicator \(W\) (binary continuous: treated vs. control), covariates \(X\) (features like age, income). 2. Tree Construction — tree grown random data/feature subset. Splits chosen maximally separate groups different treatment effects — minimize prediction error. criterion targets variance \(\tau(x)\) across branches. 3. Honest Estimation — avoid overfitting, one subsample determines tree structure (splits), held-subsample estimates treatment effects within leaf. ensures unbiased \(\tau(x)\) estimates. 4. Aggregation — trees averaged smooth, non-parametric estimate \(\tau(x)\) across covariate space. 5. Outputs — forest produces: CATE estimates \(\tau(x)\) per individual, Average Treatment Effect (ATE) \(= E[\tau(X)]\), variable importance scores showing covariates drive treatment effect heterogeneity.  diagram walks five stages end--end: Inputs (teal/purple/coral) flow tree construction, key innovation split criterion — rather minimizing prediction error, split maximizes difference treatment effects \(\Delta\tau(x)\) branches. Honest estimation (blue/amber) prevents overfitting separating data used grow tree structure data used estimate effects leaves. 1L)) # Separate explain vs background sets  # Using the same set for both leaks info — split them. set.seed(42)   n_explain <- min(80L, nrow(X_train))   n_bg      <- min(50L, nrow(X_train))   if (nrow(X_train) > n_explain + n_bg) {     # Enough rows — keep explain and background non-overlapping     idx_explain <- sample(nrow(X_train), n_explain)     idx_bg      <- sample(setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X_train)), idx_explain), n_bg)   } else {     # Small dataset — allow overlap rather than crash     idx_explain <- sample(nrow(X_train), n_explain)     idx_bg      <- sample(nrow(X_train), n_bg)   }   X_explain <- as.data.frame(X_train[idx_explain, , drop = FALSE])   bg_X      <- as.data.frame(X_train[idx_bg,      , drop = FALSE]) # Compute SHAP ks <- explain_cate(     cf_model,     X            = X_explain,     bg_X         = bg_X,     use_permshap = TRUE,     verbose      = FALSE   ) # Reset workers plan(sequential) shp <- shapviz::shapviz(ks) shapviz::sv_importance(shp, kind = "beeswarm") if (exists("shp")) {   shapviz::sv_importance(shp, show_numbers = TRUE) } if (exists("shp") && exists("xvars")) {   shapviz::sv_dependence(shp, v = xvars, share_y = TRUE) } if (exists("shp")) {   shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = 1) +     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11))    shapviz::sv_force(shp, row_id = 1) } if (exists("shp") && "sex" %in% names(shp$X)) {   idx_female <- which(shp$X$sex == 2)   row_show   <- if (length(idx_female) > 0) idx_female[1] else 1   shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = row_show) +     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11)) } else if (exists("shp")) {   shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = 2) +     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11)) }

text: Causal Forest machine learning method within Generalized Random Forests (GRF) framework, designed estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (HTE) — specifically Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) — across individuals observational experimental studies. adapts classic random forest algorithm causal inference, asking “happen?” “effect treatment type person?” Treatment Effect measures difference outcomes treated untreated individual: \[\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\] \(Y(1)\) outcome treated, \(Y(0)\) untreated, \(X\) represents covariates (age, sex, income, etc.), \(\tau(x)\) CATE — expected treatment effect individual covariates \(X = x\). Heterogeneity core motivation: treatment effects aren’t uniform. drug may work better older patients; intervention may help high-income households low-income ones. Causal forests find much effects vary. Random Forest Foundation: Like standard random forests, causal forests use ensemble decision trees — trees grown maximize heterogeneity treatment effects, prediction accuracy. 1. Data Requirements — need three things: outcome \(Y\) (e.g. survival time, test score), treatment indicator \(W\) (binary continuous: treated vs. control), covariates \(X\) (features like age, income). 2. Tree Construction — tree grown random data/feature subset. Splits chosen maximally separate groups different treatment effects — minimize prediction error. criterion targets variance \(\tau(x)\) across branches. 3. Honest Estimation — avoid overfitting, one subsample determines tree structure (splits), held-subsample estimates treatment effects within leaf. ensures unbiased \(\tau(x)\) estimates. 4. Aggregation — trees averaged smooth, non-parametric estimate \(\tau(x)\) across covariate space. 5. Outputs — forest produces: CATE estimates \(\tau(x)\) per individual, Average Treatment Effect (ATE) \(= E[\tau(X)]\), variable importance scores showing covariates drive treatment effect heterogeneity.  diagram walks five stages end--end: Inputs (teal/purple/coral) flow tree construction, key innovation split criterion — rather minimizing prediction error, split maximizes difference treatment effects \(\Delta\tau(x)\) branches. Honest estimation (blue/amber) prevents overfitting separating data used grow tree structure data used estimate effects leaves. Aggregation smooths across \(B\) trees, producing robust, non-parametric CATE surface. Outputs give per-individual CATE estimates, population-level ATE, variable importance — telling patient characteristics matter treatment response.

") Training: n = 2400 | Test: n = 600 cat("True CATE (test) — mean:", round(mean(tau_te), 3), ", sd:", round(sd(tau_te), 3), "
") True CATE (test) — mean: 0.813 , sd: 1.105 library(future)  # Detect cores and set parallel threads n_cores <- max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L)  # Fit causal forest with tuning  if (nrow(X_tr) > 5000L) {   # Large data — reduce trees slightly, rely on parallelism   n_trees          <- 500L   samp_fraction    <- 0.4   min_node         <- 10L  } else {   # Small/medium data — more trees for stability, finer nodes   n_trees          <- 200L   samp_fraction    <- 0.5   min_node         <- 5L }  cf_sim <- causal_forest(   X                = X_tr,   Y                = Y_tr,   W                = W_tr,   num.trees        = n_trees,   sample.fraction  = samp_fraction,   min.node.size    = min_node,   honesty          = TRUE,   honesty.fraction = 0.5,   tune.parameters  = "all",   # auto-tunes key hyperparameters   num.threads      = n_cores, # built-in OpenMP parallelism   seed             = 123 )  #  Summarize  summary(cf_sim) === Causal Forest Summary ===  Causal Forest -------------   Trees         : 200   Observations  : 2400   Covariates    : 20   Honesty       : TRUE (fraction = 0.50)   min.node.size : 5   mtry          : 20   alpha         : 0.050   OOB preds     : 2400 / 2400 obs covered   ATE (OOB est) : 1.5118  OOB Prediction Distribution:    Min. 1st Qu. 1L)) # Separate explain vs background sets  # Using the same set for both leaks info — split them. set.seed(42)   n_explain <- min(80L, nrow(X_train))   n_bg      <- min(50L, nrow(X_train))   if (nrow(X_train) > n_explain + n_bg) {     # Enough rows — keep explain and background non-overlapping     idx_explain <- sample(nrow(X_train), n_explain)     idx_bg      <- sample(setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X_train)), idx_explain), n_bg)   } else {     # Small dataset — allow overlap rather than crash     idx_explain <- sample(nrow(X_train), n_explain)     idx_bg      <- sample(nrow(X_train), n_bg)   }   X_explain <- as.data.frame(X_train[idx_explain, , drop = FALSE])   bg_X      <- as.data.frame(X_train[idx_bg,      , drop = FALSE]) # Compute SHAP ks <- explain_cate(     cf_model,     X            = X_explain,     bg_X         = bg_X,     use_permshap = TRUE,     verbose      = FALSE   ) # Reset workers plan(sequential) shp <- shapviz::shapviz(ks) shapviz::sv_importance(shp, kind = "beeswarm") if (exists("shp")) {   shapviz::sv_importance(shp, show_numbers = TRUE) } if (exists("shp") && exists("xvars")) {   shapviz::sv_dependence(shp, v = xvars, share_y = TRUE) } if (exists("shp")) {   shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = 1) +     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11))    shapviz::sv_force(shp, row_id = 1) } if (exists("shp") && "sex" %in% names(shp$X)) {   idx_female <- which(shp$X$sex == 2)   row_show   <- if (length(idx_female) > 0) idx_female[1] else 1   shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = row_show) +     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11)) } else if (exists("shp")) {   shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = 2) +     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11)) }

text: R package causaldata provides collection datasets causal inference. integrate {causaldata} {RCausalML} easily load datasets. tutorial, use abortion dataset, contains state-year observations gonorrhea rates among 15–19 year olds, binary indicator early repeal abortion prohibition. dataset commonly used study effects abortion legalization risky sexual behavior among teenagers, proxied gonorrhea rates. dataset commonly used study causal effects abortion legalization policies (specifically, early repeal abortion prohibitions certain U.S. states) risky sexual behavior among teenagers. Risky behavior proxied incidence gonorrhea (sexually transmitted infection) among 15–19 year olds. idea access abortion might influence sexual decision-making risk-taking behavior age group. important columns (based package documentation): fip — State FIPS code (numeric identifier U.S. state) age — Age years (focused 15–19 year olds) race — Race: 1 = white, 2 = black (similar coding) year — Calendar year t — rescaled time variable (often centered around policy change ) sex — Sex: 1 = male, 2 = female totpop — Total population (state-level) ir — Incarcerated males per 100,000 (proxy criminal justice environment) crack — Crack cocaine index (proxy drug epidemic intensity) alcohol — Alcohol consumption per capita income — Real income per capita ur — State unemployment rate poverty — Poverty rate repeal — Treatment indicator: 1 = state early repeal abortion prohibition (treatment group), 0 = otherwise (control group). main policy/treatment variable. pi — Parental involvement law effect (another policy control) bf15 — Indicator: black female 15–19 age group (useful subgroup analysis)

Causal Survival Forest extends causal forests handle time--event data — situations outcome just happened, happened, many subjects right-censored (event time never observed). Like parent method, CSF estimates Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE), \(\tau(X)\), survival timescale rather simple continuous outcome. CSFs particularly valuable medicine (drug extend survival, ?), economics (job training lead re-employment?), setting dropout, loss follow-, end--study cutoffs create incomplete outcome data. Defining treatment effect survival data requires choosing summary measure: Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST): \[\tau(X) = E[\min(T(1), h) - \min(T(0), h) \mid X = x]\] compares average survival time fixed horizon \(h\) treated control groups. Survival probability difference: \[\tau(X) = P[T(1) > h \mid X = x] - P[T(0) > h \mid X = x]\] compares probability surviving past time \(h\) treatment versus control. Right-censoring means observe \(Y = \min(T, C)\) event indicator \(D = \mathbf{1}(T \leq C)\), \(C\) censoring time. CSFs correct using Inverse Probability Censoring Weighting (IPCW), upweights observed events account censored. AIPW scores (Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting, Cui et al., 2023) provide doubly-robust pseudo-outcomes subject, combining direct outcome model propensity model. pseudo-outcomes forest actually splits , enabling unbiased CATE estimation even censoring. Honest estimation — safeguard standard causal forests — partitions data subsample used find splits strictly separate subsample used estimate effects within leaves. 1. Inputs — Covariates \(X\), observed time \(Y\), treatment \(W\), event indicator \(D\), time horizon \(h\). 2. Censoring correction — Estimate censoring probabilities \(\hat{P}(C > t \mid X)\) via survival forest, compute IPCW-corrected AIPW pseudo-outcomes \(\tilde{Y}_i\) individual. 3. Tree construction — Grow \(B\) trees random data/feature subsets. split maximizes heterogeneity pseudo-outcomes child nodes, isolating subgroups meaningfully different treatment effects. 4. Honest leaf estimation — held-subsample (\(S_2\)) estimates \(\tau(x)\) within leaf, preventing overfitting split-finding subsample (\(S_1\)). 5. Aggregation output — Average \(\tau(x)\) estimates across \(B\) trees. Final outputs: per-individual CATE \(\hat{\tau}(x)\), population ATE, confidence intervals, covariate importance.  key addition relative standard causal forest steps 2 3 — censoring correction pseudo-outcome construction. make CSF handle survival data correctly. Without IPCW, censored subjects introduce bias; without AIPW pseudo-outcomes, forest nothing meaningful split . choice \(\tau(X)\) definition (RMST vs. survival probability) made based scientific question: RMST gives time-scale interpretation (“drug adds X months survival patients like ”), survival probability difference directly interpretable clinically (“increases chance surviving 5 years X%”). honest estimation step 4 mirrors standard causal forests applied pseudo-outcomes step 3 — ensures data isn’t used carve covariate space measure effects within . Simulate n = 3000 observations with p = 8 features n <- 3000 p <- 8 X <- matrix(runif(n * p, min = -1, max = 1), n, p)   # Covariates W <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)                               # Binary treatment: 40% treatment group horizon <- 2                                         # Time horizon for RMST  # Generate failure and censoring times failure.time <- pmin(exp(X[, 2] + 0.5 * W + 0.25 * X[, 3]), horizon) censor.time <- 1.5 * runif(n) Y <- pmin(failure.time, censor.time)                 # what: Compute Kernel SHAP values for CATE using shapviz
code: library(kernelshap) library(shapviz) library(future)  #  Parallel backend  n_cores <- max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L) plan(multisession, workers = n_cores)  #  Scale sizes to data set.seed(42) n_total <- nrow(X)  if (n_total > 5000L) {   n_explain <- 400L   n_bg      <- 80L  } else if (n_total > 1000L) {   n_explain <- 250L   n_bg      <- 60L  } else {   n_explain <- min(150L, n_total)   n_bg      <- min(50L,  n_total) }  # Non-overlapping explain / background sets  if (n_total >= n_explain + n_bg) {   all_idx     <- sample(n_total)   explain_idx <- all_idx[seq_len(n_explain)]   bg_idx      <- all_idx[seq(n_explain + 1L, n_explain + n_bg)]  } else {   # Small dataset — overlap allowed   explain_idx <- sample(n_total, n_explain, replace = FALSE)   bg_idx      <- sample(n_total, n_bg,      replace = FALSE) }  X_explain <- X[explain_idx, , drop = FALSE] bg_small  <- X[bg_idx,      , drop = FALSE]  # Prediction wrapper  pred_tau <- function(object, newdata) {   predict(object, newdata = newdata)$predictions }  #  permshap instead of kernelshap (5–20x faster, same output)  shap_iv <- permshap(   object   = iv_forest,   X        = X_explain,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_tau,   verbose  = FALSE     # flip to TRUE to monitor progress )  # Reset workers  plan(sequential)

Load and modify the lung data data(lung, package = "survival") lung_data <- lung %>%   dplyr::filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(sex), !is.na(ph.ecog)) %>%   dplyr::mutate(     treatment = as.factor(sample(c("placebo", "A", "B"), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3))),     health_status = rbinom(n(), 1, prob = 0.3 + 0.1 * (treatment == "A") + 0.15 * (treatment == "B")),     log_time = log(time)   )  # Define covariates, treatment, and outcomes X <- lung_data %>% select(age, sex, ph.ecog) %>% as.matrix() W <- lung_data$treatment Y <- lung_data %>% select(log_time, health_status) %>% as.matrix() colnames(Y) <- c("log_time", "health_status")  # Split into training and test sets set.seed(123) n <- nrow(lung_data) train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n) test_idx <- setdiff(1:n, train_idx) X_train <- X[train_idx, ] X_test <- X[test_idx, ] W_train <- W[train_idx] W_test <- W[test_idx] Y_train <- Y[train_idx, ] Y_test <- Y[test_idx, ] macf_log_time <- multi_arm_causal_forest(X = X_train,                                          Y = Y_train[, "log_time"],                                           W = W_train) macf_health_status <- multi_arm_causal_forest(X = X_train,                                                Y = Y_train[, "health_status"],                                                W = W_train) # Predict treatment effects # Predict treatment effects on the test set tau_hat_log_time <- predict(macf_log_time, newdata = X_test) tau_hat_health_status <- predict(macf_health_status, newdata = X_test) # Calculate ATE for log_time ate_log_time <- average_treatment_effect(macf_log_time)  # Calculate ATE for health_status ate_health_status <- average_treatment_effect(macf_health_status)  # Display the results print("Average Treatment Effects for log_time:") [1] "Average Treatment Effects for log_time:" print(ate_log_time) estimate   std.err    contrast outcome B - A       0.2370108 0.2058838       B - A     Y.1 placebo - A 0.3267473 0.1976071 placebo - A     Y.1 print("Average Treatment Effects for health_status:") [1] "Average Treatment Effects for health_status:" print(ate_health_status) estimate   std.err    contrast outcome B - A        0.008270641 0.1062070       B - A     Y.1 placebo - A -0.144842545 0.1004455 placebo - A     Y.1 # Variable importance for log_time var_imp_log_time <- variable_importance(macf_log_time) var_imp_df_log_time <- data.frame(   Variable = colnames(X),   Importance = var_imp_log_time )  ggplot(var_imp_df_log_time, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance), y = Importance)) +   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +   coord_flip() +   labs(title = "Variable Importance for log_time", x = "Variable", y = "Importance") +   theme_minimal() # Variable importance for health_status var_imp_health_status <- variable_importance(macf_health_status) var_imp_df_health_status <- data.frame(   Variable = colnames(X),   Importance = var_imp_health_status )  ggplot(var_imp_df_health_status, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance), y = Importance)) +   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +   coord_flip() +   labs(title = "Variable Importance for health_status", x = "Variable", y = "Importance") +   theme_minimal() # Re-level so placebo is the reference (baseline) W_train <- relevel(as.factor(W_train), ref = "placebo") W_test  <- relevel(as.factor(W_test),  ref = "placebo")   # optional but consistent  # Refit both forests with the new baseline macf_log_time <- multi_arm_causal_forest(   X = X_train,   Y = Y_train[, "log_time"],   W = W_train )  macf_health_status <- multi_arm_causal_forest(   X = X_train,   Y = Y_train[, "health_status"],   W = W_train ) p <- predict(macf_log_time, newdata = head(X_test, 5)) print(colnames(p$predictions[, , 1])) [1] "A - placebo" "B - placebo" # Prediction wrapper for log_time outcome pred_A_vs_placebo_log <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "A - placebo", 1]          # extracts the scalar vector we need }  pred_B_vs_placebo_log <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "B - placebo", 1] }  # Same wrappers for health_status outcome pred_A_vs_placebo_health <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "A - placebo", 1] }  pred_B_vs_placebo_health <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "B - placebo", 1] } library(kernelshap) library(shapviz) library(future)  # ── log_time outcome ─────────────────────────────────────────────── shap_A_log <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_log_time,   X        = X_test,                    # or X[1:500, ] if you want faster   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_A_vs_placebo_log,   verbose  = FALSE )  shap_B_log <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_log_time,   X        = X_test,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_B_vs_placebo_log,   verbose  = FALSE )  # ── health_status outcome ────────────────────────────────────────── shap_A_health <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_health_status,   X        = X_test,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_A_vs_placebo_health,   verbose  = FALSE )  shap_B_health <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_health_status,   X        = X_test,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_B_vs_placebo_health,   verbose  = FALSE )  # what: Key Differences from Standard Causal Forest
text: Standard Causal Forest: Handles one treatment (binary continuous) one outcome, estimating single treatment effect per individual. Models multiple treatments (e.g., multiple drugs) /multiple outcomes (e.g., multiple health metrics). Shares information across arms/outcomes improve estimation efficiency. Uses joint objective function optimize splits treatments outcomes simultaneously.

Handles complex experiments multiple treatments outcomes. Captures heterogeneity treatment effects across subgroups. Robust non-linear relationships high-dimensional covariates. Improves efficiency sharing information across arms/outcomes.

Requires sufficient sample size treatment arm outcome. Assumes unconfoundedness (unmeasured confounders) unless combined methods (e.g., instrumental variables). Computationally intensive large datasets many outcomes. Interpretability can challenging due complex output (multiple effects per individual).

Load and modify the lung data data(lung, package = "survival") lung_data <- lung %>%   dplyr::filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(sex), !is.na(ph.ecog)) %>%   dplyr::mutate(     treatment = as.factor(sample(c("placebo", "A", "B"), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3))),     health_status = rbinom(n(), 1, prob = 0.3 + 0.1 * (treatment == "A") + 0.15 * (treatment == "B")),     log_time = log(time)   )  # Define covariates, treatment, and outcomes X <- lung_data %>% select(age, sex, ph.ecog) %>% as.matrix() W <- lung_data$treatment Y <- lung_data %>% select(log_time, health_status) %>% as.matrix() colnames(Y) <- c("log_time", "health_status")  # Split into training and test sets set.seed(123) n <- nrow(lung_data) train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n) test_idx <- setdiff(1:n, train_idx) X_train <- X[train_idx, ] X_test <- X[test_idx, ] W_train <- W[train_idx] W_test <- W[test_idx] Y_train <- Y[train_idx, ] Y_test <- Y[test_idx, ] macf_log_time <- multi_arm_causal_forest(X = X_train,                                          Y = Y_train[, "log_time"],                                           W = W_train) macf_health_status <- multi_arm_causal_forest(X = X_train,                                                Y = Y_train[, "health_status"],                                                W = W_train) # Predict treatment effects # Predict treatment effects on the test set tau_hat_log_time <- predict(macf_log_time, newdata = X_test) tau_hat_health_status <- predict(macf_health_status, newdata = X_test) # Calculate ATE for log_time ate_log_time <- average_treatment_effect(macf_log_time)  # Calculate ATE for health_status ate_health_status <- average_treatment_effect(macf_health_status)  # Display the results print("Average Treatment Effects for log_time:") [1] "Average Treatment Effects for log_time:" print(ate_log_time) estimate   std.err    contrast outcome B - A       0.2370108 0.2058838       B - A     Y.1 placebo - A 0.3267473 0.1976071 placebo - A     Y.1 print("Average Treatment Effects for health_status:") [1] "Average Treatment Effects for health_status:" print(ate_health_status) estimate   std.err    contrast outcome B - A        0.008270641 0.1062070       B - A     Y.1 placebo - A -0.144842545 0.1004455 placebo - A     Y.1 # Variable importance for log_time var_imp_log_time <- variable_importance(macf_log_time) var_imp_df_log_time <- data.frame(   Variable = colnames(X),   Importance = var_imp_log_time )  ggplot(var_imp_df_log_time, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance), y = Importance)) +   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +   coord_flip() +   labs(title = "Variable Importance for log_time", x = "Variable", y = "Importance") +   theme_minimal() # Variable importance for health_status var_imp_health_status <- variable_importance(macf_health_status) var_imp_df_health_status <- data.frame(   Variable = colnames(X),   Importance = var_imp_health_status )  ggplot(var_imp_df_health_status, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance), y = Importance)) +   geom_bar(stat = "identity") +   coord_flip() +   labs(title = "Variable Importance for health_status", x = "Variable", y = "Importance") +   theme_minimal() # Re-level so placebo is the reference (baseline) W_train <- relevel(as.factor(W_train), ref = "placebo") W_test  <- relevel(as.factor(W_test),  ref = "placebo")   # optional but consistent  # Refit both forests with the new baseline macf_log_time <- multi_arm_causal_forest(   X = X_train,   Y = Y_train[, "log_time"],   W = W_train )  macf_health_status <- multi_arm_causal_forest(   X = X_train,   Y = Y_train[, "health_status"],   W = W_train ) p <- predict(macf_log_time, newdata = head(X_test, 5)) print(colnames(p$predictions[, , 1])) [1] "A - placebo" "B - placebo" # Prediction wrapper for log_time outcome pred_A_vs_placebo_log <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "A - placebo", 1]          # extracts the scalar vector we need }  pred_B_vs_placebo_log <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "B - placebo", 1] }  # Same wrappers for health_status outcome pred_A_vs_placebo_health <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "A - placebo", 1] }  pred_B_vs_placebo_health <- function(object, newdata) {   p <- predict(object, newdata = newdata)   p$predictions[, "B - placebo", 1] } library(kernelshap) library(shapviz) library(future)  # ── log_time outcome ─────────────────────────────────────────────── shap_A_log <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_log_time,   X        = X_test,                    # or X[1:500, ] if you want faster   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_A_vs_placebo_log,   verbose  = FALSE )  shap_B_log <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_log_time,   X        = X_test,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_B_vs_placebo_log,   verbose  = FALSE )  # ── health_status outcome ────────────────────────────────────────── shap_A_health <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_health_status,   X        = X_test,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_A_vs_placebo_health,   verbose  = FALSE )  shap_B_health <- kernelshap(   object   = macf_health_status,   X        = X_test,   bg_X     = bg_small,   pred_fun = pred_B_vs_placebo_health,   verbose  = FALSE )  # For panel display  # Importance plots (beeswarm + bar) for each (treatment, outcome) plt1 <- sv_importance(shp_A_log,    kind = "both") + ggtitle("log_time: A vs placebo") plt2 <- sv_importance(shp_B_log,    kind = "both") + ggtitle("log_time: B vs placebo") plt3 <- sv_importance(shp_A_health, kind = "both") + ggtitle("health_status: A vs placebo") plt4 <- sv_importance(shp_B_health, kind = "both") + ggtitle("health_status: B vs placebo")  # Arrange plots in a 2x2 panel (plt1 | plt2) / (plt3 | plt4) # List available feature names for each SHAP object print("Available features in SHAP object (log_time):") [1] "Available features in SHAP object (log_time):" print(colnames(shp_A_log$X)) [1] "age"     "sex"     "ph.ecog" print("Available features in SHAP object (health_status):") [1] "Available features in SHAP object (health_status):" print(colnames(shp_A_health$X)) [1] "age"     "sex"     "ph.ecog" # Dependence plots for log_time outcome (A vs placebo) plt_A_log1 <- sv_dependence(shp_A_log, v = available_feats_log[1]) + ggtitle(paste("log_time (A):", available_feats_log[1])) plt_A_log2 <- sv_dependence(shp_A_log, v = available_feats_log[2]) + ggtitle(paste("log_time (A):", available_feats_log[2])) plt_A_log3 <- sv_dependence(shp_A_log, v = available_feats_log[3]) + ggtitle(paste("log_time (A):", available_feats_log[3]))  # Dependence plots for health_status outcome (A vs placebo) plt_A_health1 <- sv_dependence(shp_A_health, v = available_feats_health[1]) + ggtitle(paste("health_status (A):", available_feats_health[1])) plt_A_health2 <- sv_dependence(shp_A_health, v = available_feats_health[2]) + ggtitle(paste("health_status (A):", available_feats_health[2])) plt_A_health3 <- sv_dependence(shp_A_health, v = available_feats_health[3]) + ggtitle(paste("health_status (A):", available_feats_health[3]))  library(patchwork) # Display all dependence plots in a 2x3 grid (top: log_time, bottom: health_status) (plt_A_log1 | plt_A_log2 | plt_A_log3) / (plt_A_health1 | plt_A_health2 | plt_A_health3)

what: 1.6 The Boosted Model of Causal Inference (causalXGBoost)
text: C-XGBoost tree-boosting method estimating individual average treatment effects observational data. belongs outcome regression family causal inference methods — conceptual family TARNet DragonNet — replaces neural networks XGBoost. result model brings DragonNet-style causal masking boosted trees, combining counterfactual reasoning neural causal models XGBoost’s well-known strengths tabular data: robustness irregular boundaries, excellent calibration medium-sized datasets, minimal tuning overhead. core idea simple: train one XGBoost model two output heads simultaneously predict potential outcomes control (\(\hat{Q}_0(x)\)) treatment (\(\hat{Q}_1(x)\)). individual treatment effect falls difference. C-XGBoost operates within potential outcomes framework. unit \(\), two potential outcomes exist — \(Y_i(0)\) control \(Y_i(1)\) treatment — one observed: \[Y_i = T_i\, Y_i(1) + (1 - T_i)\, Y_i(0)\] quantities interest : \[\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \quad \text{(ITE — individual treatment effect)}\] \[\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x] \quad \text{(CATE — conditional average treatment effect)}\] \[\text{ATE} = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] \quad \text{(population average)}\] identifiable observational data \((X, T, Y)\) three standard assumptions: consistency (SUTVA — interference units), ignorability (unmeasured confounders: \((Y(0), Y(1)) \perp T \mid X\)), overlap (\(0 < e(x) < 1\), \(e(x) = P(T=1 \mid X=x)\)). fail — especially ignorability — estimates break . C-XGBoost learns two conditional expectation functions inside single model: \[\hat{Q}_0(x) \approx E[Y(0) \mid X = x], \qquad \hat{Q}_1(x) \approx E[Y(1) \mid X = x]\] ITE estimate : \[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{Q}_1(x) - \hat{Q}_0(x)\] heads share tree structure separate leaf values. key design choice: shared splits mean model learns common feature-space partitioning generalizes across heads, counterfactuals borrowed structurally similar units rather extrapolated blindly. training unit contributes gradient signal head matches observed treatment assignment: \[\mathcal{L}_i(\theta) = (1 - t_i)\bigl(\hat{Q}_0(x_i) - y_i\bigr)^2 + t_i\bigl(\hat{Q}_1(x_i) - y_i\bigr)^2\] vector form, implemented masked squared error: \[\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \| m_i \odot (\hat{q}(x_i) - \tilde{y}_i) \|_2^2, \qquad m_i = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - t_i \\ t_i \end{bmatrix}\] intuition: control units (\(t_i = 0\)) teach \(\hat{Q}_0\) head \(Y(0)\) looks like function \(X\); treated units (\(t_i = 1\)) teach \(\hat{Q}_1\) head \(Y(1)\) looks like. splits shared, information flows across heads — treated unit region \(\mathcal{R}\) covariate space indirectly informs \(\hat{Q}_0\) prediction control units region, vice versa. XGBoost builds two-output predictor additively \(M\) rounds: \[\hat{q}^{(M)}(x) = \sum_{m=1}^M f_m(x)\] \(f_m\) tree outputs two numbers per leaf — one head. round \(m\): Compute current predictions \(\hat{q}^{(m-1)}(x_i)\) units. Compute masked gradients Hessians — factual head gets non-zero curvature: \[g_{i0} = 2(1-t_i)(\hat{q}_{i0} - y_i), \quad g_{i1} = 2t_i(\hat{q}_{i1} - y_i)\] \[h_{i0} = 2(1-t_i), \quad h_{i1} = 2t_i\] Fit new tree \(f_m\) minimizes standard XGBoost second-order objective jointly across heads. Update predictions: \(\hat{q}^{(m)} = \hat{q}^{(m-1)} + \eta\, f_m(x)\), \(\eta\) learning rate. shared structure + separate leaf values lets model capture rich interactions still learning distinct counterfactual surfaces. C-XGBoost separately fits propensity model \(\hat{e}(x) = \widehat{P}(T=1 \mid X=x)\) — typically random forest. Importantly, propensity score integrated XGBoost training loss (unlike DragonNet), means model doubly robust: outcome model misspecified, propensity estimate provides correction. propensity returned purely downstream use — overlap diagnostics, inverse probability weighting, subgroup analysis. new unit \(x\), single forward pass returns \(\hat{Q}_0(x)\), \(\hat{Q}_1(x)\), \(\hat{e}(x)\), \(\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{Q}_1(x) - \hat{Q}_0(x)\). Two standard evaluation metrics apply: ATE error — absolute difference true estimated population average effect. PEHE (Precision Estimation Heterogeneous Effects) — mean squared error individual effects: \[\varepsilon_\text{PEHE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \bigl((Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)) - \hat{\tau}(x_i)\bigr)^2\] PEHE requires knowledge potential outcomes, can computed semi-synthetic benchmarks (e.g., IHDP, Jobs). real data, indirect evaluation (e.g., policy learning, subgroup validation) possible. doubly robust. Propensity estimated used training, model safety net outcome model misspecification. Binary outcome clipping. regression loss constrain outputs \([0, 1]\); post-hoc clipping calibration may needed. Classical assumptions required. Hidden confounding, SUTVA violations, lack overlap break identification. Two heads . current architecture supports binary treatment. Multi-arm extensions require additional heads revised masking scheme.  things worth emphasizing pipeline: Step 3 architectural heart. shared tree structure means splits chosen explain variation \(Y(0)\) \(Y(1)\) simultaneously. region covariate space treated control units interleaved push trees carve boundaries serve heads — effectively using treated units regularize counterfactual surface control units, vice versa. Step 4 (masked loss) makes causal rather predictive. standard multi-output XGBoost regression naively assign \(Y_i\) heads, corrupt counterfactual estimates. mask \(m_i = (1-t_i,\, t_i)\) ensures factual head receives gradient signal, keeping head honest actually observed. Step 6’s propensity caveat matters practically. \(\hat{e}(x)\) wired training objective, severe overlap violations — regions nearly units treated nearly control — degrade counterfactual head sparse group, propensity reweighting inside loss correct . Checking propensity score distribution trusting CATE estimates low-overlap regions essential. XGBoost excels nonlinearities, interactions, irregular boundaries (classic strengths tabular data). masking + shared splits give representational power neural causal models far better calibration robustness medium-sized tabular datasets. trainT <- T_syn[idx_train]; trainY <- Y_syn[idx_train] testX <- X_syn[-idx_train, ]; test_potential_Y <- potential_Y_syn[-idx_train, ] model <- CXGBoost$new(parameters = list(eta = 0.1, max_depth = 8)) model$fit(X, t, y, nrounds = 200, verbose = 0) # Optional: eval_data = list(X = X_val, t = t_val, y = y_val) for watchlist # Fit with same model configuration model_syn <- CXGBoost$new(parameters = list(                   max_depth = 5,                    eta = 1e-2,                    lambda = 5,                    alpha = 1.0,                    tree_method = "hist",                    nthread = -1 )) model_syn$fit(trainX, trainT, trainY, nrounds = 100L, verbose = 0L) # Predict (includes tau_hat = y1_hat - y0_hat) pred_syn <- model_syn$predict(testX) predicted_potential_outcomes_syn <- cbind(pred_syn$y0_hat, pred_syn$y1_hat) # Print model summary (config, fit time, propensity OOB, top variables) model_syn$summary() CXGBoost  Model Summary    Configuration    eta (learning rate)  : 0.0100   max_depth            : 5   subsample            : 0.80   colsample_bytree     : 0.80   lambda (L2)          : 5.00   alpha  (L1)          : 1.00   Boosting rounds      : two_boosters    Fit time             : 41.10 sec   Propensity Model    Ranger OOB error     : 0.2394   Ranger num.trees     : 200   Ranger max.depth     : 4   Top 10 Variables (XGBoost gain)    f0           0.5268     f1           0.4239     f4           0.0176     f3           0.0173     f2           0.0144 # Evaluate against ground truth: $evaluate() accepts matrix [Y(0), Y(1)] or ITE vector eval_syn <- model_syn$evaluate(y_true = test_potential_Y, X = testX) PEHE      : 0.569580   ATE error : 0.547519 true_ate <- mean(test_potential_Y[, 2] - test_potential_Y[, 1]) cat(sprintf("True ATE     : %.3f

C-XGBoost operates within potential outcomes framework. unit \(\), two potential outcomes exist — \(Y_i(0)\) control \(Y_i(1)\) treatment — one observed: \[Y_i = T_i\, Y_i(1) + (1 - T_i)\, Y_i(0)\] quantities interest : \[\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \quad \text{(ITE — individual treatment effect)}\] \[\tau(x) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x] \quad \text{(CATE — conditional average treatment effect)}\] \[\text{ATE} = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] \quad \text{(population average)}\] identifiable observational data \((X, T, Y)\) three standard assumptions: consistency (SUTVA — interference units), ignorability (unmeasured confounders: \((Y(0), Y(1)) \perp T \mid X\)), overlap (\(0 < e(x) < 1\), \(e(x) = P(T=1 \mid X=x)\)). fail — especially ignorability — estimates break . C-XGBoost learns two conditional expectation functions inside single model: \[\hat{Q}_0(x) \approx E[Y(0) \mid X = x], \qquad \hat{Q}_1(x) \approx E[Y(1) \mid X = x]\] ITE estimate : \[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{Q}_1(x) - \hat{Q}_0(x)\] heads share tree structure separate leaf values. key design choice: shared splits mean model learns common feature-space partitioning generalizes across heads, counterfactuals borrowed structurally similar units rather extrapolated blindly. training unit contributes gradient signal head matches observed treatment assignment: \[\mathcal{L}_i(\theta) = (1 - t_i)\bigl(\hat{Q}_0(x_i) - y_i\bigr)^2 + t_i\bigl(\hat{Q}_1(x_i) - y_i\bigr)^2\] vector form, implemented masked squared error: \[\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \| m_i \odot (\hat{q}(x_i) - \tilde{y}_i) \|_2^2, \qquad m_i = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - t_i \\ t_i \end{bmatrix}\] intuition: control units (\(t_i = 0\)) teach \(\hat{Q}_0\) head \(Y(0)\) looks like function \(X\); treated units (\(t_i = 1\)) teach \(\hat{Q}_1\) head \(Y(1)\) looks like. splits shared, information flows across heads — treated unit region \(\mathcal{R}\) covariate space indirectly informs \(\hat{Q}_0\) prediction control units region, vice versa. XGBoost builds two-output predictor additively \(M\) rounds: \[\hat{q}^{(M)}(x) = \sum_{m=1}^M f_m(x)\] \(f_m\) tree outputs two numbers per leaf — one head. round \(m\): Compute current predictions \(\hat{q}^{(m-1)}(x_i)\) units. Compute masked gradients Hessians — factual head gets non-zero curvature: \[g_{i0} = 2(1-t_i)(\hat{q}_{i0} - y_i), \quad g_{i1} = 2t_i(\hat{q}_{i1} - y_i)\] \[h_{i0} = 2(1-t_i), \quad h_{i1} = 2t_i\] Fit new tree \(f_m\) minimizes standard XGBoost second-order objective jointly across heads. Update predictions: \(\hat{q}^{(m)} = \hat{q}^{(m-1)} + \eta\, f_m(x)\), \(\eta\) learning rate. shared structure + separate leaf values lets model capture rich interactions still learning distinct counterfactual surfaces. what: Why It Works Well on Tabular Causal Data
text: XGBoost excels nonlinearities, interactions, irregular boundaries (classic strengths tabular data). masking + shared splits give representational power neural causal models far better calibration robustness medium-sized tabular datasets. Conceptually: “DragonNet-style causal masking, boosted trees instead neural nets.”

RCausalML package provides implementation C-XGBoost R via R6 class CXGBoost. create model CXGBoost$new(), optionally passing list XGBoost parameters (e.g. eta, max_depth) optional pre-fitted propensity_model (ranger). fit $fit(X, t, y, nrounds, verbose, eval_data) predict $predict(X), returns list y0_hat, y1_hat, tau_hat (ITE), propensity_score. package also provides: $summary() — formatted print model config, fit time, propensity OOB error, top variable importance. $evaluate(y_true, X) — computes PEHE ATE error ground-truth (matrix [Y(0), Y(1)] vector true ITEs) returns list PEHE, ATE_error, tau_hat, y0_hat, y1_hat. $plot_importance(top_n, metric) — ggplot2 variable importance chart (Gain, Cover, Frequency). $save_model(path) load_cxgboost(path) — save/load fitted models. $clone_reset() — return unfitted copy hyperparameters (e.g. cross-validation). package exports PEHE() ATE() two calling conventions: matrix form (y, y_hat) columns [Y(0), Y(1)], vector form (tau_true, tau_hat) ITEs.

what: Use Case: Causal XGBoost on the Abortion Dataset
text: R package causaldata provides collection datasets causal inference. integrate {causaldata} {RCausalML} easily load datasets. tutorial, use abortion dataset, contains state-year observations gonorrhea rates among 15–19 year olds, binary indicator early repeal abortion prohibition. dataset commonly used study effects abortion legalization risky sexual behavior among teenagers, proxied gonorrhea rates. dataset commonly used study causal effects abortion legalization policies (specifically, early repeal abortion prohibitions certain U.S. states) risky sexual behavior among teenagers. Risky behavior proxied incidence gonorrhea (sexually transmitted infection) among 15–19 year olds. idea access abortion might influence sexual decision-making risk-taking behavior age group. important columns (based package documentation): fip — State FIPS code (numeric identifier U.S. state) age — Age years (focused 15–19 year olds) race — Race: 1 = white, 2 = black (similar coding) year — Calendar year t — rescaled time variable (often centered around policy change ) sex — Sex: 1 = male, 2 = female totpop — Total population (state-level) ir — Incarcerated males per 100,000 (proxy criminal justice environment) crack — Crack cocaine index (proxy drug epidemic intensity) alcohol — Alcohol consumption per capita income — Real income per capita ur — State unemployment rate poverty — Poverty rate repeal — Treatment indicator: 1 = state early repeal abortion prohibition (treatment group), 0 = otherwise (control group). main policy/treatment variable. pi — Parental involvement law effect (another policy control) bf15 — Indicator: black female 15–19 age group (useful subgroup analysis) outcome variable typically lnr (logged gonorrhea rate per 100,000 population among 15–19 year olds), measures logged incidence gonorrhea proxy risky sexual behavior. ’ll split data 80% training 20% test sets using random sampling. CXGBoost R6 class fits two-head XGBoost outcome model (optional propensity model via ranger). Key arguments CXGBoost: parameters: List XGBoost hyperparameters (e.g. eta, max_depth, lambda, alpha, tree_method). Defaults include num_target = 2, multi_strategy = "multi_output_tree". $fit(X, t, y, nrounds, verbose, eval_data): X = covariate matrix (NAs median-imputed), t = binary treatment (0/1), y = observed outcome; nrounds = boosting rounds (default 100); optional eval_data watchlist verbose >= 1. $predict(X): Returns list y0_hat, y1_hat, tau_hat, propensity_score. $summary(), $evaluate(y_true, X), $plot_importance(), $save_model(path), load_cxgboost(path), $clone_reset(): see Implementation R section . Sample ATE training set (mean predicted CATE). predict() output includes tau_hat convenience. ATE average treatment effect logged gonorrhea rate (lnr) across training population—.e., much early repeal abortion prohibition associated change lnr.  C-XGBoost implement RATE/AUTOC; prioritization metrics use {grf} causal forest. summarize CATE heterogeneity test set sample ATE. ground-truth potential outcomes available (e.g. synthetic data), use $evaluate(y_true, X) (accepts matrix [Y(0), Y(1)] vector true ITEs) exported PEHE() ATE() (matrix form (y, y_hat) vector form (tau_true, tau_hat)). abortion dataset observational, observe potential outcomes [Y(0), Y(1)] unit; true PEHE ATE error computed. code illustrates placeholder case (NA) completeness. Use built-$plot_importance() method ggplot2 chart. can pass top_n metric ("Gain", "Cover", "Frequency"). model uses multi-output tree (num_target = 2); importance shared tree structure (Y(1) booster two-booster fallback mode).  use {shapviz} package SHAP analysis. package integrated {RCausalML} via explain_cate(): compute SHAP values {kernelshap} ({permshap}), pass result shapviz() importance, dependence, waterfall, force plots. SHAP values computed causal forest’s CATE predictions using explain_cate(), visualized {shapviz}. subsample training data used speed.   Dependence SHAP values covariate (patchwork object).  Waterfall force plots show feature contributes predicted CATE one observation.   can show waterfall plots subset observations (e.g., covariate). show one observation sex == 2 (female) example; bar importance plot summarizes average |SHAP| across explained rows.  C-XGBoost fits separate propensity model (ranger) returns propensity scores predictions. used XGBoost loss useful diagnostics weighting.

Define default only if not provided   if (is.null(pred_fun)) {     pred_fun <- function(m, x) rcausalml_predict_numeric(m, as.data.frame(x))   }    if (use_permshap) {     ks <- kernelshap::permshap(object, X = X, pred_fun = pred_fun, bg_X = bg_X, ...)   } else {     ks <- kernelshap::kernelshap(object, X = X, pred_fun = pred_fun, bg_X = bg_X, ...)   }   ks } # Subsample for speed (kernelshap can be slow on large data)   set.seed(42)   n_explain <- min(80, nrow(X_train))   X_explain <- as.data.frame(X_train[sample(nrow(X_train), n_explain), ])   xvars     <- colnames(X_explain)    # To avoid the "pred_fun matched by multiple actual arguments" error,   # do NOT set 'pred_fun' directly in explain_cate() when use_permshap = TRUE.    # For kernelshap (the default), passing pred_fun is acceptable: ks <- explain_cate(   cx_model,   X_explain,   bg_X = X_explain,   use_permshap = FALSE,   verbose = FALSE,   #
