what: Multi-arm uplift: T-learner forests per treatment
text: uplift_rf_multi() fits one uplift_rf_kl() object per non-control arm (control vs treatment_k). continuous outcome, T-learner ranger ensemble, KL uplift tree forest.
code: set.seed(111) idx_test <- sample(nrow(df), size = round(0.2 * nrow(df))) df_train <- df[-idx_test, ] df_test <- df[idx_test, ]

what: Shallow T-learner per arm (analogous to “one tree” depth cap)
text: regression, “n_trees = 1” means one tree ranger model (treated control) arm—useful fast sanity check, production accuracy. control treatment* columns predicted mean outcomes \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\) \(\hat{\mu}_k(x)\) arm’s training subsample (stacked control-vs-\(k\)), probabilities.
code: clf_shallow <- uplift_rf_multi(   as.matrix(df_train[, x_names]),   df_train$treatment_group_key,   df_train$outcome,   control_name = "control",   n_trees = 1,   min_node_size = 100,   max_depth = 4 ) X_test <- as.matrix(df_test[, x_names]) p_shallow <- predict(clf_shallow, X_test, full_output = TRUE) df_res_shallow <- p_shallow[, c("control", clf_shallow$treatment_names), drop = FALSE] head(df_res_shallow, 5)

what: Full multi-arm model (more trees per T-learner)
text: Predicted uplift matrix (columns = treatment arms, entries = \(\hat{\mu}_k(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\) arm’s model):
code: uplift_model <- uplift_rf_multi(   as.matrix(df_train[, x_names]),   df_train$treatment_group_key,   df_train$outcome,   control_name = "control",   n_trees = 50,   min_node_size = 50,   max_depth = 8 ) df_res <- predict(uplift_model, X_test, full_output = TRUE) cat("Shape:", nrow(df_res), "x", ncol(df_res), "\n") Shape: 800 x 9 head(df_res) y_pred <- predict(uplift_model, X_test) result <- as.data.frame(y_pred) names(result) <- uplift_model$treatment_names head(result)

text: classification notebook, build synthetic subpopulation (units assigned model’s best arm control), plot cumulative gain using observed mean outcome contrasts sorted predicted uplift.
code: uplift_cols <- uplift_model$treatment_names best_treatment <- ifelse(   apply(result[uplift_cols], 1, function(r) all(r < 0)),   "control",   uplift_cols[apply(result[uplift_cols], 1, which.max)] ) actual_is_best <- as.integer(df_test$treatment_group_key == best_treatment) actual_is_control <- as.integer(df_test$treatment_group_key == "control") synthetic <- (actual_is_best == 1) | (actual_is_control == 1) synth <- result[synthetic, , drop = FALSE] auuc_metrics <- synth auuc_metrics$is_treated <- 1 - actual_is_control[synthetic] auuc_metrics$outcome <- df_test$outcome[synthetic] auuc_metrics$uplift_model <- apply(synth, 1, max) auuc_metrics <- auuc_metrics[, c("is_treated", "outcome", "uplift_model")] head(auuc_metrics) plot_gain(auuc_metrics, outcome_col = "outcome", treatment_col = "is_treated")

text: explain \(\hat{\tau}(X)\) binary T-learner uplift_bin_rf subset training data (full training rows can slow).
code: set.seed(2026)  n_explain <- min(100L, nrow(X_train)) bg_size <- min(100L, nrow(X_train)) X_explain <- X_train[seq_len(n_explain), , drop = FALSE] bg_idx <- sample.int(nrow(X_train), bg_size) bg_X <- X_train[bg_idx, , drop = FALSE]  pred_fun <- function(object, newdata) {   as.vector(predict(object, newdata)) }  library(future) plan(multisession, workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1)  shap_ksh <- kernelshap(   object = uplift_bin_rf,   X = X_explain,   bg_X = bg_X,   pred_fun = pred_fun,   bg_w = NULL,   verbose = FALSE ) plan(sequential)  # reset after  shp_uplift <- shapviz(shap_ksh, X = X_explain) sv_importance(shp_uplift, kind = "beeswarm") sv_importance(shp_uplift, show_numbers = TRUE) important_vars <- x_names[seq_len(min(4L, length(x_names)))] sv_dependence(shp_uplift, v = important_vars, share_y = TRUE) if (length(x_names) >= 2) {   sv_dependence(shp_uplift, v = x_names[[2]], color_var = x_names[[1]]) } preds_explain <- pred_fun(uplift_bin_rf, X_explain) row_id_max <- which.max(preds_explain)  sv_waterfall(shp_uplift, row_id = row_id_max) +   ggplot2::ggtitle("SHAP waterfall — highest estimated CATE in explain set") sv_force(shp_uplift, row_id = row_id_max) n_te <- min(10L, nrow(X_test)) shap_test <- kernelshap(   uplift_bin_rf,   X = X_test[seq_len(n_te), , drop = FALSE],   bg_X = bg_X,   pred_fun = pred_fun,   verbose = FALSE )  shp_test <- shapviz(shap_test, X = X_test[seq_len(n_te), , drop = FALSE]) sv_importance(shp_test, kind = "beeswarm")

text: standard predictive model asks: “outcome expect unit?” uplift model asks different question: “much outcome change treatment unit, given covariates?” quantity Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE). unit covariates \(X = x\) continuous outcome \(Y\): \[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 1, X = x] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 0, X = x]\] \(T = 1\) treated \(T = 0\) control. Heterogeneity means \(\tau(x)\) varies \(x\): subgroups benefit strongly, others barely, may harmed. binary outcomes (e.g. conversion yes/), CATE : \[\tau(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid T = 1, X = x) - P(Y = 1 \mid T = 0, X = x)\]

text: workhorse continuous outcomes RCausalML. Choose forest style via evaluation_function: "TLearner" (default): two ranger forests, one per arm; CATE = difference predicted means. "": bagged interaction-tree forests; CATE = averaged leaf contrasts across trees. "CIT": causal inference tree variant (single tree forest). full_output = TRUE argument returns control arm prediction, treatment arm prediction, CATE (delta) unit — useful auditing downstream analysis. Model summaries: cumulative gain curve plots, move units descending order predicted CATE, much actual treatment benefit capture relative random assignment. curve bowing diagonal indicates useful uplift ranking.  Fitting full dataset gives picture heterogeneous treatment effect across observed covariate profiles.  T-Learner forest, can extract ranger variable importance arm separately average get global covariate ranking. code: set.seed(2026)  n_explain <- min(100L, nrow(X_train)) bg_size   <- min(100L, nrow(X_train)) X_explain <- X_train[seq_len(n_explain), , drop = FALSE] bg_idx    <- sample.int(nrow(X_train), bg_size) bg_X      <- X_train[bg_idx, , drop = FALSE]  pred_fun <- function(object, newdata) as.vector(predict(object, newdata))  library(future) plan(multisession, workers = max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))  shap_ksh <- kernelshap(   object   = uplift_model,   X        = X_explain,   bg_X     = bg_X,   pred_fun = pred_fun,   bg_w     = NULL,   verbose  = FALSE ) plan(sequential)  shp_uplift <- shapviz(shap_ksh, X = X_explain) sv_importance(shp_uplift, kind = "beeswarm")  # Distribution of SHAP by feature sv_importance(shp_uplift, show_numbers = TRUE) # Bar chart with mean |SHAP| important_vars <- x_names[seq_len(min(4L, length(x_names)))] sv_dependence(shp_uplift, v = important_vars, share_y = TRUE) if (length(x_names) >= 2) {   sv_dependence(shp_uplift, v = x_names[[2]], color_var = x_names[[1]]) } preds_explain <- pred_fun(uplift_model, X_explain) row_id_max    <- which.max(preds_explain)  sv_waterfall(shp_uplift, row_id = row_id_max) +   ggplot2::ggtitle("SHAP waterfall — unit with highest estimated CATE") sv_force(shp_uplift, row_id = row_id_max) n_te <- min(10L, nrow(X_test)) shap_test <- kernelshap(   uplift_model,   X        = X_test[seq_len(n_te), , drop = FALSE],   bg_X     = bg_X,   pred_fun = pred_fun,   verbose  = FALSE ) shp_test <- shapviz(shap_test, X = X_test[seq_len(n_te), , drop = FALSE]) sv_importance(shp_test, kind = "beeswarm")

tutorial applies uplift XGBoost regression RCausalML abortion dataset causaldata. dataset features continuous outcome (logged gonorrhea rate, lnr) binary treatment (early repeal abortion prohibition, repeal). cover: conceptual foundations T-learner uplift gradient boosting Data preparation feature selection Fitting uplift models uplift_xgboostRegressor() Comparing uplift XGBoost uplift_randomForestRegressor() (T-learner forests) Evaluating uplift ranking via gain curves AUUC Interpreting heterogeneity predicted CATE kernel SHAP Prerequisite: install optional xgboost package (install.packages("xgboost")). random-forest uplift workflow data, see 03-03-uplift-randomForest-r.qmd. standard predictive model asks: “outcome expect unit?” uplift model asks different question: “much outcome change treatment unit, given covariates?” quantity Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE). unit covariates \(X = x\) continuous outcome \(Y\): \[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 1, X = x] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 0, X = x]\] \(T = 1\) treated \(T = 0\) control. Heterogeneity means \(\tau(x)\) varies \(x\): subgroups benefit strongly, others barely, may harmed. binary outcomes (e.g. conversion yes/), CATE : \[\tau(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid T = 1, X = x) - P(Y = 1 \mid T = 0, X = x)\] uplift_xgboost() implements T-learner XGBoost base learner: Fit one boosted tree ensemble control units (\(T = 0\)) estimate \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\). Fit separate ensemble treated units (\(T = 1\)) estimate \(\hat{\mu}_1(x)\). Predict CATE difference: \[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\] Compared uplift random forests (bagged uplift trees treatment-aware splits), uplift XGBoost: Aspect | Uplift random forest | Uplift XGBoost | |||***| | Base learner | Bagged uplift / ranger trees | Gradient-boosted trees (xgboost) | | Splitting rule | KL / ED / / T-learner ranger | T-learner | | Strengths | Interpretable tree ensembles; /CIT forests | Flexible nonlinear surfaces; strong predictive performance | | RCausalML API | uplift_randomForestRegressor() | uplift_xgboostRegressor() | model output \(\hat{\tau}(x)\) scale \(Y\). notebook, \(Y\) lnr (log gonorrhea rate per 100,000), CATE \(-0.12\) means model estimates early repeal associated 0.12 log-point lower gonorrhea rate covariate profile — raw rate drops 12%. average treatment effect (ATE) summarises treatment one number. uplift model estimates full profile \(\tau(x)\), enabling: CATE region | Interpretation | Targeting decision | |||*| | High positive \(\tau(x)\) | Large expected benefit treatment | Priority targets | | Near zero | Treatment adds little | Skip / low priority | | Negative** \(\tau(x)\) | Treatment may worsen outcomes | Actively avoid treating | Standard outcome prediction ranks high-baseline units highly even treatment adds nothing. text: standard predictive model asks: “outcome expect unit?” uplift model asks different question: “much outcome change treatment unit, given covariates?” quantity Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE). unit covariates \(X = x\) continuous outcome \(Y\): \[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 1, X = x] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 0, X = x]\] \(T = 1\) treated \(T = 0\) control. Heterogeneity means \(\tau(x)\) varies \(x\): subgroups benefit strongly, others barely, may harmed. binary outcomes (e.g. conversion yes/), CATE : \[\tau(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid T = 1, X = x) - P(Y = 1 \mid T = 0, X = x)\]

uplift_xgboost() implements T-learner XGBoost base learner: Fit one boosted tree ensemble control units (\(T = 0\)) estimate \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\). Fit separate ensemble treated units (\(T = 1\)) estimate \(\hat{\mu}_1(x)\). Predict CATE difference: \[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\] Compared uplift random forests (bagged uplift trees treatment-aware splits), uplift XGBoost: Aspect | Uplift random forest | Uplift XGBoost | |||***| | Base learner | Bagged uplift / ranger trees | Gradient-boosted trees (xgboost) | | Splitting rule | KL / ED / / T-learner ranger | T-learner | | Strengths | Interpretable tree ensembles; /CIT forests | Flexible nonlinear surfaces; strong predictive performance | | RCausalML API | uplift_randomForestRegressor() | uplift_xgboostRegressor() | model output \(\hat{\tau}(x)\) scale \(Y\). notebook, \(Y\) lnr (log gonorrhea rate per 100,000), CATE \(-0.12\) means model estimates early repeal associated 0.12 log-point lower gonorrhea rate covariate profile — raw rate drops 12%. average treatment effect (ATE) summarises treatment one number. uplift model estimates full profile \(\tau(x)\), enabling: CATE region | Interpretation | Targeting decision | |||*| | High positive \(\tau(x)\) | Large expected benefit treatment | Priority targets | | Near zero | Treatment adds little | Skip / low priority | | Negative** \(\tau(x)\) | Treatment may worsen outcomes | Actively avoid treating | Standard outcome prediction ranks high-baseline units highly even treatment adds nothing. parts notebook use partially linear regression (PLR) model, separates linear treatment effect \(\theta_0\) nonparametric confounding functions \(g_0\) \(m_0\): \[Y = D\,\theta_0 + g_0(X) + \zeta, \quad \mathbb{E}(\zeta \mid D, X) = 0\] \[D = m_0(X) + V, \quad \mathbb{E}(V \mid X) = 0\]

Throughout notebook use doubleml_plr() RCausalML (R/DMLearner.R), thin wrapper around DoubleML’s DoubleMLPLR. accepts covariate matrix X, treatment vector d, outcome vector y, forwards score, n_folds, apply_cross_fitting directly underlying PLR implementation. Data simulation 401(k) dataset loaded DoubleML package (make_plr_CCDDHNR2018, fetch_401k); mlr3 learners used unchanged.

what: Part A: Diagnosing Bias with Synthetic Data
text: Part uses Monte Carlo simulation make bias problems visible. run 100 replications partially linear model Chernozhukov et al. (2018) compare distribution rescaled estimator \((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0) / \hat{\text{se}}\) \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) three approaches. valid estimator produces histogram matches standard normal; deviations expose regularization overfitting bias. data-generating process : \[y_i = \theta_0\, d_i + g_0(x_i) + \zeta_i, \quad \zeta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\] \[d_i = m_0(x_i) + v_i, \quad v_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\] Covariates \(x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)\) \(\Sigma_{kj} = 0.7^{|j-k|}\). true causal parameter \(\theta_0 = 0.5\). Nuisance functions: \[m_0(x_i) = x_{,1} + \frac{1}{4}\frac{\exp(x_{,3})}{1 + \exp(x_{,3})}\] \[g_0(x_i) = \frac{\exp(x_{,1})}{1 + \exp(x_{,1})} + \frac{1}{4}x_{,3}\] true causal parameter \(\theta_0 = 0.5\). replication draws \(n = 500\) observations \(p = 5\) covariates. helper extracts covariate matrix PLR data frame dropping outcome y treatment d columns.
code: plr_x_matrix <- function(df) {    as.matrix(df[, setdiff(names(df), c("y", "d")), drop = FALSE])  } set.seed(1234)  n_rep  <- 100   # replications (set to 1000 for full replication) n_obs  <- 500 n_vars <- 5 alpha  <- 0.5   # true theta_0  data_sim <- vector("list", n_rep) for (i_rep in seq_len(n_rep)) {   data_sim[[i_rep]] <- make_plr_CCDDHNR2018(     alpha       = alpha,     n_obs       = n_obs,     dim_x       = n_vars,     return_type = "data.frame"   ) }  head(data_sim[[1]])

what: Part B: Real-World Application — 401(k) Eligibility and Net Financial Assets
text: Part B applies DML 401(k) dataset (Chernozhukov et al., 2020) estimate average causal effect employer-sponsored 401(k) eligibility (e401) net total financial assets (net_tfa), controlling age, income, education, family structure, background variables. workflow four stages: (1) 80/20 stratified train–test split; (2) causal estimation via doubleml_plr() training fold; (3) --sample validation nuisance models held-test fold; (4) SHAP interpretation treatment effect heterogeneity using LinearDML explain_cate(). Note formal PLR inference (summary, confint) applies training sample doubleml_plr() fit; test fold used exclusively predictive sanity-checking nuisance regressions.

what: B.1 Load and Inspect the 401(k) Data
code: df_401k <- fetch_401k(return_type = "data.frame", instrument = FALSE)  # Variables: #   net_tfa : net total financial assets (outcome Y) #   e401    : = 1 if employer offers 401(k) (treatment D) #   age, inc, fsize, educ, db, marr, twoearn, pira, hown : covariates (X)  cat("Dimensions:", nrow(df_401k), "x", ncol(df_401k), "\n") Dimensions: 9915 x 11 head(df_401k)

what: B.2 Outcome, Treatment, Covariates, and Train–Test Split
text: split stratified e401 (80% train / 20% test) folds retain similar treatment prevalence. Stratification prevents imbalance artificially improve degrade nuisance model performance test fold.
code: x_cols_401k <- c("age", "inc", "fsize", "educ", "db", "marr", "twoearn", "pira", "hown") X_401k      <- as.matrix(df_401k[, x_cols_401k, drop = FALSE]) y_401k      <- df_401k$net_tfa t_401k      <- df_401k$e401  set.seed(3141) train_frac <- 0.8 i1 <- which(t_401k == 1L) i0 <- which(t_401k == 0L) n1_tr <- max(1L, floor(train_frac * length(i1))) n0_tr <- max(1L, floor(train_frac * length(i0))) train_idx <- c(sample(i1, n1_tr), sample(i0, n0_tr)) test_idx  <- setdiff(seq_along(t_401k), train_idx)  X_tr <- X_401k[train_idx, , drop = FALSE] X_te <- X_401k[test_idx, , drop = FALSE] y_tr <- y_401k[train_idx] y_te <- y_401k[test_idx] t_tr <- t_401k[train_idx] t_te <- t_401k[test_idx]  cat(   "Train n =", length(train_idx), "| Test n =", length(test_idx),   "| mean(e401) train =", round(mean(t_tr), 3),   "test =", round(mean(t_te), 3), "\n" ) Train n = 7931 | Test n = 1984 | mean(e401) train = 0.371 test = 0.371

text: nuisance models use random forest via ranger (500 trees, max depth 5, min node size 2). Random forests well-suited : 401(k) dataset moderate-dimensional likely non-linear covariate effects, ranger fast enough 5-fold cross-fitting sample size.
code: learner_rf <- lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 500, max.depth = 5, min.node.size = 2) ml_l_401k  <- learner_rf$clone() ml_m_401k  <- learner_rf$clone()

text: LinearDML, SparseLinearDML, CausalForestDML variants within DML framework heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE) — meaning treatment effect \(\theta(X)\) allowed vary across individuals based covariates \(X\), rather single constant \(\theta0\). shared backbone : residualize \(Y\) \(D\) using ML nuisance models, estimate treatment effect residuals. differs final stage models \(\theta(X)\). underlying model : \[Y = \theta(X) \cdot D + g0(X) + \varepsilon\] partialling nuisances: \[\tilde{Y} = Y - \hat{\ell}(X), \qquad \tilde{D} = D - \hat{m}(X)\] residualized relationship becomes: \[\tilde{Y} = \theta(X) \cdot \tilde{D} + \text{noise}\] three estimators differ model \(\theta(X)\) final stage. Assumption: \(\theta(X)\) linear function effect modifiers \(Z \subseteq X\): \[\theta(X) = \beta0 + \beta1 Z1 + \beta2 Z2 + \cdots\] Final stage: OLS regression \(\tilde{Y}\) \(\tilde{D} \cdot Z\) (residualized treatment interacted effect modifiers). use: • small moderate number effect modifiers • want interpretable coefficients modifier • can defend linear specification heterogeneity • need fast, standard-error-ready inference \(\betak\) Strengths: Fast, interpretable, standard asymptotic confidence intervals. Limitation: Misspecified true \(\theta(X)\) nonlinear \(Z\). Assumption: \(\theta(X)\) still linear effect modifiers, modifier space high-dimensional — many candidate interactions, zero: \[\theta(X) = Z^\top \beta, \quad \text{} \beta \text{ sparse}\] Final stage: Lasso (another penalized regression) \(\tilde{Y}\) \(\tilde{D} \cdot Z\), followed post-selection inference (typically via desparsified/debiased Lasso) recover valid confidence intervals. use: • many potential effect modifiers (e.g., dozens hundreds) • believe truly drive heterogeneity • still want coefficient-level inference selection Strengths: Handles high-dimensional \(Z\); automatic variable selection; valid inference via debiasing. Limitation: Still assumes linearity \(Z\); debiased Lasso inference machinery adds complexity. Assumption: \(\theta(X)\) arbitrary nonparametric function \(X\) — linearity assumed. Final stage: Fits causal forest (Wager & Athey, 2018) residuals \((\tilde{Y}, \tilde{D})\), producing separate local estimate \(\hat{\theta}(x)\) point \(x\). causal forest grows trees explicitly optimize treatment effect heterogeneity rather prediction accuracy, using criterion based : \[\hat{\theta}(x) = \arg\min\theta \sum{\\text{leaf}(x)} \left(\tilde{Y}- \theta \cdot \tilde{D}\right)^2\] use: • expect complex, nonlinear, non-additive heterogeneity • want individual-level subgroup treatment effect estimates • enough data forest reliable • want variable importance rankings effect modifiers Strengths: Fully nonparametric; honest inference via subsampling-based confidence intervals; produces \(\hat{\theta}(xi)\) unit. Limitation: Requires grf package; computationally heavier; less interpretable coefficient table; needs data reliable. three share first stage (ML nuisance estimation cross-fitting), inherit DML’s valid inference properties — difference entirely flexibly interpretably second stage captures treatment effect variation.

what: The Shared Setup: Partial Linear Model with Heterogeneity
text: underlying model : \[Y = \theta(X) \cdot D + g0(X) + \varepsilon\] partialling nuisances: \[\tilde{Y} = Y - \hat{\ell}(X), \qquad \tilde{D} = D - \hat{m}(X)\] residualized relationship becomes: \[\tilde{Y} = \theta(X) \cdot \tilde{D} + \text{noise}\] three estimators differ model \(\theta(X)\) final stage.

Assumption: \(\theta(X)\) linear function effect modifiers \(Z \subseteq X\): \[\theta(X) = \beta0 + \beta1 Z1 + \beta2 Z2 + \cdots\] Final stage: OLS regression \(\tilde{Y}\) \(\tilde{D} \cdot Z\) (residualized treatment interacted effect modifiers). use: • small moderate number effect modifiers • want interpretable coefficients modifier • can defend linear specification heterogeneity • need fast, standard-error-ready inference \(\betak\) Strengths: Fast, interpretable, standard asymptotic confidence intervals. Limitation: Misspecified true \(\theta(X)\) nonlinear \(Z\).

Assumption: \(\theta(X)\) still linear effect modifiers, modifier space high-dimensional — many candidate interactions, zero: \[\theta(X) = Z^\top \beta, \quad \text{} \beta \text{ sparse}\] Final stage: Lasso (another penalized regression) \(\tilde{Y}\) \(\tilde{D} \cdot Z\), followed post-selection inference (typically via desparsified/debiased Lasso) recover valid confidence intervals. use: • many potential effect modifiers (e.g., dozens hundreds) • believe truly drive heterogeneity • still want coefficient-level inference selection Strengths: Handles high-dimensional \(Z\); automatic variable selection; valid inference via debiasing. Limitation: Still assumes linearity \(Z\); debiased Lasso inference machinery adds complexity.

Assumption: \(\theta(X)\) arbitrary nonparametric function \(X\) — linearity assumed. Final stage: Fits causal forest (Wager & Athey, 2018) residuals \((\tilde{Y}, \tilde{D})\), producing separate local estimate \(\hat{\theta}(x)\) point \(x\). causal forest grows trees explicitly optimize treatment effect heterogeneity rather prediction accuracy, using criterion based : \[\hat{\theta}(x) = \arg\min\theta \sum{\\text{leaf}(x)} \left(\tilde{Y}- \theta \cdot \tilde{D}\right)^2\] use: • expect complex, nonlinear, non-additive heterogeneity • want individual-level subgroup treatment effect estimates • enough data forest reliable • want variable importance rankings effect modifiers Strengths: Fully nonparametric; honest inference via subsampling-based confidence intervals; produces \(\hat{\theta}(xi)\) unit. Limitation: Requires grf package; computationally heavier; less interpretable coefficient table; needs data reliable.
three share first stage (ML nuisance estimation cross-fitting), inherit DML’s valid inference properties — difference entirely flexibly interpretably second stage captures treatment effect variation.

what: 1. Single Continuous Treatment (Synthetic) and Model Selection
text: use DGP Chernozhukov et al.: \[T = \langle W, \beta\rangle + \eta\] \[Y = T\cdot \theta(X) + \langle W, \gamma\rangle + \epsilon\] \(\theta(x) = \exp(2\cdot x_1)\). Confounders \(W\) effect modifier \(X\) independent. R DMLearner expects treatment include control value (0); binarize median: \[T_{\text{bin}} = (T > \text{median}(T))\] compare LinearDML (default), SparseLinearDML polynomial features (degree 3), SparseLinearDML degree-10 polynomial + Lasso, CausalForestDML. Figure 1: Estimated vs true treatment effect (single continuous treatment) use mean squared error (MSE) predicted CATE vs true CATE test grid proxy model quality. (EconML’s score() R DMLearner; use instead.)
code: exp_te <- function(x) exp(2 * x[1]) epsilon_sample <- function(n) runif(n, -1, 1) eta_sample <- function(n) runif(n, -1, 1) n <- 2000 n_w <- 30 support_size <- 5 n_x <- 1  support_Y <- sample(seq_len(n_w), size = support_size, replace = FALSE) coefs_Y <- runif(support_size, 0, 1) support_T <- support_Y coefs_T <- runif(support_size, 0, 1)  W <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_w), n, n_w) X <- matrix(runif(n * n_x), n, n_x) TE <- apply(X, 1, exp_te) T_vec <- as.numeric(W[, support_T] %*% coefs_T + eta_sample(n)) Y <- TE * T_vec + as.numeric(W[, support_Y] %*% coefs_Y) + epsilon_sample(n)  # R DMLearner expects treatment to include control_name (0). Binarize at median. T_bin <- as.integer(T_vec > median(T_vec))  # Train/validation split idx <- sample.int(n, size = round(0.2 * n)) idx_val <- idx idx_train <- setdiff(seq_len(n), idx_val) Y_train <- Y[idx_train] Y_val <- Y[idx_val] T_train <- T_bin[idx_train] T_val <- T_bin[idx_val] X_train <- X[idx_train, , drop = FALSE] X_val <- X[idx_val, , drop = FALSE] W_train <- W[idx_train, , drop = FALSE] W_val <- W[idx_val, , drop = FALSE]  # Full covariate for first stage (X and W). DMLearner uses single X matrix. X_all_train <- cbind(X_train, W_train) X_all_val <- cbind(X_val, W_val) colnames(X_all_train) <- paste0("V", seq_len(ncol(X_all_train))) colnames(X_all_val) <- colnames(X_all_train)  # Test grid (effect modifier only); for prediction we pair with mean W X_test <- matrix(seq(0, 1, by = 0.01), ncol = 1) W_rep <- matrix(colMeans(W_train), nrow = nrow(X_test), ncol = ncol(W_train), byrow = TRUE) X_all_test <- cbind(X_test, W_rep) colnames(X_all_test) <- colnames(X_all_train) est <- LinearDML(model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", n_fold = 5L, seed = 123L) est <- fit(est, X_all_train, T_train, Y_train) te_pred <- predict(est, X_all_test) # Polynomial degree 3 on effect modifier; confounders W as-is X_poly3_train <- cbind(poly(X_train[, 1], degree = 3, raw = TRUE), W_train) X_poly3_val <- cbind(poly(X_val[, 1], degree = 3, raw = TRUE), W_val) X_poly3_test <- cbind(poly(X_test[, 1], degree = 3, raw = TRUE), W_rep) colnames(X_poly3_train) <- paste0("V", seq_len(ncol(X_poly3_train))) colnames(X_poly3_val) <- colnames(X_poly3_train) colnames(X_poly3_test) <- colnames(X_poly3_train)  est1 <- SparseLinearDML(model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", alpha = 0.01, n_fold = 5L, seed = 123L) est1 <- fit(est1, X_poly3_train, T_train, Y_train) te_pred1 <- predict(est1, X_poly3_test) # Polynomial degree 10 + Lasso final stage X_poly10_train <- cbind(poly(X_train[, 1], degree = 10, raw = TRUE), W_train) X_poly10_val <- cbind(poly(X_val[, 1], degree = 10, raw = TRUE), W_val) X_poly10_test <- cbind(poly(X_test[, 1], degree = 10, raw = TRUE), W_rep) colnames(X_poly10_train) <- paste0("V", seq_len(ncol(X_poly10_train))) colnames(X_poly10_val) <- colnames(X_poly10_train) colnames(X_poly10_test) <- colnames(X_poly10_train)  est2 <- SparseLinearDML(model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", alpha = 0.1, n_fold = 5L, seed = 123L) est2 <- fit(est2, X_poly10_train, T_train, Y_train) te_pred2 <- predict(est2, X_poly10_test) if (requireNamespace("grf", quietly = TRUE)) {   est3 <- CausalForestDML(     model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger",     n_fold = 5L, seed = 123L, num_trees = 1000L, min_node_size = 5L   )   est3 <- fit(est3, X_all_train, T_train, Y_train)   te_pred3 <- predict(est3, X_all_test) } else {   te_pred3 <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(X_all_test))   message("Package 'grf' not installed; CausalForestDML skipped.") } expected_te <- apply(X_test, 1, exp_te) df_plot <- data.frame(   x = rep(X_test[, 1], 5),   te = c(te_pred, te_pred1, te_pred2, te_pred3, expected_te),   method = rep(c("LinearDML", "SparseLinearDML (poly 3)", "SparseLinearDML (poly 10 + Lasso)",                  "CausalForestDML", "True effect"), each = length(te_pred)) ) ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = x, y = te, colour = method, linetype = method)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = c(rep("solid", 4), "dashed")) +   labs(y = "Treatment Effect", x = "x", colour = "", linetype = "") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(legend.position = "bottom") mse_te <- c(   "LinearDML" = mean((expected_te - te_pred)^2),   "SparseLinearDML (poly 3)" = mean((expected_te - te_pred1)^2),   "SparseLinearDML (poly 10 + Lasso)" = mean((expected_te - te_pred2)^2),   "CausalForestDML" = if (all(!is.na(te_pred3))) mean((expected_te - te_pred3)^2) else NA_real_ ) print(mse_te) LinearDML          SparseLinearDML (poly 3)                         7.97847741                        0.07211196  SparseLinearDML (poly 10 + Lasso)                   CausalForestDML                         0.90497396                        0.46968272 print("Best by MSE of TE:") [1] "Best by MSE of TE:" print(names(which.min(mse_te[!is.na(mse_te)]))) [1] "SparseLinearDML (poly 3)"

what: 3. Single Continuous Treatment with Polynomial Features
text: Section 1 already fits DGP three linear final stages: LinearDML raw X W (est), SparseLinearDML degree-3 polynomials \(x_1\) plus W (est1), SparseLinearDML degree-10 polynomials plus W stronger Lasso penalty (est2). interpret fitted CATE linear model columns passed fit: \[\hat{\theta}(z) = \hat{\beta}_0 + z^\top \hat{\beta},\] \(z\) one row design matrix (raw covariates, polynomial terms \(x_1\) plus \(W\), etc.). coef() returns \(\hat{\beta}\) aligned column names V1, V2, …; intercept() returns \(\hat{\beta}_0\). LinearDML (OLS final stage): coef() intercept() CATE parameters \(\hat{\theta}(z) = \hat{\beta}_0 + z^\top\hat{\beta}\), agree direct dot product (ordering columns newdata). SparseLinearDML (glmnet final stage): glmnet fits extra global intercept top column named intercept (residualized treatment scale). Reconstruct CATE \(\hat{\eta} = b_0 + \tilde{z}^\top b_{1:p}\) \(\tilde{z} = (1, z^\top)^\top\) matches predict()’s cbind(intercept = 1, newdata); use full coef(fit, s = "lambda.1se") vector, call predict() directly.

text: EconML DML stack supports matrix continuous treatments T (e.g. log prices per brand Dominick’s OJ example). RCausalML mirrors pattern: pass treatment \(n \times d\) numeric matrix data.frame \(d > 1\) columns. First stage: cross-fitted \(\hat{E}[Y \mid X]\) , \(j=1,\ldots,d\), \(\hat{E}[T_j \mid X]\) using model_y / model_t learners scalar treatment (continuous columns use regression nuisances, EconML). Second stage: joint residual--residual regression \(\tilde{Y}\) cross-product CATE featurizer \(\phi(X)\) \(\tilde{T}\) (analogue EconML’s cross_product econml.dml), treatment dimension gets heterogeneous coefficient \(\hat{\theta}_j(X)\). API: fit(est, X, T_matrix, y), predict(est, newdata) returns \(n_{\mathrm{new}} \times d\) matrix marginal CATEs (one column per treatment). estimate_ate(..., return_ci = TRUE) returns vector ate, ate_lb, ate_ub one element per treatment dimension. Supported classes: LinearDML, SparseLinearDML, KernelDML (model_final "lm", "glmnet", "kernel"). CausalForestDML NonParamDML (ranger/xgb) still require single treatment dimension. panel / sequential settings, DynamicDMLearner remains dedicated native-R entry point. Multiple outcomes (vector Y) implemented DMLearner; use separate fits per outcome Python EconML need joint multi-outcome model. See original EconML notebook full Dominick’s-style setup.
code: set.seed(123) n <- 350 X_m <- data.frame(income = rnorm(n, 50, 15), age = rnorm(n, 40, 10)) # Two correlated continuous treatments (observational) T_m <- cbind(   T1 = 0.08 * X_m$income + 0.02 * X_m$age + rnorm(n),   T2 = -0.05 * X_m$income + 0.06 * X_m$age + rnorm(n) ) Y_m <- 2 + 1.1 * T_m[, 1] + 0.6 * T_m[, 2] + 0.25 * X_m$income - 0.1 * X_m$age + rnorm(n)  library(RCausalML) est_m <- LinearDML(n_fold = 5L, seed = 123) est_m <- fit(est_m, X_m, T_m, Y_m)  cate_m <- predict(est_m, X_m) cat("Dimensions of predicted CATE matrix (n x d):", paste(dim(cate_m), collapse = " x "), "\n") Dimensions of predicted CATE matrix (n x d): 350 x 2 print(head(cate_m, 3L)) T1        T2 [1,] 1.1056177 0.5440505 [2,] 0.7469703 0.6733157 [3,] 0.7313425 0.4460835 ate_m <- estimate_ate(est_m, X_m, T_m, Y_m, return_ci = TRUE, pretrain = TRUE) cat("ATE per treatment dimension (with CI):\n") ATE per treatment dimension (with CI): print(ate_m) $ate        T1        T2  0.9313875 0.5504409   $ate_lb        T1        T2  0.9156536 0.5408941   $ate_ub        T1        T2  0.9471214 0.5599876

text: Double Machine Learning Difference--Differences (DML-) combines identification credibility flexibility ML estimate causal effects high-dimensional observational panel settings. classic two-way fixed effects model assumes: \[Y_{} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \theta (D_{} \times Post_t) + \varepsilon_{}\] DML-extends allowing flexible, nonparametric control high-dimensional confounders \(X_{}\): \[\Delta Y_{} = \theta D_{} + g(X_{}) + \zeta_{}\] \(\Delta Y_{} = Y_{} - Y_{,t-1}\) first-differenced outcome \(g(\cdot)\) estimated cross-fitted ML model rather linear parametric form. DML-accommodates: Two-period : Classic treatment vs. control, pre/post design Staggered adoption: Units treated different times (group-time ATT) [[19]] Continuous treatments: Dose-response using kernel weighting + GPS [[6]] Repeated cross-sections balanced panels DoubleML package implements via DoubleMLPLR, DoubleMLIRM, custom wrappers package [[10]]. Parallel trends still required. DML adjusts observed covariates \(X\); unobserved time-varying confounders remain threat identification. Sample size. Cross-fitting requires sufficient observations per fold; small panels may yield unstable nuisance estimates. Interpretability. \(\hat{\theta}\) valid causal estimate, ML nuisance functions \(g(X)\) \(\ell(X)\) black boxes. Implementation complexity. Requires careful choice ML hyperparameters number cross-fitting folds.

text: Callaway Sant’Anna (2021) examined causal impact higher state minimum wages (federal level) teen employment across U.S. counties, using data roughly 2001–2007. demonstration uses cleaned, balanced panel dataset study (called mpdta R package; see package documentation details). data employed purely example illustrate key differences DoubleML packages. similar notebook using data appears package documentation. Following original example, report results two identification strategies: - Unconditional parallel trends assumption - Conditional parallel trends assumption (adjusting covariates) Double Machine Learning (DML) fit three RCausalML wrappers—doubleml_did_linear, doubleml_did_rf, doubleml_did_xgboost—compare aggregated ATTs, dispersion group-time estimates, illustrative nuisance metrics (via doubleml_did_eval_*). Small differences versus default expected cross-fitting flexible nuisances. package includes mpdta dataset: county-level teen employment (log employment) 2003–2007, variation timing minimum-wage increases across states. use illustrate DoubleML real data. Part B: simple aggregate ATT wrapper Part B: RMSE group-time ATTs across wrappers Part B: illustrative nuisance scores (two covariates) simple aggregate ATT summarizes average effect minimum-wage treatment log teen employment across group-time cells, using linear wrapper’s cross-fitted nuisances. aggregate ATT gives single summary estimate minimum-wage effect log teen employment, averaging across treated cohort-time cells covariate adjustment lpop. Compare cmp_agg_b see RF XGBoost wrappers differ. ::att_gt() doubleml_did_* wrappers operates many internal 2×2 slices returns group-time ATTs plus influence functions. expose single global object predict(object, newdata) method, RCausalML::explain_cate() applied directly att_gt fit. Instead, illustrate SHAP workflow single slice: fit LinearDML Part B toy sample (x1, x2, D2, \(\Delta Y = y_{1} - y_{0}\)) compute permutation SHAP predicted \(\hat{\tau}(X)\). SHAP values descriptive summary CATE heterogeneity within DML model — group-time ATTs reported . keep runtime manageable, explanation background rows subsampled deduplicated covariate rows, using non-overlapping sets possible avoid leakage. Parallel SHAP via {future} used package available. Bar plot — average |SHAP| per feature, useful ranking overall feature importance.  Dependence plots show feature drives predicted treatment effect. Colour encodes second variable chosen automatically potential interaction effects.  toy DGP, larger x1 shifts treatment propensity \(\\Delta Y\); may see SHAP x1 x2 align roles. 1L)) }  dy_shap <- as.numeric(y1_2 - y0_2) X_df <- as.data.frame(X_ev2) X_shap_pool <- X_df[!duplicated(X_df), , drop = FALSE]  set.seed(102) ldml_shap <- LinearDML(model_y = "lm", model_t = "lm", n_fold = 5L, seed = 102) ldml_shap <- fit(ldml_shap, X_df, D2, dy_shap)  nexplain <- min(80L, nrow(X_shap_pool)) nbg <- min(50L, nrow(X_shap_pool))  if (nrow(X_shap_pool) > nexplain + nbg) {   idxexplain <- sample(nrow(X_shap_pool), nexplain)   idxbg <- sample(setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X_shap_pool)), idxexplain), nbg) } else {   idxexplain <- sample(nrow(X_shap_pool), nexplain)   idxbg <- sample(nrow(X_shap_pool), nbg) }  Xexplain <- X_shap_pool[idxexplain, , drop = FALSE] bg_X_df <- X_shap_pool[idxbg, , drop = FALSE] fg_prev <- getOption("future.globals.maxSize", default = 500 * 1024^2) if (has_future) {   options(future.globals.maxSize = max(2 * 1024^3, fg_prev)) } ks_args <- list(   object = ldml_shap,   X = Xexplain,   bg_X = bg_X_df,   use_permshap = TRUE,   parallel = has_future,   verbose = FALSE ) if (has_future) {   ks_args$parallel_args <- list(packages = c("RCausalML")) } ks <- tryCatch(   do.call(explain_cate, ks_args),   finally = {     if (has_future) {       future::plan(future::sequential)       options(future.globals.maxSize = fg_prev)     }   } ) shp <- shapviz::shapviz(ks, X = Xexplain) shapviz::sv_importance(shp, kind = "beeswarm") +   ggplot2::labs(title = "SHAP (beeswarm): predicted CATE, LinearDML on DiD-style slice") shapviz::sv_importance(shp, show_numbers = TRUE) +   ggplot2::labs(title = "SHAP importance (bar): predicted CATE, LinearDML on DiD-style slice") xvars <- colnames(shp$X) shapviz::sv_dependence(shp, v = xvars, share_y = TRUE) shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = 1) shapviz::sv_force(shp, row_id = 1) row_show <- if (nrow(shp$X) >= 1L) as.integer(which.max(shp$X$x1)) else 1L shapviz::sv_waterfall(shp, row_id = row_show)

text: Double Machine Learning Instrumental Variables (DML-IV) combines IV identification double/debiased machine learning. instrument \(Z\) addresses endogeneity treatment \(D\), ML nuisance models cross-fitting prevent overfitting bias. DMLIVLearner() RCausalML builds cross-fitted estimates \(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y \mid X,W]\), \(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[T \mid X,W]\), \(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[T \mid X,W,Z]\), forms DML-IV pseudo-outcome, fits linear CATE \(X\) (see ?DMLIVLearner). standard IV directed acyclic graph (DAG): naive regression \(Y\) \(D\) biased \(D\) correlated \(C\). Classical 2SLS projects \(D\) onto \(Z\) covariates first stage. DML-IV generalises first-stage steps optional ML learners ("ranger", "glmnet", "xgb") cross-fitting, targeting local average treatment effect (LATE) standard IV assumptions. Standard DML (LinearDML) applies cross-fitted nuisance idea without instrument. correct unobserved confounders affect \(D\) \(Y\); included show IV vs non-IV estimates side side first-stage learner.

1L))   } else {     1L   }   use_parallel <- n_workers > 1L && requireNamespace("future", quietly = TRUE)    fg_prev <- getOption("future.globals.maxSize", default = 500 * 1024^2)   if (use_parallel) {     options(future.globals.maxSize = max(2 * 1024^3, fg_prev))     future::plan(future::multisession, workers = n_workers)   }    explain_one <- function(fit_obj, label) {     tryCatch(       {         args <- list(           fit_obj,           X = X_explain,           bg_X = bg_X_df,           use_permshap = TRUE,           verbose = FALSE,           max_iter = 60L,           tol = 0.02,           parallel = use_parallel,           parallel_args = list(packages = c("RCausalML", "ranger", "xgboost"))         )         if (!requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)) {           args$parallel_args$packages <- setdiff(args$parallel_args$packages, "xgboost")         }         do.call(explain_cate, args)       },       error = function(e) {         warning("SHAP failed for ", label, ": ", conditionMessage(e))         NULL       }     )   }    tryCatch(     {       ks_iv <- mapply(         explain_one,         fits_iv,         paste0("DML-IV (", names(fits_iv), ")"),         SIMPLIFY = FALSE       )       ks_pl <- mapply(         explain_one,         fits_pl,         paste0("Linear DML (", names(fits_pl), ")"),         SIMPLIFY = FALSE       )       shp_iv <- lapply(ks_iv, function(k) {         if (!is.null(k)) shapviz::shapviz(k) else NULL       })       shp_pl <- lapply(ks_pl, function(k) {         if (!is.null(k)) shapviz::shapviz(k) else NULL       })     },     finally = {       if (use_parallel) {         future::plan(future::sequential)         options(future.globals.maxSize = fg_prev)       }     }   ) }

code: packages <- c(   "RCausalML",   "ggplot2" ) # Install missing packages # new_packages <- packages[!(packages %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"])] # if (length(new_packages)) install.packages(new_packages) # Verify installation cat("Installed packages:\n") Installed packages: print(sapply(packages, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE)) RCausalML   ggplot2       TRUE      TRUE # Load packages with suppressed messages invisible(lapply(packages, function(pkg) {   suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)) })) # Check loaded packages cat("Successfully loaded packages:\n") Successfully loaded packages: print(search()[grepl("package:", search())]) [1] "package:ggplot2"   "package:RCausalML" "package:stats"     [4] "package:graphics"  "package:grDevices" "package:utils"     [7] "package:datasets"  "package:methods"   "package:base" set.seed(123) n_panels   <- 800L   # number of panels (units) n_periods  <- 3L     # time periods per panel n_treatments <- 2L   # treatments per period n_w        <- 20L    # control variables n_x        <- 100L   # total features (for Section 2) s_x        <- 10L    # support size for controls # One row per (unit, period). Outcome Y is the final-period outcome for that unit. n <- n_panels * n_periods groups <- rep(seq_len(n_panels), each = n_periods)  # True effects: (n_periods * n_treatments) coefficients true_effect <- c(0.04, 0.07, 0.32, 0.24, 0.13, 0.61)  # Controls W (time-varying): same dimension for all rows W <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_w), n, n_w) colnames(W) <- paste0("W", seq_len(n_w))  # Treatments T: (n_periods * n_treatments) columns; for row in period p, fill period 1..p, rest 0 T_mat <- matrix(0, n, n_periods * n_treatments) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   for (p in seq_len(n_periods)) {     row <- (i - 1) * n_periods + p     T_mat[row, ((p - 1) * n_treatments + 1):(p * n_treatments)] <- rnorm(n_treatments, 0.5, 0.5)   } } colnames(T_mat) <- paste0("T", seq_len(n_periods * n_treatments))  # Outcome at last period: Y = T %*% theta + W %*% gamma + noise (per unit) gamma_w <- runif(n_w, 0, 0.3) Y_last <- numeric(n_panels) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   T_i <- T_mat[idx, , drop = FALSE]   # Use period-specific T for this unit (row n_periods has all treatments)   Ti_full <- T_i[n_periods, ]   W_i <- W[idx[n_periods], , drop = FALSE]   Y_last[i] <- sum(true_effect * Ti_full) + as.numeric(W_i %*% gamma_w) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5) } # Repeat last-period outcome for each row of the panel (for fit API) Y <- rep(Y_last, each = n_periods) est <- DynamicDMLearner(   model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", cv = 3L, random_state = 123L,   fit_cate_intercept = FALSE  # intercept-only when X = NULL (avoids collinearity) ) est <- fit(est, Y = Y, T = T_mat, X = NULL, W = W, groups = groups) # Predicted CATE at each row (intercept-only model: same for all) cate_pred <- predict(est, newdata = NULL) ate_approx <- mean(cate_pred, na.rm = TRUE) print(paste0("Average effect (mean predicted CATE): ", round(ate_approx, 2))) [1] "Average effect (mean predicted CATE): -0.03" baseline_policy <- matrix(0, 1, n_periods * n_treatments) target_policy   <- matrix(1, 1, n_periods * n_treatments) # Effect = sum(theta * (T1 - T0)); text: Standard DML works great static (one-time) treatments high-dimensional complex confounders. However, many real-world scenarios involve dynamic treatments: - Treatments period \(t\) depend past treatments evolving states. Outcomes accumulate time. Confounders (variables affect treatment decisions outcomes) high-dimensional unknown functional forms. Dynamic DML solves using machine learning flexibly model “nuisance” relationships (confounding dynamics) delivering robust, semi-parametric estimates treatments different periods affect final outcome — heterogeneity driven initial conditions. assumes data follow Markov decision process-like structure observed dynamic confounders. ’s core logic: Data Structure provide panel data indexed unit (e.g., individual, firm) time \(t = 1, \ldots, m\): \[ \{X_t, W_t, T_t, Y_t\}_{t=1}^m \] \(X_t\): State variables time \(t\) (can high-dimensional). \(W_t\): Additional confounders/controls time \(t\). \(T_t\): Treatment(s) assigned time \(t\) (can continuous, binary, multi-valued). \(Y_t\): Outcome observed time \(t\). groups array tells model rows belong unit across time. Underlying Structural Model method built equations (data-generating process): \[ XW_t = \cdot T_{t-1} + B \cdot XW_{t-1} + \eta_t \] (state/confounder evolution) \[ T_t = p(T_{t-1}, XW_t, \zeta_t) \] (treatment policy — treatments chosen adaptively) \[ Y_t = \theta_0(X_0)' T_t + \mu' XW_t + \epsilon_t \] (outcome equation) \(XW_t\) concatenation states confounders. \(\theta_0(X_0)\) heterogeneous treatment effect want estimate — depends initial state \(X_0\). effect treatments periods ultimately measured final-period outcome. Errors \(\eta_t, \zeta_t, \epsilon_t\) assumed mean-independent covariates (standard DML exogeneity). Estimation via Double Machine Learning (“Double” part) Dynamic DML uses classic DML trick get unbiased estimates even nuisance functions estimated ML (can overfit): Step : Nuisance estimation Use flexible ML models estimate two “nuisance” functions: Treatment model: \(\hat{p}(T_t \mid T_{t-1}, XW_t)\) (conditional expectation continuous). Outcome model: \(\hat{E}[Y_t \mid T_t, XW_t, \text{past}]\). Step B: Residualization & orthogonalization Create residuals “partial ” confounding. dynamic structure, done recursively across time periods respecting panel structure. Step C: Cross-fitting Data split folds. Nuisance models trained one fold used predict residuals held-fold (prevents overfitting ensures valid inference). Step D: Solve moment condition final estimator solves score equation isolates \(\theta_0(X_0)\), yielding consistent asymptotically normal estimates even ML nuisance models slightly misspecified (long converge fast enough). result estimate \(\theta_0(X_0)\) new \(X_0\), telling much sequence treatments change final outcome units different initial characteristics. model_t: ML model treatment (nuisance). model_y: ML model outcome (nuisance). X: Initial time-varying state features. W: Additional high-dimensional controls. groups: Panel identifier. code: n_panels   <- 800L   # number of panels (units) n_periods  <- 3L     # time periods per panel n_treatments <- 2L   # treatments per period n_w        <- 20L    # control variables n_x        <- 100L   # total features (for Section 2) s_x        <- 10L    # support size for controls # One row per (unit, period). Outcome Y is the final-period outcome for that unit. n <- n_panels * n_periods groups <- rep(seq_len(n_panels), each = n_periods)  # True effects: (n_periods * n_treatments) coefficients true_effect <- c(0.04, 0.07, 0.32, 0.24, 0.13, 0.61)  # Controls W (time-varying): same dimension for all rows W <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_w), n, n_w) colnames(W) <- paste0("W", seq_len(n_w))  # Treatments T: (n_periods * n_treatments) columns; for row in period p, fill period 1..p, rest 0 T_mat <- matrix(0, n, n_periods * n_treatments) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   for (p in seq_len(n_periods)) {     row <- (i - 1) * n_periods + p     T_mat[row, ((p - 1) * n_treatments + 1):(p * n_treatments)] <- rnorm(n_treatments, 0.5, 0.5)   } } colnames(T_mat) <- paste0("T", seq_len(n_periods * n_treatments))  # Outcome at last period: Y = T %*% theta + W %*% gamma + noise (per unit) gamma_w <- runif(n_w, 0, 0.3) Y_last <- numeric(n_panels) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   T_i <- T_mat[idx, , drop = FALSE]   # Use period-specific T for this unit (row n_periods has all treatments)   Ti_full <- T_i[n_periods, ]   W_i <- W[idx[n_periods], , drop = FALSE]   Y_last[i] <- sum(true_effect * Ti_full) + as.numeric(W_i %*% gamma_w) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5) } # Repeat last-period outcome for each row of the panel (for fit API) Y <- rep(Y_last, each = n_periods) est <- DynamicDMLearner(   model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", cv = 3L, random_state = 123L,   fit_cate_intercept = FALSE  # intercept-only when X = NULL (avoids collinearity) ) est <- fit(est, Y = Y, T = T_mat, X = NULL, W = W, groups = groups) # Predicted CATE at each row (intercept-only model: same for all) cate_pred <- predict(est, newdata = NULL) ate_approx <- mean(cate_pred, na.rm = TRUE) print(paste0("Average effect (mean predicted CATE): ", round(ate_approx, 2))) [1] "Average effect (mean predicted CATE): -0.03" baseline_policy <- matrix(0, 1, n_periods * n_treatments) target_policy   <- matrix(1, 1, n_periods * n_treatments) # Effect = sum(theta * (T1 - T0)); with T1 - T0 = 1 for all, effect = sum(period effects) intercept_est_full <- vapply(est$model_cate$models, function(fit) as.numeric(stats::coef(fit)[1]), numeric(1)) eff_policy <- sum(intercept_est_full * as.numeric(target_policy - baseline_policy)) print(paste0("Effect of target vs baseline policy (sum of period effects): ", round(eff_policy, 2))) [1] "Effect of target vs baseline policy (sum of period effects): 0.37" m <- est$model_cate if (m$type == "lm_multi") {   intercepts <- vapply(m$models, function(fit) as.numeric(stats::coef(fit)[1]), numeric(1)) } else {   intercepts <- as.numeric(stats::coef(m$model)[1]) } dim(intercepts) <- c(n_treatments, n_periods) for (p in seq_len(n_periods)) {   print(paste0("Marginal effect of treatments in period ", p, " on final outcome: ",                paste(round(intercepts[, p], 4), collapse = ", "))) } [1] "Marginal effect of treatments in period 1 on final outcome: -0.0278, 0.0084" [1] "Marginal effect of treatments in period 2 on final outcome: 0.0534, -0.085" [1] "Marginal effect of treatments in period 3 on final outcome: 0.0447, 0.3774" if (est$model_cate$type == "lm_multi") {   conf_ints <- t(vapply(est$model_cate$models, function(fit) {     ci <- stats::confint(fit, parm = 1, level = 0.95)     c(ci[1], ci[2])   }, numeric(2)))   conf_lower <- conf_ints[, 1]   conf_upper <- conf_ints[, 2]   intercept_est <- vapply(est$model_cate$models, function(fit) as.numeric(stats::coef(fit)[1]), numeric(1)) } else {   intercept_est <- as.numeric(stats::coef(est$model_cate$model)[1])   ci <- stats::confint(est$model_cate$model, parm = 1, level = 0.95)   conf_lower <- ci[1]; conf_upper <- ci[2] } idx_est <- seq_len(length(true_effect)) df_plot <- data.frame(   param = factor(idx_est),   estimate = if (length(intercept_est) == length(true_effect)) intercept_est else rep(intercept_est[1], length(true_effect)),   true = true_effect,   lower = if (length(conf_lower) == length(true_effect)) conf_lower else NA_real_,   upper = if (length(conf_upper) == length(true_effect)) conf_upper else NA_real_ ) # If we have one intercept only, plot it once if (length(intercept_est) != length(true_effect)) {   df_plot$estimate <- intercept_est[1]   df_plot$lower <- NA   df_plot$upper <- NA } ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = param)) +   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, y = estimate), width = 0.2, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_point(aes(y = estimate, colour = "DynamicDMLearner"), size = 3) +   geom_point(aes(y = true, colour = "Ground truth"), size = 3, shape = 18) +   geom_vline(xintercept = seq(2.5, 6, by = 2), linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.4) +   scale_x_discrete(labels = paste0("theta_", rep(0:(n_periods - 1), each = n_treatments))) +   labs(y = "Effect", x = "Parameter", colour = "") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(legend.position = "bottom") het_strength <- 0.5 n_hetero    <- 2L   # number of effect modifiers n_x_use     <- 5L   # use first 5 X columns for heterogeneity set.seed(12) X_full <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_x_use), n, n_x_use) colnames(X_full) <- paste0("X", seq_len(n_x_use))  # Heterogeneous effect: true_effect + X[, 1:n_hetero] %*% het_coef  het_coef <- matrix(het_strength * runif(n_hetero * (n_periods * n_treatments)), n_hetero, n_periods * n_treatments) true_effect_het <- true_effect  # baseline # For each unit, Y_last = T %*% (true_effect + het_coef' %*% x) + ... Y_last_het <- numeric(n_panels) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   x_i <- X_full[idx[1], 1:n_hetero, drop = FALSE]   theta_i <- true_effect + as.numeric(x_i %*% het_coef)   Ti_full <- T_mat[idx[n_periods], ]   W_i <- W[idx[n_periods], , drop = FALSE]   Y_last_het[i] <- sum(theta_i * Ti_full) + as.numeric(W_i %*% gamma_w) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5) } Y_het <- rep(Y_last_het, each = n_periods) est_het <- DynamicDMLearner(model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", cv = 3L, random_state = 1L) est_het <- fit(est_het, Y = Y_het, T = T_mat, X = X_full, W = W, groups = groups) X_test_idx <- seq(1, min(25, n_panels), by = 3) X_test <- X_full[(X_test_idx[1] - 1) * n_periods + 1, , drop = FALSE] for (j in seq_along(X_test_idx)[-1]) {   row_j <- (X_test_idx[j] - 1) * n_periods + 1   X_test <- rbind(X_test, X_full[row_j, , drop = FALSE]) } cate_het <- predict(est_het, newdata = X_test) print(paste0("Average effect (mean CATE on test set): ", round(mean(cate_het), 2))) [1] "Average effect (mean CATE on test set): -0.17" eff_het <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(X_test)), function(i) {   effect(est_het, newdata = X_test[i, , drop = FALSE],          T0 = as.numeric(baseline_policy), T1 = as.numeric(target_policy)) }, numeric(1)) print("Effect of target vs baseline for test units:") [1] "Effect of target vs baseline for test units:" print(round(eff_het, 4)) [1] -0.0163 -0.5412  0.6095 -2.6782 -2.3637 -0.4089 -1.3400 -0.3608 -2.2846 m_het <- est_het$model_cate if (m_het$type == "lm_multi") {   intercept_het <- vapply(m_het$models, function(fit) {     cf <- stats::coef(fit)     if ("intercept" %in% names(cf)) cf["intercept"] else cf[1]   }, numeric(1))   coef_het <- vapply(m_het$models, function(fit) {     cf <- stats::coef(fit)     unname(cf[names(cf) != "intercept"])   }, FUN.VALUE = numeric(n_x_use)) } else {   intercept_het <- stats::coef(m_het$model)["intercept"]   cf <- stats::coef(m_het$model)   coef_het <- unname(cf[names(cf) != "intercept"]) } print("Intercepts (period/treatment effects):") [1] "Intercepts (period/treatment effects):" print(round(intercept_het, 4)) [1] -0.0463  0.0015  0.0573  0.0201  0.0783  0.3954 param_hat <- c(intercept_het, as.numeric(coef_het)) n_params <- length(param_hat) df_het <- data.frame(   param = factor(seq_len(n_params)),   estimate = param_hat ) ggplot(df_het, aes(x = param, y = estimate)) +   geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3) +   labs(y = "Coefficient", x = "Parameter") +   theme_minimal()

Outcome Y is the final-period outcome for that unit. n <- n_panels * n_periods groups <- rep(seq_len(n_panels), each = n_periods)  # True effects: (n_periods * n_treatments) coefficients true_effect <- c(0.04, 0.07, 0.32, 0.24, 0.13, 0.61)  # Controls W (time-varying): same dimension for all rows W <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_w), n, n_w) colnames(W) <- paste0("W", seq_len(n_w))  # Treatments T: (n_periods * n_treatments) columns; for row in period p, fill period 1..p, rest 0 T_mat <- matrix(0, n, n_periods * n_treatments) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   for (p in seq_len(n_periods)) {     row <- (i - 1) * n_periods + p     T_mat[row, ((p - 1) * n_treatments + 1):(p * n_treatments)] <- rnorm(n_treatments, 0.5, 0.5)   } } colnames(T_mat) <- paste0("T", seq_len(n_periods * n_treatments))  # Outcome at last period: Y = T %*% theta + W %*% gamma + noise (per unit) gamma_w <- runif(n_w, 0, 0.3) Y_last <- numeric(n_panels) for (i in seq_len(n_panels)) {   idx <- ((i - 1) * n_periods + 1):(i * n_periods)   T_i <- T_mat[idx, , drop = FALSE]   # Use period-specific T for this unit (row n_periods has all treatments)   Ti_full <- T_i[n_periods, ]   W_i <- W[idx[n_periods], , drop = FALSE]   Y_last[i] <- sum(true_effect * Ti_full) + as.numeric(W_i %*% gamma_w) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5) } # Repeat last-period outcome for each row of the panel (for fit API) Y <- rep(Y_last, each = n_periods)

Average treatment effect: approximate “default policy” effect averaging predicted CATE sample (using baseline vs target policy). Effect moving baseline policy (zeros) target policy (ones). 6 treatment dimensions, effect sum estimated period effects (since T1 - T0 = 1 ). Period treatment effects: R DynamicDMLearner stores one linear model per treatment column. fit_cate_intercept = FALSE \(X\), single coefficient per model marginal effect period/treatment.
code: est <- DynamicDMLearner(   model_y = "ranger", model_t = "ranger", cv = 3L, random_state = 123L,   fit_cate_intercept = FALSE  # intercept-only when X = NULL (avoids collinearity) ) est <- fit(est, Y = Y, T = T_mat, X = NULL, W = W, groups = groups) # Predicted CATE at each row (intercept-only model: same for all) cate_pred <- predict(est, newdata = NULL) ate_approx <- mean(cate_pred, na.rm = TRUE) print(paste0("Average effect (mean predicted CATE): ", round(ate_approx, 2))) [1] "Average effect (mean predicted CATE): -0.03" baseline_policy <- matrix(0, 1, n_periods * n_treatments) target_policy   <- matrix(1, 1, n_periods * n_treatments) # Effect = sum(theta * (T1 - T0)); with T1 - T0 = 1 for all, effect = sum(period effects) intercept_est_full <- vapply(est$model_cate$models, function(fit) as.numeric(stats::coef(fit)[1]), numeric(1)) eff_policy <- sum(intercept_est_full * as.numeric(target_policy - baseline_policy)) print(paste0("Effect of target vs baseline policy (sum of period effects): ", round(eff_policy, 2))) [1] "Effect of target vs baseline policy (sum of period effects): 0.37" m <- est$model_cate if (m$type == "lm_multi") {   intercepts <- vapply(m$models, function(fit) as.numeric(stats::coef(fit)[1]), numeric(1)) } else {   intercepts <- as.numeric(stats::coef(m$model)[1]) } dim(intercepts) <- c(n_treatments, n_periods) for (p in seq_len(n_periods)) {   print(paste0("Marginal effect of treatments in period ", p, " on final outcome: ",                paste(round(intercepts[, p], 4), collapse = ", "))) } [1] "Marginal effect of treatments in period 1 on final outcome: -0.0278, 0.0084" [1] "Marginal effect of treatments in period 2 on final outcome: 0.0534, -0.085" [1] "Marginal effect of treatments in period 3 on final outcome: 0.0447, 0.3774"

code: packages <- c(   "RCausalML",   "ggplot2" ) # Install missing packages # new_packages <- packages[!(packages %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"])] # if (length(new_packages)) install.packages(new_packages) # Verify installation cat("Installed packages:\n") Installed packages: print(sapply(packages, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE)) RCausalML   ggplot2       TRUE      TRUE # Load packages with suppressed messages invisible(lapply(packages, function(pkg) {   suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)) })) # Check loaded packages cat("Successfully loaded packages:\n") Successfully loaded packages: print(search()[grepl("package:", search())]) [1] "package:ggplot2"   "package:RCausalML" "package:stats"     [4] "package:graphics"  "package:grDevices" "package:utils"     [7] "package:datasets"  "package:methods"   "package:base" set.seed(123) n <- 10000L   # number of raw samples d <- 10L      # number of binary features + 1  # Binary features; first 4 used for heterogeneity, rest as controls X_raw <- matrix(rbinom(n * d, 1, 0.5), n, d) # First column is treatment: imbalanced A/B test log_odds <- qlogis(pmin(pmax(X_raw[, 2], 0.001), 0.999))  # expit(X[,2])-like X_raw[, 1] <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(log_odds)) # Outcome: heterogeneity from first binary feature, confounding, heteroskedastic errors y_raw <- (-1 + 2 * X_raw[, 2]) * X_raw[, 1] + X_raw[, 2] +   (1 * X_raw[, 2] + 1) * rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Treatment = first column; X = effect modifiers (cols 2--5); W = controls (cols 6--10) treatment <- X_raw[, 1] X_effect <- X_raw[, 2:5, drop = FALSE] W_control <- X_raw[, 6:d, drop = FALSE] colnames(X_effect) <- c("A", "B", "C", "D") # Full X for first stage (effect modifiers + controls). CATE will be linear in X_effect. X_full <- cbind(X_effect, W_control) colnames(X_full) <- c(colnames(X_effect), paste0("W", seq_len(ncol(W_control))))  est <- LinearDML(   model_y = "ranger",   model_t = "ranger",   fit_cate_intercept = TRUE,   n_fold = 3L,   seed = 123L ) # Fit on full X so first stage uses all covariates; CATE is linear in all columns. # For CATE linear only in A--D, we would fit on X_effect only (weaker first stage). est <- fit(est, X_full, treatment, y_raw) # Segment with features [1, 0, 0, 0] (A=1, B=0, C=0, D=0); use mean controls for W x_segment <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 1) colnames(x_segment) <- c("A", "B", "C", "D") # For prediction we need full X (effect modifiers + controls). Use sample means for W. W_mean <- matrix(colMeans(W_control), nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(W_control), byrow = TRUE) newdata_segment <- cbind(x_segment, W_mean) colnames(newdata_segment) <- colnames(X_full)  effect_segment <- predict(est, newdata_segment) print(paste0("Treatment effect for segment [A=1, B=0, C=0, D=0]: ", round(effect_segment, 4))) [1] "Treatment effect for segment [A=1, B=0, C=0, D=0]: 1.4059" ate_ci <- estimate_ate(est, X_full, treatment, y_raw, return_ci = TRUE) print("ATE with 95% confidence interval:") [1] "ATE with 95% confidence interval:" print(ate_ci) $ate [1] 0.9999682  $ate_lb [1] 0.9816215  $ate_ub [1] 1.018315 coef_est <- coef(est) int_est <- intercept(est) cnames <- if (!is.null(names(coef_est))) names(coef_est) else paste0("V", seq_along(coef_est)) print("Coefficients of the linear CATE model (effect modifiers + controls):") [1] "Coefficients of the linear CATE model (effect modifiers + controls):" print(data.frame(feature = cnames, coef = round(as.numeric(coef_est), 4))) feature    coef 1       A -0.1522 2       B  0.3839 3       C -1.4603 4       D  0.0786 5      W1  0.2291 6      W2 -0.7001 7      W3  0.4543 8      W4 -0.1757 9      W5  0.6145 print(paste0("Intercept: ", round(int_est, 4))) [1] "Intercept: 1.3453" # Interaction-only polynomial features for effect modifiers (A--D) poly_X <- stats::model.matrix(~ .^2 - 1, data = as.data.frame(X_effect)) # Drop intercept-like column if present; keep interactions and main effects X_poly_full <- cbind(poly_X, W_control) colnames(X_poly_full) <- paste0("V", seq_len(ncol(X_poly_full)))  est_poly <- LinearDML(   model_y = "ranger",   model_t = "ranger",   fit_cate_intercept = TRUE,   n_fold = 3L,   seed = 123L ) est_poly <- fit(est_poly, X_poly_full, treatment, y_raw) m <- est_poly$model_cate if (!is.null(m$model) && inherits(m$model, "lm")) {   ci_int <- stats::confint(m$model, level = 0.99)   all_coef <- stats::coef(m$model)   point_int <- as.numeric(all_coef[1])   point_coef <- as.numeric(all_coef[-1])   lower_int <- ci_int[1, 1]   upper_int <- ci_int[1, 2]   lower_coef <- ci_int[-1, 1]   upper_coef <- ci_int[-1, 2]   n_coef <- length(point_coef) } else {   point_int <- intercept(est_poly)   point_coef <- coef(est_poly)   n_coef <- length(point_coef)   lower_int <- upper_int <- lower_coef <- upper_coef <- NA_real_ } idx <- seq_len(n_coef + 1) pts <- c(point_int, point_coef) lo <- c(lower_int, lower_coef) hi <- c(upper_int, upper_coef) labels <- c("intercept", if (!is.null(est_poly$X_names) && length(est_poly$X_names) == n_coef) est_poly$X_names else paste0("V", seq_len(n_coef))) df_coef <- data.frame(   param = factor(idx),   point = pts,   lower = lo,   upper = hi,   label = labels ) ggplot(df_coef, aes(x = param, y = point)) +   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_point(size = 3) +   scale_x_discrete(labels = df_coef$label) +   labs(y = "Coefficient", x = "Parameter") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)) lst <- expand.grid(A = 0:1, B = 0:1, C = 0:1, D = 0:1) feat_names_abbrev <- c("A", "B", "C", "D") segment_labels <- apply(lst, 1, function(r) paste(feat_names_abbrev[r > 0], collapse = " ")) segment_labels[segment_labels == ""] <- "(none)"  W_mean_all <- matrix(colMeans(W_control), nrow = nrow(lst), ncol = ncol(W_control), byrow = TRUE) newdata_all <- cbind(as.matrix(lst), W_mean_all) colnames(newdata_all) <- colnames(X_full)  point_cate <- predict(est, newdata_all) # Approximate CI using the lm variance: for linear CATE, Var(theta(x)) = x' V x if (!is.null(est$model_cate$model) && inherits(est$model_cate$model, "lm")) {   V <- stats::vcov(est$model_cate$model)   # Design for each segment: intercept + x (effect modifiers + W means)   D_seg <- cbind(1, newdata_all)   se_cate <- sqrt(diag(D_seg %*% V %*% t(D_seg)))   z <- qnorm(0.995)   lower_cate <- point_cate - z * se_cate   upper_cate <- point_cate + z * se_cate } else {   lower_cate <- upper_cate <- rep(NA_real_, length(point_cate)) } stat_sig <- (lower_cate > 0) | (upper_cate < 0) df_seg <- data.frame(   segment = factor(segment_labels, levels = segment_labels),   point = point_cate,   lower = lower_cate,   upper = upper_cate,   significant = stat_sig ) ggplot(df_seg, aes(x = segment, y = point, colour = significant)) +   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.25, linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(size = 3) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "red", "TRUE" = "black"), labels = c("insig", "stat_sig")) +   labs(y = "CATE", x = "Segment", colour = "") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5), legend.position = "bottom") if (requireNamespace("grf", quietly = TRUE)) {   est_forest <- CausalForestDML(     model_y = "ranger",     model_t = "ranger",     n_fold = 3L,     seed = 123L,     num_trees = 1000L,     min_node_size = 2L   )   est_forest <- fit(est_forest, X_full, treatment, y_raw)   cate_forest <- predict(est_forest, newdata_all)   print("CausalForestDML fitted (no sample weights in R). CATE for first 5 segments:")   print(round(cate_forest[1:5], 4)) } else {   message("Package 'grf' not installed; CausalForestDML skipped.")   cate_forest <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(newdata_all)) } [1] "CausalForestDML fitted (no sample weights in R). tutorial shows perform cluster robust double machine learning (DML) R RCausalML’ package. follow DoubleML R Cluster Robust example implement one-way two-way cluster robust DML using simulated data Chiang et al. (2021) real-world data (U.S. automobile demand, BLP 1995). data clustered, observations within cluster may correlated, violating ..d. assumption. example, panel dataset, errors may correlated within individuals time (one-way clustering), multi-dimensional setting, errors may correlated within two dimensions (e.g., firms markets) leading two-way clustering. Clustering affects DML two ways: Variance–covariance: Standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals must use cluster robust variance estimator (Cameron et al. 2011). Sample splitting: Standard cross-fitting put observations cluster train test folds, errors correlated across folds. Chiang et al. (2021) propose splitting cluster: two-way clustering \(K\) folds per dimension, data split \(K^2\) folds nuisance functions estimated clusters disjoint used evaluate score. Cluster Robust Double Machine Learning (Cluster Robust DML) extension standard Double Machine Learning framework designed data observations independent. standard DML, assumed every data point (row) independent identically distributed (..d.). However, many real-world datasets, observations grouped clusters (e.g., students within schools, patients within hospitals, firms within industries, repeated time periods individual). Within clusters, errors correlated. apply standard DML clustered data, standard errors underestimated, leading invalid confidence intervals false positives (Type errors). Cluster Robust DML fixes adjusting cross-fitting procedure variance estimation. Cluster Robust DML modifies two specific steps standard DML algorithm: standard DML, split data \(K\) folds randomly row. Cluster Robust DML, must split Cluster ID. Standard: Fold 1 might contain Student Classroom 1, Fold 2 might contain Student B Classroom 1. causes data leakage ML model learns information Classroom 1 Fold 1 predicts Fold 2. Cluster Robust: students Classroom 1 must fold. ensures nuisance models (\(\hat{g}, \hat{m}\)) trained completely independent clusters ones predicting . final step, calculating standard error \(\theta\), sum scores across individual observations. must aggregate scores cluster level first. Calculate orthogonal score \(\psi_i\) every observation. Sum scores within cluster: \(\Psi_c = \sum_{\\text{cluster } c} \psi_i\). Calculate variance based variation \(\Psi_c\) across clusters, \(\psi_i\) across observations. \[ \hat{\sigma}^2_{cluster} = \frac{1}{C(C-1)} \sum_{c=1}^{C} (\Psi_c - \bar{\Psi})^2 \] (\(C\) number clusters, observations) use variant whenever data hierarchical panel structure: Panel Data: Multiple time periods unit (Cluster = Individual ID). Multi-Site Experiments: Participants nested within locations (Cluster = Site ID). Network Data: Individuals connected within network component. Survey Data: Complex survey designs stratification clustering. Difference--Differences: Especially staggered adoption units observed time (Cluster = Unit ID). Valid Inference: Prevents false positives caused intra-cluster correlation. Flexible Nuisance Control: Still allows use ML (XGBoost, RF) control high-dimensional confounders within clusters. Easy Implementation: DoubleML package, requires one additional argument (cluster_cols). Rule Thumb: 10,000 observations 10 clusters, Cluster Robust DML work well. asymptotic theory relies \(C \\infty\) (number clusters), \(N \\infty\). Generally, want least 30–50 clusters reliable inference. Imbalanced Clusters: cluster sizes vary wildly (e.g., one cluster 5 observations, another 5,000), variance estimation can become unstable. Computational Cost: Clustered cross-fitting can slightly slower clusters large, training/test splits less granular. DoubleML package provides DoubleMLClusterData, DoubleMLPLIV, simulator make_pliv_multiway_cluster_CKMS2021() Chiang et al. (2021) DGP. RCausalML implements thin, documented wrappers around DoubleML data backend R/DMLearner.R: doubleml_data_from_data_frame() (doubleml_data_from_matrix()) delegate DoubleML::double_ml_data_from_data_frame() / double_ml_data_from_matrix(). notebook constructs BLP analysis data doubleml_data_from_data_frame() workflow explicitly tied DMLearner.R; simulated CKMS2021 block still calls DoubleML’s generator directly (DGP duplicated RCausalML). tutorial covers: Following R packages required run notebook. packages installed, can install using code : RCausalML, DoubleML, mlr3, mlr3learners, hdm, ggplot2, reshape2, gridExtra, lgr use partially linear IV (PLIV) model data generating process Chiang et al. (2021). Data double-indexed: \(\{W_{ij}: =1,\ldots,N,\, j=1,\ldots,M\}\). text: data clustered, observations within cluster may correlated, violating ..d. assumption. example, panel dataset, errors may correlated within individuals time (one-way clustering), multi-dimensional setting, errors may correlated within two dimensions (e.g., firms markets) leading two-way clustering. Clustering affects DML two ways: Variance–covariance: Standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals must use cluster robust variance estimator (Cameron et al. 2011). Sample splitting: Standard cross-fitting put observations cluster train test folds, errors correlated across folds. Chiang et al. (2021) propose splitting cluster: two-way clustering \(K\) folds per dimension, data split \(K^2\) folds nuisance functions estimated clusters disjoint used evaluate score. Cluster Robust Double Machine Learning (Cluster Robust DML) extension standard Double Machine Learning framework designed data observations independent. standard DML, assumed every data point (row) independent identically distributed (..d.). However, many real-world datasets, observations grouped clusters (e.g., students within schools, patients within hospitals, firms within industries, repeated time periods individual). Within clusters, errors correlated. apply standard DML clustered data, standard errors underestimated, leading invalid confidence intervals false positives (Type errors). Cluster Robust DML fixes adjusting cross-fitting procedure variance estimation. Cluster Robust DML modifies two specific steps standard DML algorithm: standard DML, split data \(K\) folds randomly row. Cluster Robust DML, must split Cluster ID. Standard: Fold 1 might contain Student Classroom 1, Fold 2 might contain Student B Classroom 1. causes data leakage ML model learns information Classroom 1 Fold 1 predicts Fold 2. Cluster Robust: students Classroom 1 must fold. ensures nuisance models (\(\hat{g}, \hat{m}\)) trained completely independent clusters ones predicting . final step, calculating standard error \(\theta\), sum scores across individual observations. must aggregate scores cluster level first. Calculate orthogonal score \(\psi_i\) every observation. Sum scores within cluster: \(\Psi_c = \sum_{\\text{cluster } c} \psi_i\). Calculate variance based variation \(\Psi_c\) across clusters, \(\psi_i\) across observations. \[ \hat{\sigma}^2_{cluster} = \frac{1}{C(C-1)} \sum_{c=1}^{C} (\Psi_c - \bar{\Psi})^2 \] (\(C\) number clusters, observations) use variant whenever data hierarchical panel structure: Panel Data: Multiple time periods unit (Cluster = Individual ID). Multi-Site Experiments: Participants nested within locations (Cluster = Site ID). Network Data: Individuals connected within network component. Survey Data: Complex survey designs stratification clustering. Difference--Differences: Especially staggered adoption units observed time (Cluster = Unit ID). Valid Inference: Prevents false positives caused intra-cluster correlation. Flexible Nuisance Control: Still allows use ML (XGBoost, RF) control high-dimensional confounders within clusters. Easy Implementation: DoubleML package, requires one additional argument (cluster_cols). Rule Thumb: 10,000 observations 10 clusters, Cluster Robust DML work well. asymptotic theory relies \(C \\infty\) (number clusters), \(N \\infty\). Generally, want least 30–50 clusters reliable inference. Imbalanced Clusters: cluster sizes vary wildly (e.g., one cluster 5 observations, another 5,000), variance estimation can become unstable. Computational Cost: Clustered cross-fitting can slightly slower clusters large, training/test splits less granular.

what: Part 1: Two-Way Cluster Robust DML (Simulated Data)
text: use partially linear IV (PLIV) model data generating process Chiang et al. (2021). Data double-indexed: \(\{W_{ij}: =1,\ldots,N,\, j=1,\ldots,M\}\). Model: \[Y_{ij} = D_{ij} \theta_0 + g_0(X_{ij}) + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_{ij} \mid X_{ij}, Z_{ij}) = 0\] \[Z_{ij} = m_0(X_{ij}) + V_{ij}, \quad \mathbb{E}(V_{ij} \mid X_{ij}) = 0\] Errors covariates can correlated within dimension \(\), within dimension \(j\), (two-way clustering). DoubleML provides make_pliv_multiway_cluster_CKMS2021() generate data DGP. use default parameters (e.g. \(\theta=1\), \(N=M=25\), \(p_x=100\)). Cluster robust DML uses DoubleMLClusterData backend. Cluster variables specified construction (set later). object carries cluster information sample splitting variance estimation. set ML learners three nuisances (l, m, r) use \(K=3\) folds per cluster dimension, giving \(K^2=9\) folds total. output shows . folds: 9 (.e. \(3^2\)) Cluster variable(s): cluster_var_i, cluster_var_j. fit() uses cluster-based sample splitting; standard errors confidence intervals computed cluster robust variance estimator Chiang et al. (2021). estimate close true \(\theta_0 = 1\), reported standard errors p-values valid two-way clustering.

text: replicate consumer demand application Chiang et al. (2021) using Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes (1995) automobile data hdm package. outcome demand (y), treatment log price, use instruments covariates. Observations clustered product (model.id) market (cdid); compare clustering, one-way (product market), two-way clustering. use formula DoubleML documentation build design matrix instruments. use doubleml_data_from_data_frame() RCausalML R/DMLearner.R, wraps DoubleML::double_ml_data_from_data_frame(). Passing cluster_cols returns DoubleMLClusterData object. fit PLIV model four specifications store coefficients standard errors. cluster_cols = NULL, doubleml_data_from_data_frame() builds standard DoubleMLData object (DMLearner.R helper). Interpretation: price coefficient (effect log price demand) similar across specifications, standard errors increase account clustering. Two-way clustering yields largest standard errors allow correlation within products within markets. Inference ignores clustering anti-conservative.
code: data(BLP, package = "hdm") blp_data <- BLP$BLP blp_data$price <- blp_data$price + 11.761 blp_data$log_p <- log(blp_data$price) x_cols <- c("hpwt", "air", "mpd", "space") head(blp_data[x_cols]) iv_vars <- as.data.frame(hdm:::constructIV(blp_data$firm.id,                                            blp_data$cdid,                                            blp_data$id,                                            blp_data[x_cols]))  formula <- formula(paste0(" ~ -1 + (hpwt + air + mpd + space)^2",                          "+ I(hpwt^2)*(air + mpd + space)",                          "+ I(air^2)*(hpwt + mpd + space)",                          "+ I(mpd^2)*(hpwt + air + space)",                          "+ I(space^2)*(hpwt + air + mpd)",                          "+ I(space^2) + I(hpwt^3) + I(air^3) + I(mpd^3) + I(space^3)")) data_transf <- data.frame(model.matrix(formula, blp_data)) y_col <- "y" d_col <- "log_p" cluster_cols <- c("model.id", "cdid") all_z_cols <- c("sum.other.hpwt", "sum.other.mpd", "sum.other.space") z_col <- all_z_cols[1]  dml_df <- cbind(blp_data[c(y_col, d_col, cluster_cols)],                 data_transf,                 iv_vars[all_z_cols]) dml_data <- doubleml_data_from_data_frame(   dml_df,   y_col = y_col,   d_cols = d_col,   z_cols = z_col,   cluster_cols = cluster_cols,   x_cols = names(data_transf) ) stopifnot(!is.null(dml_data), inherits(dml_data, "DoubleMLClusterData")) print(dml_data) ================= DoubleMLClusterData Object ==================   ------------------ Data summary
