text: Ensemble learners pipelines allow us combine multiple machine learning algorithms preprocessing steps improve estimation nuisance functions DoubleML. using mlr3pipelines, can create complex workflows include feature engineering, multiple learners, tuning, wrapped single learner object DoubleML can use cross-fitting score computation. Key idea: mlr3pipelines defines pipeline (e.g., preprocessing → learner, multiple learners → average). pipeline converted Learner as_learner(), DoubleML uses like nuisance learner cross-fitting score computation.

R use mlr3 ecosystem machine learning pipelines, DoubleML package double machine learning estimation. Data backends PLR built RCausalML R/DMLearner.R: doubleml_data_from_matrix() (simulated PLR), doubleml_data_from_data_frame() (Bonus sample), doubleml_fetch_bonus() download Bonus data (DoubleML::fetch_bonus). single call fits PLR existing DoubleMLData object learners (including GraphLearner pipelines ensembles), use doubleml_plr_fit_data(); $tune() $fit(), use doubleml_plr_tune_data() (requires mlr3tuning). tutorial covers:

code: if (!requireNamespace("causaldata", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("causaldata") data(nsw_mixtape, package = "causaldata") df <- as.data.frame(nsw_mixtape) df$treat <- as.integer(df$treat) y_col <- "re78" t_col <- "treat" x_cols <- c("age", "educ", "black", "hisp", "marr", "nodegree", "re74", "re75") df <- df[complete.cases(df[, c(y_col, t_col, x_cols)]), ]  p_train <- 0.8 n <- nrow(df) idx <- sample.int(n, size = round(p_train * n)) df_train <- df[idx, ] df_val <- df[-idx, ]  X_train_raw <- as.matrix(df_train[, x_cols]) X_val_raw <- as.matrix(df_val[, x_cols]) cm <- colMeans(X_train_raw) cs <- apply(X_train_raw, 2, stats::sd) cs[cs == 0] <- 1 X_train <- scale(X_train_raw, center = cm, scale = cs) X_val <- scale(X_val_raw, center = cm, scale = cs)  t_train <- as.integer(df_train[[t_col]]) y_train <- as.numeric(df_train[[y_col]]) t_val <- as.integer(df_val[[t_col]]) y_val <- as.numeric(df_val[[y_col]])  cat(   "Train n =", nrow(X_train), "| Val n =", nrow(X_val),   "| p =", ncol(X_train), "| TARNet/CFRNet source: R/causalDeepNet.R\n" ) Train n = 356 | Val n = 89 | p = 8 | TARNet/CFRNet source: R/causalDeepNet.R

code: pred_ite_repr <- function(fit, Xm) {   r <- predict(fit, as.matrix(Xm))   if (is.list(r)) {     if (!is.null(r$ite)) return(as.numeric(r$ite))     if (!is.null(r$predictions)) return(as.numeric(r$predictions))     num_el <- r[sapply(r, is.numeric)]     if (length(num_el)) {       v <- as.numeric(unlist(num_el))       nr <- nrow(as.matrix(Xm))       if (length(v) >= nr) return(v[seq_len(nr)])     }     stop("Cannot extract ITE vector from predict() for this fit.")   }   as.numeric(r) }  repr_for_perm <- list(   TARNet = fit_tarnet,   CFRNet = fit_cfrnet )  imp_repr <- NULL if (nrow(X_val) >= 10L) {   p <- ncol(X_val)   feat_names <- colnames(X_val)   if (is.null(feat_names)) feat_names <- x_cols    n_rep <- 8L   set.seed(4343L)    imp_chunks <- vector("list", length(repr_for_perm))   names(imp_chunks) <- names(repr_for_perm)    for (lab in names(repr_for_perm)) {     fit_i <- repr_for_perm[[lab]]     ite_base <- pred_ite_repr(fit_i, X_val)     imp_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_rep, ncol = p)     for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {       for (j in seq_len(p)) {         Xp <- X_val         Xp[, j] <- sample(Xp[, j])         imp_mat[r, j] <- mean(abs(ite_base - pred_ite_repr(fit_i, Xp)), na.rm = TRUE)       }     }     imp_mean <- colMeans(imp_mat, na.rm = TRUE)     imp_chunks[[lab]] <- data.frame(       feature = feat_names,       importance = imp_mean,       model = lab,       stringsAsFactors = FALSE     )   }   imp_repr <- dplyr::bind_rows(imp_chunks)    n_facets <- length(repr_for_perm)   print(     ggplot2::ggplot(       imp_repr,       ggplot2::aes(         x = stats::reorder(factor(feature), importance),         y = importance       )     ) +       ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "#8F4CB3", width = 0.72) +       ggplot2::facet_wrap(~model, scales = "free_y", ncol = min(3L, n_facets)) +       ggplot2::coord_flip() +       ggplot2::labs(         title = "TARNet / CFRNet: permutation importance for predicted CATE (validation)",         subtitle = paste0("Mean |\u03c4\u0302(X) \u2212 \u03c4\u0302(X_perm)|; ", n_rep, " rounds per feature"),         x = NULL,         y = "Mean |\u0394 predicted ITE|"       ) +       ggplot2::theme_bw() +       ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"))   ) }

what: 5.1.3 DragonNet: Propensity-Adjusted Networks for Causal Inference
text: DragonNet introduced Shi, Blei & Veitch (2019) “Adapting Neural Networks Estimation Treatment Effects.” addresses fundamental weakness TARNet CFRNet: neither uses propensity score information guide representation learning. DragonNet deep learning architecture explicitly incorporates propensity score estimation training process. consists shared representation layer followed three separate heads: one predicting propensity score two predicting potential outcomes treatment control. key innovation targeted regularization term derived theory targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE), encourages model learn representations sufficient causal estimation. result model can achieve doubly-robust ATE estimation — meaning even either outcome model propensity model misspecified, ATE estimate remains consistent. shared representation Φ(x) feeds three heads:  propensity score e(x) = P(T=1 | X=x) probability unit receives treatment, given covariates. fundamental tool classical causal inference de-confounding observational data. key theoretical result behind DragonNet comes sufficient representation theorem (Shi et al., 2019): representation Φ(x) sufficient predicting propensity score, also sufficient estimating causal quantity. plain terms: don’t need capture X — need capture parts X relevant treatment assignment. variation X irrelevant noise causal estimation can discarded. much targeted form dimension reduction TARNet CFRNet apply. Step 1 — Shared backbone. patients passed shared deep network Φ(x), producing learned representation. structurally identical TARNet’s shared layer, training signal receives fundamentally different. Step 2 — Three-headed output. representation feeds three separate heads simultaneously: - \(g(\Phi(x))\) — propensity head, outputs sigmoid probability \(\hat{e}(x) = \hat{P}(T=1 \mid x)\). binary classifier trained treatment assignment. - \(Q_0(\Phi(x))\) — control outcome head - \(Q_1(\Phi(x))\) — treated outcome head Step 3 — Targeted regularization. DragonNet’s unique contribution. Rather just adding propensity prediction loss top, DragonNet applies targeted regularization term derived theory targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). regularizer nudges outcome predictions \(Q_0\) \(Q_1\) toward doubly robust — meaning even either outcome model propensity model slightly wrong, final ATE estimate remains consistent. Step 4 — Joint backpropagation. combined loss flows back three heads shared backbone simultaneously. propensity head outcome heads share Φ, backbone forced learn features predictive treatment assignment outcomes — targeted regularizer ensures features align causally necessary. Step 5 — ITE inference. \(\text{ITE}(x) = \hat{Q}_1(\Phi(x)) - \hat{Q}_0(\Phi(x))\). propensity head discarded — needed training shape representation. targeted regularization mathematically novel part. computes:  targeted regularization term derived doubly-robust (DR) ATE estimator: \[\widehat{\text{DR-ATE}} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{Q}_1 - \hat{Q}_0 + \frac{T(Y - \hat{Q}_1)}{\hat{e}(x)} - \frac{(1-T)(Y - \hat{Q}_0)}{1 - \hat{e}(x)}\right]\] two correction terms — IPW-weighted residuals — penalize network outcome predictions inconsistent propensity score. residuals zero, model achieved double robustness. targeted regularization adds quantity training loss small weight, gently steering backbone toward representations consistency holds. key practical advantage DragonNet CFRNet doesn’t need flatten entire representation distribution — forces representation capture propensity-relevant information, much surgical theoretically justified constraint. benchmarks like IHDP Jobs, DragonNet consistently matches outperforms CFRNet, especially low-data regimes -regularization IPM can hurt. fit DragonNet RCausalML::dragonnet() (R/causalDeepNet.R), uses torch available (Adam SGD, shared trunk, three heads, targeted regularization). use real-world dataset TARNet/CFRNet tutorial (NSW/Lalonde causaldata) consistency. ") Successfully loaded packages: print(search()[grepl("package:", search())]) [1] "package:future"       "package:xgboost"      "package:mlbench"       [4] "package:ForCausality" "package:torch"        "package:causaldata"    [7] "package:RCausalML"    "package:plyr"         "package:lubridate"    [10] "package:forcats"      "package:stringr"      "package:dplyr"        [13] "package:purrr"        "package:readr"        "package:tidyr"        [16] "package:tibble"       "package:ggplot2"      "package:tidyverse"    [19] "package:stats"        "package:graphics"     "package:grDevices"    [22] "package:utils"        "package:datasets"     "package:methods"      [25] "package:base" set.seed(42) torch_manual_seed(42) data(nsw_mixtape, package = "causaldata") df <- as.data.frame(nsw_mixtape) df$treat <- as.integer(df$treat)  y_col <- "re78" t_col <- "treat" x_cols <- c("age", "educ", "black", "hisp", "marr", "nodegree", "re74", "re75")  df <- df[complete.cases(df[, c(y_col, t_col, x_cols)]), ]  X <- as.matrix(df[, x_cols]) X <- scale(X)                    # standardize covariates (already in your code)  t_vec <- as.integer(df[[t_col]]) y_vec <- as.numeric(df[[y_col]])  # === NEW: Scale the outcome (critical for DragonNet stability) === y_mean <- mean(y_vec) y_sd   <- sd(y_vec) y_scaled <- (y_vec - y_mean) / y_sd  n <- nrow(X) input_dim <- ncol(X) cat("Sample size:", n, "| Covariates:", input_dim,      "| Treated:", sum(t_vec), "| Control:", sum(1L - t_vec), "

") DragonNet factual MSE (val): 31675688 # Propensity calibration dragon_res <- predict(fit_dn, X_val, propensity = TRUE) cat("Mean predicted propensity | T=0:",      round(mean(dragon_res$propensity[t_val == 0]), 3),     "| T=1:", round(mean(dragon_res$propensity[t_val == 1]), 3), "
") Mean predicted propensity | T=0: 0.43 | T=1: 0.439 # Helper function to safely extract predicted ITE / CATE pred_ite_mat <- function(Xm) {   r <- predict(fit_dn, Xm)      if (is.list(r)) {     # Common names returned by DragonNet / causal ML packages     if (!is.null(r$ite)) {       return(as.numeric(r$ite))     } else if (!is.null(r$predictions)) {       return(as.numeric(r$predictions))     } else if (!is.null(r$pred) || !is.null(r$cate)) {       return(as.numeric(r$pred %||% r$cate))     } else {       # fallback: take first numeric element       return(as.numeric(unlist(r[sapply(r, is.numeric)]))[1:length(nrow(Xm))])     }   } else {     return(as.numeric(r))   } }  # Main permutation importance ite_base <- pred_ite_mat(X_val)  p <- ncol(X_val) n_rep <- 8L set.seed(4343L)  imp_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_rep, ncol = p)  for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {   for (j in seq_len(p)) {     Xp <- X_val     Xp[, j] <- sample(Xp[, j])          # random permutation of column j     imp_mat[r, j] <- mean(abs(ite_base - pred_ite_mat(Xp)), na.rm = TRUE)   } }  imp_mean <- colMeans(imp_mat, na.rm = TRUE)  # Feature names feat_names <- colnames(X_val) if (is.null(feat_names)) {   feat_names <- paste0("X", seq_len(p))   # better fallback than relying on x_cols }  impdf <- data.frame(   feature   = feat_names,   importance = imp_mean,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) head(impdf) # Plot library(ggplot2)  ggplot(impdf, aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance)) +   geom_col(fill = "#1B998B", width = 0.72) +   coord_flip() +   labs(     title    = "DragonNet: Permutation Importance for Predicted CATE (Validation)",     subtitle = paste0(       "Mean |τ̂(X) − τ̂(X_perm)| per feature; ",       n_rep, " permutation rounds — descriptive of model surface"     ),     x = NULL,     y = "Mean |Δ predicted ITE|"   ) +   theme_bw() +   theme(     plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),     axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)   )

Step 2 — Three-headed output. representation feeds three separate heads simultaneously: - \(g(\Phi(x))\) — propensity head, outputs sigmoid probability \(\hat{e}(x) = \hat{P}(T=1 \mid x)\). binary classifier trained treatment assignment. - \(Q_0(\Phi(x))\) — control outcome head - \(Q_1(\Phi(x))\) — treated outcome head Step 3 — Targeted regularization. DragonNet’s unique contribution. Rather just adding propensity prediction loss top, DragonNet applies targeted regularization term derived theory targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). regularizer nudges outcome predictions \(Q_0\) \(Q_1\) toward doubly robust — meaning even either outcome model propensity model slightly wrong, final ATE estimate remains consistent. Step 4 — Joint backpropagation. combined loss flows back three heads shared backbone simultaneously. propensity head outcome heads share Φ, backbone forced learn features predictive treatment assignment outcomes — targeted regularizer ensures features align causally necessary. Step 5 — ITE inference. \(\text{ITE}(x) = \hat{Q}_1(\Phi(x)) - \hat{Q}_0(\Phi(x))\). propensity head discarded — needed training shape representation.

targeted regularization mathematically novel part. computes:  targeted regularization term derived doubly-robust (DR) ATE estimator: \[\widehat{\text{DR-ATE}} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{Q}_1 - \hat{Q}_0 + \frac{T(Y - \hat{Q}_1)}{\hat{e}(x)} - \frac{(1-T)(Y - \hat{Q}_0)}{1 - \hat{e}(x)}\right]\] two correction terms — IPW-weighted residuals — penalize network outcome predictions inconsistent propensity score. residuals zero, model achieved double robustness. targeted regularization adds quantity training loss small weight, gently steering backbone toward representations consistency holds.

key practical advantage DragonNet CFRNet doesn’t need flatten entire representation distribution — forces representation capture propensity-relevant information, much surgical theoretically justified constraint. benchmarks like IHDP Jobs, DragonNet consistently matches outperforms CFRNet, especially low-data regimes -regularization IPM can hurt.

") Final epsilon (targeted reg): 0.00194 dragon_res <- predict(fit_dn, X_val, propensity = TRUE) ite_val <- dragon_res$ite ate_val <- mean(ite_val) cat("DragonNet ATE (val):", round(ate_val, 2), "

") DragonNet factual MSE (val): 31675688 # Propensity calibration dragon_res <- predict(fit_dn, X_val, propensity = TRUE) cat("Mean predicted propensity | T=0:",      round(mean(dragon_res$propensity[t_val == 0]), 3),     "| T=1:", round(mean(dragon_res$propensity[t_val == 1]), 3), "
") Mean predicted propensity | T=0: 0.43 | T=1: 0.439 # Helper function to safely extract predicted ITE / CATE pred_ite_mat <- function(Xm) {   r <- predict(fit_dn, Xm)      if (is.list(r)) {     # Common names returned by DragonNet / causal ML packages     if (!is.null(r$ite)) {       return(as.numeric(r$ite))     } else if (!is.null(r$predictions)) {       return(as.numeric(r$predictions))     } else if (!is.null(r$pred) || !is.null(r$cate)) {       return(as.numeric(r$pred %||% r$cate))     } else {       # fallback: take first numeric element       return(as.numeric(unlist(r[sapply(r, is.numeric)]))[1:length(nrow(Xm))])     }   } else {     return(as.numeric(r))   } }  # Main permutation importance ite_base <- pred_ite_mat(X_val)  p <- ncol(X_val) n_rep <- 8L set.seed(4343L)  imp_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_rep, ncol = p)  for (r in seq_len(n_rep)) {   for (j in seq_len(p)) {     Xp <- X_val     Xp[, j] <- sample(Xp[, j])          # random permutation of column j     imp_mat[r, j] <- mean(abs(ite_base - pred_ite_mat(Xp)), na.rm = TRUE)   } }  imp_mean <- colMeans(imp_mat, na.rm = TRUE)  # Feature names feat_names <- colnames(X_val) if (is.null(feat_names)) {   feat_names <- paste0("X", seq_len(p))   # better fallback than relying on x_cols }  impdf <- data.frame(   feature   = feat_names,   importance = imp_mean,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) head(impdf) # Plot library(ggplot2)  ggplot(impdf, aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance)) +   geom_col(fill = "#1B998B", width = 0.72) +   coord_flip() +   labs(     title    = "DragonNet: Permutation Importance for Predicted CATE (Validation)",     subtitle = paste0(       "Mean |τ̂(X) − τ̂(X_perm)| per feature; ",       n_rep, " permutation rounds — descriptive of model surface"     ),     x = NULL,     y = "Mean |Δ predicted ITE|"   ) +   theme_bw() +   theme(     plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),     axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)   )

what: 5.1.4 GANITE: Generative Adversarial Network for Inference of Treatment Effects
text: GANITE (Yoon, Jordon, van der Schaar, 2018) estimates individual treatment effects (ITE) recasting counterfactual inference problem generative modeling task. core challenge addresses fundamental causal inference: individual, outcome treatment actually received ever observed, outcome alternative treatment remains counterfactual unknowable. Rather imputing single point estimate missing outcome, GANITE uses Generative Adversarial Network learn full distribution potential outcomes — capturing uncertainty remaining grounded observed data distribution. GANITE (Yoon, Jordon, van der Schaar, 2018) estimates individual treatment effects (ITE) recasting counterfactual inference generative modeling task. core challenge addresses fundamental causal inference: individual, outcome treatment actually received observable, outcome alternative treatment remains counterfactual unknowable. Rather imputing single point estimate missing outcome, GANITE uses two-block GAN learn full distribution potential outcomes — capturing epistemic uncertainty remaining grounded observed data distribution. potential outcomes framework, individual observe covariates \(X_i\), treatment \(T_i \\{0, 1\}\), factual outcome \(Y_i^F = Y_i(T_i)\). counterfactual outcome \(Y_i^{CF} = Y_i(1 - T_i)\) never observed. individual treatment effect therefore: \[\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\] Standard regression models impute single value missing \(Y_i^{CF}\). GANITE instead learns conditional generative model \(p(Y(0), Y(1) \mid X)\), potential outcomes uncertainty can sampled. GANITE cleanly separates two sub-problems: imputing missing counterfactuals (Block 1) estimating treatment effects completed data (Block 2). diagram shows GANITE’s overall two-block pipeline inputs ITE estimate.  Block 1 — counterfactual generator. generator \(G\) takes observed tuple \((X_i, T_i, Y_i^F)\) together noise vector \(Z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, )\) outputs imputed counterfactual \(\tilde{Y}_i^{CF}\). discriminator \(D\) trained distinguish real factual outcomes generator-imputed counterfactuals, forcing \(G\) produce counterfactuals indistinguishable distribution real outcomes. factual reconstruction term \(\mathcal{L}_\text{factual}\) anchors generator observed arm, preventing producing well-distributed causally meaningless imputations. Block 2 — ITE generator. Block 1 produced imputed counterfactuals every training individual, second generator \(\hat{G}\) trained now-complete dataset \(\{X_i, \tilde{Y}_i^{CF}, Y_i^F\}\). Unlike \(G\), takes covariates noise input — treatment factual outcome longer needed missing data problem resolved. second discriminator \(\hat{D}\) distinguishes \(\hat{G}\)’s joint outcome pairs Block 1 pairs, ensuring joint distribution \((Y(0), Y(1))\) respected rather just marginals independently. final ITE estimate averages multiple noise draws: \[\hat{\tau}_i = \mathbb{E}_Z[\hat{G}(X_i, Z)_1 - \hat{G}(X_i, Z)_0]\] Combined training objective: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_\text{GAN}^\text{Block 1} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_\text{factual} + \mathcal{L}_\text{GAN}^\text{Block 2}\] shows three loss terms combine direction gradient flow training.  GANITE encodes three standard causal assumptions architecture. assumes ignorability — \(T \perp (Y(0), Y(1)) \mid X\), meaning confounding captured observed covariates. enforces consistency factual reconstruction loss, requires \(\hat{Y}_i(T_i) \approx Y_i^F\). explicitly enforce overlap, adversarial training implicitly pressures generator produce plausible outcomes across treatment arms covariate values. One GANITE’s distinctive properties relative deterministic estimators like TARNet DragonNet native uncertainty quantification. generators stochastic, repeated forward passes \(\hat{G}\) yield distribution ITE estimates: \[\{\hat{\tau}_i^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K = \{\hat{G}(X_i, Z^{(k)})_1 - \hat{G}(X_i, Z^{(k)})_0\}_{k=1}^K\] distribution reflects genuine epistemic uncertainty unobservable counterfactual — merely variance model fitting. Point-estimate models provide without additional machinery bootstrapping conformal prediction. GANITE’s generative approach captures directly model’s output distribution. GANITE generative model captures uncertainty operating observed covariate space like TARNet, rather learning latent confounder structure. Assumptions: - Strong ignorability holds observed covariate space X - GAN generator expressive enough capture true distribution potential outcomes - Sufficient sample size train two coupled adversarial networks stably Limitations: - GAN training notoriously unstable — mode collapse, vanishing gradients, sensitivity hyperparameters practical concerns - two-block training sequential, meaning errors Block 1 (counterfactual imputation) propagate Block 2 (ITE estimation) mechanism correct - Evaluation difficult counterfactuals never observed; standard loss functions directly measure counterfactual accuracy real data - Computationally expensive relative simpler regression-based ITE estimators implement GANITE R using {RCausalML} package compare meta-learners (S, T, X, R) IHDP semi-synthetic dataset synthetic dataset hidden confounding. text: GANITE (Yoon, Jordon, van der Schaar, 2018) estimates individual treatment effects (ITE) recasting counterfactual inference generative modeling task. core challenge addresses fundamental causal inference: individual, outcome treatment actually received observable, outcome alternative treatment remains counterfactual unknowable. Rather imputing single point estimate missing outcome, GANITE uses two-block GAN learn full distribution potential outcomes — capturing epistemic uncertainty remaining grounded observed data distribution. potential outcomes framework, individual observe covariates \(X_i\), treatment \(T_i \\{0, 1\}\), factual outcome \(Y_i^F = Y_i(T_i)\). counterfactual outcome \(Y_i^{CF} = Y_i(1 - T_i)\) never observed. individual treatment effect therefore: \[\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\] Standard regression models impute single value missing \(Y_i^{CF}\). GANITE instead learns conditional generative model \(p(Y(0), Y(1) \mid X)\), potential outcomes uncertainty can sampled.

GANITE cleanly separates two sub-problems: imputing missing counterfactuals (Block 1) estimating treatment effects completed data (Block 2). diagram shows GANITE’s overall two-block pipeline inputs ITE estimate.  Block 1 — counterfactual generator. generator \(G\) takes observed tuple \((X_i, T_i, Y_i^F)\) together noise vector \(Z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, )\) outputs imputed counterfactual \(\tilde{Y}_i^{CF}\). discriminator \(D\) trained distinguish real factual outcomes generator-imputed counterfactuals, forcing \(G\) produce counterfactuals indistinguishable distribution real outcomes. factual reconstruction term \(\mathcal{L}_\text{factual}\) anchors generator observed arm, preventing producing well-distributed causally meaningless imputations. Block 2 — ITE generator. Block 1 produced imputed counterfactuals every training individual, second generator \(\hat{G}\) trained now-complete dataset \(\{X_i, \tilde{Y}_i^{CF}, Y_i^F\}\). Unlike \(G\), takes covariates noise input — treatment factual outcome longer needed missing data problem resolved. second discriminator \(\hat{D}\) distinguishes \(\hat{G}\)’s joint outcome pairs Block 1 pairs, ensuring joint distribution \((Y(0), Y(1))\) respected rather just marginals independently. final ITE estimate averages multiple noise draws: \[\hat{\tau}_i = \mathbb{E}_Z[\hat{G}(X_i, Z)_1 - \hat{G}(X_i, Z)_0]\] Combined training objective: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_\text{GAN}^\text{Block 1} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_\text{factual} + \mathcal{L}_\text{GAN}^\text{Block 2}\] shows three loss terms combine direction gradient flow training.  GANITE encodes three standard causal assumptions architecture. assumes ignorability — \(T \perp (Y(0), Y(1)) \mid X\), meaning confounding captured observed covariates. enforces consistency factual reconstruction loss, requires \(\hat{Y}_i(T_i) \approx Y_i^F\). explicitly enforce overlap, adversarial training implicitly pressures generator produce plausible outcomes across treatment arms covariate values.

One GANITE’s distinctive properties relative deterministic estimators like TARNet DragonNet native uncertainty quantification. generators stochastic, repeated forward passes \(\hat{G}\) yield distribution ITE estimates: \[\{\hat{\tau}_i^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K = \{\hat{G}(X_i, Z^{(k)})_1 - \hat{G}(X_i, Z^{(k)})_0\}_{k=1}^K\] distribution reflects genuine epistemic uncertainty unobservable counterfactual — merely variance model fitting. Point-estimate models provide without additional machinery bootstrapping conformal prediction. GANITE’s generative approach captures directly model’s output distribution. GANITE generative model captures uncertainty operating observed covariate space like TARNet, rather learning latent confounder structure. what: Fit GANITE on the IHDP dataset
text: fit GANITE semi-synthetic dataset compare performance meta-learners. Following original Python example, training uses nine IHDP files (ihdp_npci_1.csv ihdp_npci_9.csv), concatenated replicated 100 times, evaluation held-validation set. run_fast = TRUE, smaller replication factor used speed rendering. dataset follows standard IHDP column layout: treatment, y_factual, y_cfactual, mu0, mu1, 25 covariates. Covariates reordered binary features come first (indices 6–24 Python; columns 7–25 R), followed continuous features (indices 0–5 Python; columns 1–6 R). fit GANITE (torch available, else placeholder) training set predict ITE train validation. CUDA available, training runs GPU speed. run_fast TRUE, fewer iterations smaller network used faster rendering. fit propensity elastic net (like Python’s ElasticNetPropensityModel) S-, T-, X-, R-Learners ranger (Python uses LGBM). X- R-Learners use propensity scores. Build prediction data frame (S, T, X, R, GANITE, tau, w, y) compute ATE, MAE (vs. true τ), AUUC (mean normalized cumulative gain). plot cumulative gain.  metrics gain plot validation set.
code: base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uber/causalml/master/docs/examples/data" cols <- c("treatment", "y_factual", "y_cfactual", "mu0", "mu1", paste0("X", 0:24)) df <- NULL for (i in 1:9) {   url <- sprintf("%s/ihdp_npci_%d.csv", base_url, i)   tmp <- tryCatch({     read.csv(url, header = FALSE)   }, error = function(e) NULL)   if (!is.null(tmp) && nrow(tmp) > 0) {     colnames(tmp) <- cols[seq_len(ncol(tmp))]     if (is.null(df)) df <- tmp else df <- rbind(df, tmp)   } } if (!is.null(df) && nrow(df) > 0) {   replications <- if (run_fast) 2L else 10L   df <- do.call(rbind, replicate(replications, df, simplify = FALSE))   message("Loaded IHDP (all 9 files × ", replications, " replications): ", nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) } else {   df <- NULL }  if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) {   d <- synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 5000, p = 25, sigma = 1.0, adj = 0)   df <- as.data.frame(d$X)   colnames(df) <- paste0("X", 0:(ncol(df) - 1))   df$treatment <- d$w   df$y_factual <- d$y   df$y_cfactual <- ifelse(d$w == 1, d$b - 0.5 * d$tau, d$b + 0.5 * d$tau)   df$mu0 <- d$b - 0.5 * d$tau   df$mu1 <- d$b + 0.5 * d$tau   message("Using synthetic fallback: ", nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) }  # Feature order: binary first (Python indices 6-24 -> R columns 7-25), then continuous (0-5 -> 1-6) binfeats <- 7:25 contfeats <- 1:6 perm <- c(binfeats, contfeats) xcols <- paste0("X", 0:24) X <- as.matrix(df[, xcols][, perm]) treatment <- as.integer(df$treatment) y <- as.numeric(df$y_factual) y_cf <- as.numeric(df$y_cfactual) mu0 <- as.numeric(df$mu0) mu1 <- as.numeric(df$mu1) tau <- ifelse(df$treatment == 1, df$y_factual - df$y_cfactual, df$y_cfactual - df$y_factual)  # Train/validation split (80/20, random_state=1 like Python) n <- nrow(X) set.seed(1) ite <- sample(n, size = round(0.2 * n)) itr <- setdiff(seq_len(n), ite) X_train <- X[itr, ] treatment_train <- treatment[itr] y_train <- y[itr] tau_train <- tau[itr] mu_0_train <- mu0[itr] mu_1_train <- mu1[itr] X_val <- X[ite, ] treatment_val <- treatment[ite] y_val <- y[ite] tau_val <- tau[ite] cat("Train size:", length(itr), "| Val size:", length(ite), "\n") Train size: 10757 | Val size: 2689 gn <- ganite(X_train, treatment_train, y_train,               iterations = if (run_fast) 100L else 500L,               h_dim = if (run_fast) 25L else 50L,               batch_size = if (run_fast) 128L else 64L,               verbose = !run_fast, device = device_use) ite_train_ganite <- as.vector(predict(gn, X_train)) ite_val_ganite <- as.vector(predict(gn, X_val)) ate_train_ganite <- mean(ite_train_ganite) ate_val_ganite <- mean(ite_val_ganite) cat("GANITE — ATE (train):", round(ate_train_ganite, 4), "| ATE (val):", round(ate_val_ganite, 4), "\n") GANITE — ATE (train): -1.4695 | "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train) tl <- fit(TLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train) xl <- fit(XLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train, p = p_train) rl <- fit(RLearner(learner = "ranger", n_fold = n_fold_meta), X_train, treatment_train, y_train, p = p_train)  s_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(sl, X_train)) s_ite_val <- as.vector(predict(sl, X_val)) t_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(tl, X_train)) t_ite_val <- as.vector(predict(tl, X_val)) x_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(xl, X_train)) x_ite_val <- as.vector(predict(xl, X_val)) r_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(rl, X_train)) r_ite_val <- as.vector(predict(rl, X_val)) df_preds_train <- data.frame(   S = s_ite_train,   T = t_ite_train,   X = x_ite_train,   R = r_ite_train,   GANITE = ite_train_ganite,   tau = tau_train,   w = treatment_train,   y = y_train ) df_result_train <- data.frame(   Method = c("S", "T", "X", "R", "GANITE", "actual"),   ATE = c(     mean(s_ite_train), mean(t_ite_train), mean(x_ite_train), mean(r_ite_train),     ate_train_ganite, mean(tau_train)   ) ) tau_train_1d <- as.numeric(tau_train) df_result_train$MAE <- c(   mean(abs(s_ite_train - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(t_ite_train - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(x_ite_train - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(r_ite_train - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(ite_train_ganite - tau_train_1d)),   NA_real_ ) # AUUC = mean of normalized cumulative gain (like Python auuc_score) gain_train <- get_cumgain(df_preds_train, outcome_col = "y", treatment_col = "w",                          treatment_effect_col = "tau", normalize = TRUE) model_cols <- c("S", "T", "X", "R",  "GANITE", "tau") model_cols <- intersect(model_cols, colnames(gain_train)) auuc_train <- colMeans(gain_train[, model_cols, drop = FALSE]) df_result_train$AUUC <- NA_real_ for (m in names(auuc_train)) {   idx <- which(df_result_train$Method == if (m == "tau") "actual" else m) NA_real_ ) gain_val <- get_cumgain(df_preds_val, outcome_col = "y", treatment_col = "w",                        treatment_effect_col = "tau", normalize = TRUE) auuc_val <- colMeans(gain_val[, Standard causal methods condition X directly therefore fail fully eliminate confounding. CEVAE addresses learning Z data using Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework performing causal inference latent space. Methods TARNet, CFRNet, DragonNet, GANITE rely standard ignorability assumption — confounders observed X. practice rarely satisfied. patient’s true health status Z never fully measured; clinician sees noisy proxies blood pressure readings, laboratory values, clinical notes. Conditioning proxies Z leaves residual confounding biases causal estimates. CEVAE (Louizos et al., NeurIPS 2017) takes different approach: uses VAE infer latent confounder Z proxy measurements, trains causal model top inferred representation. Treatment outcome information fed encoder training, giving model every available signal disentangle underlying confounder measurement noise. standard potential outcomes setup, observe: X — proxy covariates (e.g., test scores, survey responses, clinical measurements) T — binary treatment indicator Y — observed outcome key assumption exists latent Z : \[T \perp Y(t) \mid Z \quad \text{(ignorability holds latent space)}\] necessarily \(T \perp Y(t) \mid X\). X imperfect, noisy measurement true confounder Z, conditioning X leaves residual bias. CEVAE recovers Z conditions instead. CEVAE specifies joint generative process observed variables, driven latent confounder Z: \[p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(0, )\] \[p(X \mid Z) = \prod_j p(x_j \mid Z) \quad \text{(factored, mixed likelihood)}\] \[p(T \mid Z) = \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma(f_T(Z))\right)\] \[p(Y \mid T, Z) = p(Y \mid T=0, Z)\cdot(1-T) + p(Y \mid T=1, Z)\cdot T\] \(f_T\) outcome distributions parameterized neural networks. outcome likelihood Gaussian continuous outcomes Bernoulli binary outcomes. Critically, T Y conditionally independent given Z, enforces ignorability assumption latent space. Z unobserved, CEVAE must infer data. defines variational posterior \[q(Z \mid X, T, Y) \approx p(Z \mid X, T, Y)\] implemented neural network takes observed variables input outputs parameters \((\mu_Z, \sigma_Z^2)\) Gaussian approximate posterior. Feeding treatment outcome encoder training allows model use available signal latent confounder. reparameterization trick makes end--end backpropagation stochastic Z samples possible. CEVAE trained maximizing Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), balances reconstruction fidelity regularization latent space: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q(Z|X,T,Y)}\!\left[\log p(X|Z) + \log p(T|Z) + \log p(Y|T,Z)\right] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(Z|X,T,Y) \,\|\, p(Z)\right)\] reconstruction terms ensure generative model explains observed data well. KL divergence regularizes Z toward unit Gaussian prior, preventing overfitting encouraging smooth, well-structured latent space. Optimizing objective jointly trains encoder decoder heads. trained, CEVAE estimates individual treatment effects (ITE) three-step procedure: Encode: given \((X_i, T_i, Y_i)\), sample \(Z_i \sim q(Z \mid X_i, T_i, Y_i)\) Predict potential outcomes: \(\hat{Y}_i(0) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T{=}0, Z_i]\) \(\hat{Y}_i(1) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T{=}1, Z_i]\) Estimate ITE: \(\hat{\tau}_i = \hat{Y}_i(1) - \hat{Y}_i(0)\) potential outcomes predicted inferred Z, gives CEVAE counterfactual coherence — factual counterfactual grounded underlying confounder estimate. figure illustrates full data flow CEVAE. left side shows inference path (encoder), right side shows generative path (decoder prediction heads). text: CEVAE deep generative model causal inference introduced Louizos et al. (2017). central insight many real-world settings observed covariates X true confounders — noisy proxies underlying latent variable Z simultaneously influences treatment assignment outcomes. Standard causal methods condition X directly therefore fail fully eliminate confounding. CEVAE addresses learning Z data using Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework performing causal inference latent space. Methods TARNet, CFRNet, DragonNet, GANITE rely standard ignorability assumption — confounders observed X. practice rarely satisfied. patient’s true health status Z never fully measured; clinician sees noisy proxies blood pressure readings, laboratory values, clinical notes. Conditioning proxies Z leaves residual confounding biases causal estimates. CEVAE (Louizos et al., NeurIPS 2017) takes different approach: uses VAE infer latent confounder Z proxy measurements, trains causal model top inferred representation. Treatment outcome information fed encoder training, giving model every available signal disentangle underlying confounder measurement noise. standard potential outcomes setup, observe: X — proxy covariates (e.g., test scores, survey responses, clinical measurements) T — binary treatment indicator Y — observed outcome key assumption exists latent Z : \[T \perp Y(t) \mid Z \quad \text{(ignorability holds latent space)}\] necessarily \(T \perp Y(t) \mid X\). X imperfect, noisy measurement true confounder Z, conditioning X leaves residual bias. CEVAE recovers Z conditions instead. CEVAE specifies joint generative process observed variables, driven latent confounder Z: \[p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(0, )\] \[p(X \mid Z) = \prod_j p(x_j \mid Z) \quad \text{(factored, mixed likelihood)}\] \[p(T \mid Z) = \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma(f_T(Z))\right)\] \[p(Y \mid T, Z) = p(Y \mid T=0, Z)\cdot(1-T) + p(Y \mid T=1, Z)\cdot T\] \(f_T\) outcome distributions parameterized neural networks. outcome likelihood Gaussian continuous outcomes Bernoulli binary outcomes. Critically, T Y conditionally independent given Z, enforces ignorability assumption latent space. Z unobserved, CEVAE must infer data. defines variational posterior \[q(Z \mid X, T, Y) \approx p(Z \mid X, T, Y)\] implemented neural network takes observed variables input outputs parameters \((\mu_Z, \sigma_Z^2)\) Gaussian approximate posterior. Feeding treatment outcome encoder training allows model use available signal latent confounder. reparameterization trick makes end--end backpropagation stochastic Z samples possible. CEVAE trained maximizing Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), balances reconstruction fidelity regularization latent space: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q(Z|X,T,Y)}\!\left[\log p(X|Z) + \log p(T|Z) + \log p(Y|T,Z)\right] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(Z|X,T,Y) \,\|\, p(Z)\right)\] reconstruction terms ensure generative model explains observed data well. KL divergence regularizes Z toward unit Gaussian prior, preventing overfitting encouraging smooth, well-structured latent space. Optimizing objective jointly trains encoder decoder heads. trained, CEVAE estimates individual treatment effects (ITE) three-step procedure: Encode: given \((X_i, T_i, Y_i)\), sample \(Z_i \sim q(Z \mid X_i, T_i, Y_i)\) Predict potential outcomes: \(\hat{Y}_i(0) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T{=}0, Z_i]\) \(\hat{Y}_i(1) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T{=}1, Z_i]\) Estimate ITE: \(\hat{\tau}_i = \hat{Y}_i(1) - \hat{Y}_i(0)\) potential outcomes predicted inferred Z, gives CEVAE counterfactual coherence — factual counterfactual grounded underlying confounder estimate. figure illustrates full data flow CEVAE. left side shows inference path (encoder), right side shows generative path (decoder prediction heads).  CEVAE strictly general confounding assumptions. trade-harder train, sensitive generative model misspecification, computationally heavier discriminative approaches TARNet. Assumptions: Ignorability holds latent space Z, necessarily X generative model structure (way Z produces X, T, Y) correctly specified variational posterior approximation sufficiently flexible Practical limitations: Sensitive choice decoder architecture X — misspecifying \(p(X \mid Z)\) can corrupt inferred Z Identifiability Z guaranteed general; structured causal graph helps anchor latent space, guarantee Harder train stably TARNet CFRNet, especially small datasets Counterfactual quality depends well encoder separates confounding signal measurement noise X Subsequent work refined extended CEVAE framework: DCEVAE disentangles latent space components independent treatment versus correlated , improving counterfactual generation quality. See ojs.aaai.org details. VCI (Variational Causal Inference) argues vanilla CEVAE formulation fully aligned Pearl’s counterfactual semantics, proposes stricter framework disentangled exogenous noise abduction — particularly important high-dimensional outcomes gene expression profiles. See arxiv.org full treatment. primary limitation shared approaches X must sufficiently informative Z allow reliable recovery. proxy measurements weak, confounder posterior poorly identified causal estimates degrade.

what: Fitting CEVAE on the IHDP Dataset (semi-synthetic)
text: first benchmark CEVAE Infant Health Development Program (IHDP) dataset, widely used semi-synthetic benchmark treatment effect estimation. dataset simulates randomized early childhood intervention augments real-world covariates simulated potential outcomes, giving us access ground-truth individual treatment effects. load nine IHDP replication files (ihdp_npci_1.csv ihdp_npci_9.csv) CausalML repository concatenate . combined dataset replicated match scale used original CEVAE experiments (Louizos et al., 2017). Columns follow standard IHDP convention: treatment, y_factual, y_cfactual, mu0, mu1, 25 covariates. Covariates reordered binary features come first (Python indices 6–24; R columns 7–25), followed continuous features (Python indices 0–5; R columns 1–6), matching feature ordering Python CausalML CEVAE example. fit CEVAE training set obtain ITE predictions training validation splits. run_fast = TRUE, use smaller networks, fewer epochs, single deterministic prediction pass rapid rendering. Setting run_fast = FALSE switches full hyperparameter configuration Louizos et al. (2017) — 200-unit hidden layers, 20-dimensional latent space, 100 Monte Carlo samples per prediction. comparison, fit propensity scores elastic net regularization (matching Python’s ElasticNetPropensityModel) four meta-learners — S-, T-, X-, R-Learners — using random forest (ranger) base learner (Python uses LightGBM). X- R-Learners additionally receive estimated propensity scores. assemble prediction data frame compute ATE, MAE (relative ground-truth \(\tau\)), AUUC (area uplift curve, normalized) models. plot cumulative gain curve. Training set: ATE, MAE, AUUC method  repeat evaluation held-validation set assess generalization. Validation set: ATE, MAE, AUUC method
code: base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uber/causalml/master/docs/examples/data" cols <- c("treatment", "y_factual", "y_cfactual", "mu0", "mu1", paste0("X", 0:24)) df <- NULL for (i in 1:9) {   url <- sprintf("%s/ihdp_npci_%d.csv", base_url, i)   tmp <- tryCatch({     read.csv(url, header = FALSE)   }, error = function(e) NULL)   if (!is.null(tmp) && nrow(tmp) > 0) {     colnames(tmp) <- cols[seq_len(ncol(tmp))]     if (is.null(df)) df <- tmp else df <- rbind(df, tmp)   } } if (!is.null(df) && nrow(df) > 0) {   replications <- if (run_fast) 2L else 10L   df <- do.call(rbind, replicate(replications, df, simplify = FALSE))   message("Loaded IHDP (all 9 files × ", replications, " replications): ",           nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) } else {   df <- NULL }  # Fallback to a synthetic dataset if the IHDP files cannot be downloaded if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) {   d <- synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 5000, p = 25, sigma = 1.0, adj = 0)   df <- as.data.frame(d$X)   colnames(df) <- paste0("X", 0:(ncol(df) - 1))   df$treatment  <- d$w   df$y_factual  <- d$y   df$y_cfactual <- ifelse(d$w == 1, d$b - 0.5 * d$tau, d$b + 0.5 * d$tau)   df$mu0        <- d$b - 0.5 * d$tau   df$mu1        <- d$b + 0.5 * d$tau   message("Using synthetic fallback: ", nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) }  # Feature ordering: binary first, continuous second (matches the Python example) binfeats  <- 7:25 contfeats <- 1:6 perm      <- c(binfeats, contfeats) xcols     <- paste0("X", 0:24) X         <- as.matrix(df[, xcols][, perm]) treatment <- as.integer(df$treatment) y         <- as.numeric(df$y_factual) y_cf      <- as.numeric(df$y_cfactual) mu0       <- as.numeric(df$mu0) mu1       <- as.numeric(df$mu1) tau       <- ifelse(df$treatment == 1,                     df$y_factual - df$y_cfactual,                     df$y_cfactual - df$y_factual)  # 80/20 train–validation split (random_state = 1, matching the Python example) n <- nrow(X) set.seed(1) ite <- sample(n, size = round(0.2 * n)) itr <- setdiff(seq_len(n), ite)  X_train         <- X[itr, ]; X_val       <- X[ite, ] treatment_train <- treatment[itr]; treatment_val <- treatment[ite] y_train         <- y[itr];   y_val       <- y[ite] tau_train       <- tau[itr]; tau_val     <- tau[ite] mu_0_train      <- mu0[itr]; mu_1_train  <- mu1[itr]  cat("Train size:", length(itr), "| Val size:", length(ite), "\n") Train size: 10757 | Val size: 2689 n_samp_pred <- if (run_fast) 1L else 100L  # 1 = deterministic; >1 = MC averaging  cv <- cevae(   X_train, treatment_train, y_train,   device     = device_use,   num_epochs = if (run_fast) 10L else 50L,   num_samples= if (run_fast) 20L else 1000L,   batch_size = if (run_fast) 256L else 100L,   hidden_dim = if (run_fast) 64L else 200L,   num_layers = if (run_fast) 2L else 3L,   latent_dim = if (run_fast) 10L else 20L,   verbose    = !run_fast )  ite_train_cevae <- predict(cv, X_train, num_samples = n_samp_pred) ite_val_cevae   <- predict(cv, X_val,   num_samples = n_samp_pred)  if (is.matrix(ite_train_cevae)) ite_train_cevae <- ite_train_cevae[, 1] if (is.matrix(ite_val_cevae))   ite_val_cevae   <- ite_val_cevae[, 1]  ate_train_cevae <- mean(ite_train_cevae) ate_val_cevae   <- mean(ite_val_cevae)  cat("CEVAE — ATE (train):", round(ate_train_cevae, 4),     "| ATE (val):",         round(ate_val_cevae,   4), "\n") CEVAE — ATE (train): -1.1218 | ATE (val): -1.0867 p_train <- propensity_glmnet(X_train, treatment_train) p_val   <- propensity_glmnet(X_val,   treatment_val)  n_fold_meta <- if (run_fast) 3L else 5L  sl <- fit(SLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train) tl <- fit(TLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train) xl <- fit(XLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train, p = p_train) rl <- fit(RLearner(learner = "ranger", n_fold = n_fold_meta),           X_train, treatment_train, y_train, p = p_train)  s_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(sl, X_train)) s_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(sl, X_val)) t_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(tl, X_train)) t_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(tl, X_val)) x_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(xl, X_train)) x_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(xl, X_val)) r_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(rl, X_train)) r_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(rl, X_val)) df_preds_train <- data.frame(   S     = s_ite_train,   T     = t_ite_train,   X     = x_ite_train,   R     = r_ite_train,   CEVAE = ite_train_cevae,   tau   = tau_train,   w     = treatment_train,   y     = y_train ) df_result_train <- data.frame(   Method = c("S", "T", "X", "R", "CEVAE", "actual"),   ATE    = c(mean(s_ite_train), mean(t_ite_train), mean(x_ite_train),              mean(r_ite_train), ate_train_cevae, mean(tau_train)) ) tau_train_1d <- as.numeric(tau_train) df_result_train$MAE <- c(   mean(abs(s_ite_train   - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(t_ite_train   - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(x_ite_train   - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(r_ite_train   - tau_train_1d)),   mean(abs(ite_train_cevae - tau_train_1d)),   NA_real_ )  gain_train  <- get_cumgain(df_preds_train, outcome_col = "y",                            treatment_col = "w", treatment_effect_col = "tau",                            normalize = TRUE) model_cols  <- intersect(c("S", "T", "X", "R", "CEVAE", "tau"),                          colnames(gain_train)) auuc_train  <- colMeans(gain_train[, model_cols, drop = FALSE])  df_result_train$AUUC <- NA_real_ for (m in names(auuc_train)) {   idx <- which(df_result_train$Method == if (m == "tau") "actual" else m)   if (length(idx)) df_result_train$AUUC[idx] <- auuc_train[m] } knitr::kable(df_result_train, digits = 4,              caption = "Training set: ATE, MAE, and AUUC by method") plot_gain(df_preds_train, outcome_col = "y", treatment_col = "w",           treatment_effect_col = "tau",           model_cols = c("S", "T", "X", "R", "CEVAE", "tau"),           main = "Cumulative gain — training set", normalize = TRUE) df_preds_val <- data.frame(   S     = s_ite_val,   T     = t_ite_val,   X     = x_ite_val,   R     = r_ite_val,   CEVAE = ite_val_cevae,   tau   = tau_val,   w     = treatment_val,   y     = y_val ) df_result_val <- data.frame(   Method = c("S", "T", "X", "R", "CEVAE", "actual"),   ATE    = c(mean(s_ite_val), mean(t_ite_val), mean(x_ite_val),              mean(r_ite_val), ate_val_cevae, mean(tau_val)) ) tau_val_1d <- as.numeric(tau_val) df_result_val$MAE <- c(   mean(abs(s_ite_val   - tau_val_1d)),   mean(abs(t_ite_val   - tau_val_1d)),   mean(abs(x_ite_val   - tau_val_1d)),   mean(abs(r_ite_val   - tau_val_1d)),   mean(abs(ite_val_cevae - tau_val_1d)),   NA_real_ )  gain_val   <- get_cumgain(df_preds_val, outcome_col = "y",                           treatment_col = "w", treatment_effect_col = "tau",                           normalize = TRUE) auuc_val   <- colMeans(gain_val[, model_cols, drop = FALSE])  df_result_val$AUUC <- NA_real_ for (m in names(auuc_val)) {   idx <- which(df_result_val$Method == if (m == "tau") "actual" else m)   if (length(idx)) df_result_val$AUUC[idx] <- auuc_val[m] } knitr::kable(df_result_val, digits = 4,              caption = "Validation set: ATE, MAE, and AUUC by method") plot_gain(df_preds_val, outcome_col = "y", treatment_col = "w",           treatment_effect_col = "tau",           model_cols = c("S", "T", "X", "R", "CEVAE", "tau"),           main = "Cumulative gain — validation set", normalize = TRUE)

1))   df$treatment  <- d$w   df$y_factual  <- d$y   df$y_cfactual <- ifelse(d$w == 1, d$b - 0.5 * d$tau, d$b + 0.5 * d$tau)   df$mu0        <- d$b - 0.5 * d$tau   df$mu1        <- d$b + 0.5 * d$tau   message("Using synthetic fallback: ", nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) }  # Feature ordering: binary first, continuous second (matches the Python example) binfeats  <- 7:25 contfeats <- 1:6 perm      <- c(binfeats, contfeats) xcols     <- paste0("X", 0:24) X         <- as.matrix(df[, xcols][, perm]) treatment <- as.integer(df$treatment) y         <- as.numeric(df$y_factual) y_cf      <- as.numeric(df$y_cfactual) mu0       <- as.numeric(df$mu0) mu1       <- as.numeric(df$mu1) tau       <- ifelse(df$treatment == 1,                     df$y_factual - df$y_cfactual,                     df$y_cfactual - df$y_factual)  # 80/20 train–validation split (random_state = 1, matching the Python example) n <- nrow(X) set.seed(1) ite <- sample(n, size = round(0.2 * n)) itr <- setdiff(seq_len(n), ite)  X_train         <- X[itr, ]; X_val       <- X[ite, ] treatment_train <- treatment[itr]; treatment_val <- treatment[ite] y_train         <- y[itr];   y_val       <- y[ite] tau_train       <- tau[itr]; tau_val     <- tau[ite] mu_0_train      <- mu0[itr]; mu_1_train  <- mu1[itr]  cat("Train size:", length(itr), "| Val size:", length(ite), "\n") Train size: 10757 | Val size: 2689

text: fit CEVAE training set obtain ITE predictions training validation splits. run_fast = TRUE, use smaller networks, fewer epochs, single deterministic prediction pass rapid rendering. Setting run_fast = FALSE switches full hyperparameter configuration Louizos et al. (2017) — 200-unit hidden layers, 20-dimensional latent space, 100 Monte Carlo samples per prediction.
code: n_samp_pred <- if (run_fast) 1L else 100L  # 1 = deterministic; >1 = MC averaging  cv <- cevae(   X_train, treatment_train, y_train,   device     = device_use,   num_epochs = if (run_fast) 10L else 50L,   num_samples= if (run_fast) 20L else 1000L,   batch_size = if (run_fast) 256L else 100L,   hidden_dim = if (run_fast) 64L else 200L,   num_layers = if (run_fast) 2L else 3L,   latent_dim = if (run_fast) 10L else 20L,   verbose    = !run_fast )  ite_train_cevae <- predict(cv, X_train, num_samples = n_samp_pred) ite_val_cevae   <- predict(cv, X_val,   num_samples = n_samp_pred)  if (is.matrix(ite_train_cevae)) ite_train_cevae <- ite_train_cevae[, 1] if (is.matrix(ite_val_cevae))   ite_val_cevae   <- ite_val_cevae[, 1]  ate_train_cevae <- mean(ite_train_cevae) ate_val_cevae   <- mean(ite_val_cevae)  cat("CEVAE — ATE (train):", round(ate_train_cevae, 4),     "| ATE (val):",         round(ate_val_cevae,   4), "\n") CEVAE — ATE (train): -1.1218 | ATE (val): -1.0867

text: comparison, fit propensity scores elastic net regularization (matching Python’s ElasticNetPropensityModel) four meta-learners — S-, T-, X-, R-Learners — using random forest (ranger) base learner (Python uses LightGBM). X- R-Learners additionally receive estimated propensity scores.
code: p_train <- propensity_glmnet(X_train, treatment_train) p_val   <- propensity_glmnet(X_val,   treatment_val)  n_fold_meta <- if (run_fast) 3L else 5L  sl <- fit(SLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train) tl <- fit(TLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train) xl <- fit(XLearner(learner = "ranger"), X_train, treatment_train, y_train, p = p_train) rl <- fit(RLearner(learner = "ranger", n_fold = n_fold_meta),           X_train, treatment_train, y_train, p = p_train)  s_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(sl, X_train)) s_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(sl, X_val)) t_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(tl, X_train)) t_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(tl, X_val)) x_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(xl, X_train)) x_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(xl, X_val)) r_ite_train <- as.vector(predict(rl, X_train)) r_ite_val   <- as.vector(predict(rl, X_val))

what: Fitting CEVAE on a Synthetic Dataset with Hidden Confounding
text: IHDP benchmark involves semi-synthetic outcomes layered onto real covariates. stress-test CEVAE setting proxy-confounder structure known design, use simulate_hidden_confounder(), generates data generating process observed X explicitly constructed noisy proxies underlying latent confounder. generate dataset simulate_hidden_confounder(n, p = 5, sigma = 1.0, adj = 0) compare S-, T-, X-, R-Learners (linear random forest base learners) CEVAE. mirrors Python CausalML example, uses linear regression XGBoost base learners. Summary metrics include ATE, MSE, absolute percentage error ATE, AUUC; results reported training validation splits. Synthetic training set: ATE, MSE, Abs % Error ATE, AUUC Synthetic validation set: ATE, MSE, Abs % Error ATE, AUUC
code:

text: training loop implements several practical stability measures: LR warmup (first 10 epochs): optimizer starts fraction target learning rate ramps linearly, preventing large early updates disrupting nascent causal structure. Capped gamma schedule: DAG penalty weight \(\gamma\) introduced gradually first 50 epochs capped 0.35, preventing acyclicity constraint overwhelming reconstruction early training. Gradient clipping (max norm 0.5): prevents gradient explosions, especially common matrix exponential \(h()\) produces large gradients. NaN/Inf detection: batches numerically unstable losses skipped rather allowed corrupt model weights. Early stopping: training halts 10 epochs validation loss stops improving, best checkpoint restored end.

") Treatment prevalence — train: 0.184 | val: 0.196 # Standardize continuous covariates (cols 20–25 in the permuted matrix, # corresponding to the original continuous features X0–X5). # Binary covariates (cols 1–19) are left unchanged. preprocess_features <- function(train_x, test_x) {   scaled_train <- train_x   scaled_test  <- test_x   cont_cols    <- 20:25   means <- colMeans(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE])   sds   <- apply(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)   sds[sds == 0] <- 1   scaled_train[, cont_cols] <- scale(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE],                                      center = means, scale = sds)   scaled_test[, cont_cols]  <- scale(test_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE],                                      center = means, scale = sds)   list(train_x = scaled_train, test_x = scaled_test, means = means, sds = sds) }  # Random subsampling with reproducible seed — keeps training times manageable # while preserving the treatment ratio approximately. build_training_arrays <- function(x, t, y, subsample = 5000L, seed = 42L) {   set.seed(seed)   idx <- sample.int(nrow(x), size = min(subsample, nrow(x)), replace = FALSE)   list(x = x[idx, , drop = FALSE],        t = as.numeric(t[idx]),        y = as.numeric(y[idx]),        idx = idx) }  # ATE and ITE evaluation against known potential outcomes. # Returns ATE bias, absolute ATE error, and sqrt(PEHE) — # the three metrics most commonly reported in the IHDP literature. estimate_ate_cdvae <- function(model, x_eval, mu0_true, mu1_true) {   y0_hat   <- predict(model, x_eval, type = "mu0")   y1_hat   <- predict(model, x_eval, type = "mu1")   ite_hat  <- y1_hat - y0_hat   ite_true <- mu1_true - mu0_true   ate_pred <- mean(ite_hat)   ate_true <- mean(ite_true)   list(     ite_hat   = ite_hat,     ite_true  = ite_true,     ate_pred  = ate_pred,     ate_true  = ate_true,     ate_bias  = ate_pred - ate_true,     ate_error = abs(ate_true - ate_pred),     pehe      = sqrt(mean((ite_hat - ite_true)^2))   ) }  # Plot all four loss components over training epochs on a log scale. # A healthy run sees reconstruction and KL decline steadily while MMD # converges toward zero, confirming causal alignment is improving. plot_training_history_cdvae <- function(history) {   h <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(history$train), function(i) {     as.data.frame(history$train[[i]]) |> dplyr::mutate(epoch = i)   }))   h_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(h, cols = c(total, kl, mmd),                                 names_to = "component", values_to = "value")   ggplot(h_long, aes(epoch, value, color = component)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +     scale_y_log10() +     facet_wrap(~component, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +     labs(title = "CD-VAE: training loss components (log scale)",          x = "Epoch", y = "Loss") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "none") }  # MMD-only convergence plot — separating this out makes it easy to see # whether causal alignment has stabilized before reconstruction has. plot_mmd_convergence_cdvae <- function(history) {   h <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(history$train), function(i) {     as.data.frame(history$train[[i]]) |> dplyr::mutate(epoch = i)   }))   ggplot(h, aes(epoch, mmd)) +     geom_line(color = "#993556", linewidth = 0.9) +     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",                color = "gray60", linewidth = 0.5) +     labs(title = "MMD causal alignment convergence",          x = "Epoch", y = "MMD") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) }  # Latent space PCA: color by treatment group. # In a well-trained CD-VAE the two groups should overlap substantially — # the MMD penalty has removed the statistical separation that raw covariates show. plot_latent_space_cdvae <- function(model, x_data, t_data,                                     title = "Latent space (PCA)") {   z_mu <- predict(model, x_data, type = "latent")   pc   <- prcomp(z_mu, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)   z2   <- pc$x[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]   dfz  <- data.frame(     PC1       = z2[, 1],     PC2       = z2[, 2],     treatment = factor(t_data, levels = c(0, 1),                        labels = c("Control", "Treated"))   )   ggplot(dfz, aes(PC1, PC2, color = treatment)) +     geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) +     scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#185FA5", "Treated" = "#993C1D")) +     labs(title = title, x = "PC1", y = "PC2", color = "") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "top") }  # ITE scatter and distribution comparison. plot_ite_analysis_cdvae <- function(ite_hat, ite_true, ate_pred, ate_true) {   df <- data.frame(ite_true = ite_true, ite_hat = ite_hat)   p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(ite_true, ite_hat)) +     geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.0, color = "#534AB7") +     geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,                 linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +     geom_hline(yintercept = ate_pred, linetype = "dotted",                color = "#BA7517", linewidth = 0.7) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dotted",                color = "#0F6E56", linewidth = 0.7) +     annotate("text", x = min(ite_true) + 0.1, y = ate_pred + 0.05,              label = sprintf("Pred ATE = %.3f", ate_pred),              hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#BA7517") +     annotate("text", x = ate_true + 0.05, y = max(ite_hat) - 0.1,              label = sprintf("True ATE = %.3f", ate_true),              hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#0F6E56") +     labs(title = "Predicted vs true ITE",          x = "True ITE", y = "Predicted ITE") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11)    dfh <- dplyr::bind_rows(     data.frame(value = ite_true, type = "True ITE"),     data.frame(value = ite_hat,  type = "Predicted ITE")   )   p2 <- ggplot(dfh, aes(value, fill = type)) +     geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.5, bins = 40) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dashed",                color = "#0F6E56", linewidth = 0.7) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_pred, linetype = "dashed",                color = "#993C1D", linewidth = 0.7) +     scale_fill_manual(values = c("True ITE" = "#185FA5",                                  "Predicted ITE" = "#993C1D")) +     labs(title = "ITE distribution",          x = "ITE", y = "Count", fill = "") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "top")    list(scatter = p1, hist = p2) } # what: Where CD-VAE Fits in the Causal VAE Family
text: series covered four increasingly expressive models. Understanding CD-VAE fits clarifies use . core trade-supervision richness versus data requirements. CEVAE, iVAE, CausalVAE work purely observational data (plus partial graph knowledge CausalVAE). CD-VAE requires real interventional data gains much direct robust training signal return. real experimental data exists — Perturb-Seq studies, randomized trials, /B tests — CD-VAE grounded option family.

Variational Autoencoder learns encode data \(x\) latent representation \(z\) reconstruct , optimizing Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}\!\left[\log p_\theta(x|z)\right] - D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z|x) \,\|\, p(z)\right)\] first term rewards faithful reconstruction; second regularizes posterior toward standard Gaussian prior. works well generative modelling, notion causality — latent space organizes information statistical co-occurrence, causal mechanism.

what: The Causal Extension: Adding the MMD Penalty
text: CD-VAE augments ELBO third term measures closely model’s predicted response virtual intervention matches observed response real one: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{CD-VAE}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}} - \lambda \cdot \text{MMD}\!\left(\hat{p}_{\text{int}},\, p_{\text{int}}\right)\] \(\hat{p}_{\text{int}}\) model’s predicted post-intervention distribution \(p_{\text{int}}\) distribution actually observed real intervention. parameter \(\lambda\) controls strength causal alignment. \(\lambda = 0\) model reduces standard VAE; \(\lambda\) increases model devotes capacity making causal predictions faithful real experimental data.

CD-VAE architecture: encoder, decoder, virtual intervention mechanism, MMD alignment real interventional data. virtual intervention mechanism — latent modification produces predicted interventional distribution — distinctive part CD-VAE worth showing separately.  Virtual intervention latent space: latent modification produces predicted interventional distribution compared observed outcomes via MMD.

MMD kernel-based distance two probability distributions. Given samples distributions \(P\) \(Q\), compares mean embeddings Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS): \[\text{MMD}^2(P, Q) = \left\|\, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[\phi(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{y \sim Q}[\phi(y)] \,\right\|^2_{\mathcal{H}}\] Using kernel trick kernel \(k\) (typically mixture RBF/Gaussian kernels multiple bandwidths), expands sum three kernel expectations: \[\text{MMD}^2(P, Q) = \mathbb{E}_{x,x' \sim P}[k(x,x')] - 2\,\mathbb{E}_{x \sim P,\, y \sim Q}[k(x,y)] + \mathbb{E}_{y,y' \sim Q}[k(y,y')]\] Using mixture kernels rather single one makes estimator robust scale differences across dimensions — important practical consideration two distributions compared live high-dimensional gene expression covariate space.

what: Virtual Interventions in the Latent Space
text: “causal” part CD-VAE relies -calculus intuition. virtual intervention \(\text{}(X_i = v)\) simulated : Encoding unperturbed observation \(x\) latent space: \(z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)\) Modifying specific latent dimension learned intervention subspace corresponding feature \(\) — virtual perturbation \(\tilde{z}\) Decoding modified \(\tilde{z}\) back observation space produce \(\hat{x}_{\text{int}}\) predicted post-intervention distribution \(\hat{p}_{\text{int}}\) compared real distribution \(p_{\text{int}}\) observed experiment using MMD. MMD differentiable, gradient discrepancy flows back decoder, intervention, encoder — forcing latent space organize way makes causal predictions accurate, just reconstructions faithful.

\[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}\!\left[\log p_\theta(x|z)\right]}_{\text{reconstruction}} - \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z|x) \,\|\, p(z)\right)}_{\text{latent regularization}} - \underbrace{\lambda \sum_k \text{MMD}\!\left(\hat{p}_{\text{int}}^{(k)},\, p_{\text{int}}^{(k)}\right)}_{\text{causal discrepancy penalty}} - \underbrace{\lambda_Y \,\mathcal{L}_{\text{outcome}}}_{\text{outcome head}}\] sum \(k\) runs intervention conditions training data (e.g., distinct gene knockout treatment arm). term checks: intervention \(k\), model’s simulation match observed response? outcome head \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{outcome}}\) MSE loss trains separate prediction network \(Y\) given \(z\) \(T\), enabling ATE estimation inference time. Strengths: CD-VAE leverages real interventional data direct supervisory signal, causal VAEs lack entirely. base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uber/causalml/master/docs/examples/data" cols <- c("treatment", "y_factual", "y_cfactual", "mu0", "mu1", paste0("X", 0:24)) df <- NULL for (i in 1:9) {   url <- sprintf("%s/ihdp_npci_%d.csv", base_url, i)   tmp <- tryCatch(read.csv(url, header = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)   if (!is.null(tmp) && nrow(tmp) > 0) {     colnames(tmp) <- cols[seq_len(ncol(tmp))]     df <- if (is.null(df)) tmp else rbind(df, tmp)   } }  if (!is.null(df) && nrow(df) > 0) {   replications <- if (run_fast) 2L else 10L   df <- do.call(rbind, replicate(replications, df, simplify = FALSE))   message("IHDP loaded (", replications, " replications): ",           nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) } else {   df <- NULL }  if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) {   d <- tryCatch(     synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 5000, p = 25, sigma = 1.0, adj = 0),     error = function(e) synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 5000, p = 25, sigma = 1.0)   )   df <- as.data.frame(d$X)   colnames(df) <- paste0("X", 0:(ncol(df) - 1))   df$treatment  <- d$w   df$y_factual  <- d$y   df$y_cfactual <- ifelse(d$w == 1, d$b - 0.5 * d$tau, d$b + 0.5 * d$tau)   df$mu0 <- d$b - 0.5 * d$tau   df$mu1 <- d$b + 0.5 * d$tau   message("Synthetic fallback: ", nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) }  # Feature ordering: binary first (cols 7–25), continuous second (cols 1–6) # — matches the Python tutorial's feature permutation xcols    <- paste0("X", 0:24) perm     <- c(7:25, 1:6) X        <- as.matrix(df[, xcols][, perm]) treatment <- as.integer(df$treatment) y         <- as.numeric(df$y_factual) y_cf      <- as.numeric(df$y_cfactual) mu0       <- as.numeric(df$mu0) mu1       <- as.numeric(df$mu1) tau       <- ifelse(df$treatment == 1,                     df$y_factual - df$y_cfactual,                     df$y_cfactual - df$y_factual)  # 80/20 train–validation split (seed 1 matches the Python tutorial) n <- nrow(X) set.seed(1) ite <- sample(n, size = round(0.2 * n)) itr <- setdiff(seq_len(n), ite)  X_train         <- X[itr, ];  X_val         <- X[ite, ] treatment_train <- treatment[itr]; treatment_val <- treatment[ite] y_train         <- y[itr];   y_val         <- y[ite] tau_train       <- tau[itr]; tau_val       <- tau[ite] mu_0_train      <- mu0[itr]; mu_0_val      <- mu0[ite] mu_1_train      <- mu1[itr]; mu_1_val      <- mu1[ite]  cat("Train:", length(itr), "| Val:", length(ite), "
") Train: 10757 | Val: 2689 cat("Treatment prevalence — train:",     round(mean(treatment_train), 3),     "| val:", round(mean(treatment_val), 3), "
") Treatment prevalence — train: 0.184 | val: 0.196 # Standardize continuous covariates (cols 20–25 in the permuted matrix, # corresponding to the original continuous features X0–X5). # Binary covariates (cols 1–19) are left unchanged. preprocess_features <- function(train_x, test_x) {   scaled_train <- train_x   scaled_test  <- test_x   cont_cols    <- 20:25   means <- colMeans(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE])   sds   <- apply(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)   sds[sds == 0] <- 1   scaled_train[, cont_cols] <- scale(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE],                                      center = means, scale = sds)   scaled_test[, cont_cols]  <- scale(test_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE],                                      center = means, scale = sds)   list(train_x = scaled_train, test_x = scaled_test, means = means, sds = sds) }  # Random subsampling with reproducible seed — keeps training times manageable # while preserving the treatment ratio approximately. build_training_arrays <- function(x, t, y, subsample = 5000L, seed = 42L) {   set.seed(seed)   idx <- sample.int(nrow(x), size = min(subsample, nrow(x)), replace = FALSE)   list(x = x[idx, , drop = FALSE],        t = as.numeric(t[idx]),        y = as.numeric(y[idx]),        idx = idx) }  # ATE and ITE evaluation against known potential outcomes. # Returns ATE bias, absolute ATE error, and sqrt(PEHE) — # the three metrics most commonly reported in the IHDP literature. estimate_ate_cdvae <- function(model, x_eval, mu0_true, mu1_true) {   y0_hat   <- predict(model, x_eval, type = "mu0")   y1_hat   <- predict(model, x_eval, type = "mu1")   ite_hat  <- y1_hat - y0_hat   ite_true <- mu1_true - mu0_true   ate_pred <- mean(ite_hat)   ate_true <- mean(ite_true)   list(     ite_hat   = ite_hat,     ite_true  = ite_true,     ate_pred  = ate_pred,     ate_true  = ate_true,     ate_bias  = ate_pred - ate_true,     ate_error = abs(ate_true - ate_pred),     pehe      = sqrt(mean((ite_hat - ite_true)^2))   ) }  # Plot all four loss components over training epochs on a log scale. # A healthy run sees reconstruction and KL decline steadily while MMD # converges toward zero, confirming causal alignment is improving. plot_training_history_cdvae <- function(history) {   h <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(history$train), function(i) {     as.data.frame(history$train[[i]]) |> dplyr::mutate(epoch = i)   }))   h_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(h, cols = c(total, kl, mmd),                                 names_to = "component", values_to = "value")   ggplot(h_long, aes(epoch, value, color = component)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +     scale_y_log10() +     facet_wrap(~component, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +     labs(title = "CD-VAE: training loss components (log scale)",          x = "Epoch", y = "Loss") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "none") }  # MMD-only convergence plot — separating this out makes it easy to see # whether causal alignment has stabilized before reconstruction has. plot_mmd_convergence_cdvae <- function(history) {   h <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(history$train), function(i) {     as.data.frame(history$train[[i]]) |> dplyr::mutate(epoch = i)   }))   ggplot(h, aes(epoch, mmd)) +     geom_line(color = "#993556", linewidth = 0.9) +     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",                color = "gray60", linewidth = 0.5) +     labs(title = "MMD causal alignment convergence",          x = "Epoch", y = "MMD") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) }  # Latent space PCA: color by treatment group. # In a well-trained CD-VAE the two groups should overlap substantially — # the MMD penalty has removed the statistical separation that raw covariates show. plot_latent_space_cdvae <- function(model, x_data, t_data,                                     title = "Latent space (PCA)") {   z_mu <- predict(model, x_data, type = "latent")   pc   <- prcomp(z_mu, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)   z2   <- pc$x[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]   dfz  <- data.frame(     PC1       = z2[, 1],     PC2       = z2[, 2],     treatment = factor(t_data, levels = c(0, 1),                        labels = c("Control", "Treated"))   )   ggplot(dfz, aes(PC1, PC2, color = treatment)) +     geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) +     scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#185FA5", "Treated" = "#993C1D")) +     labs(title = title, x = "PC1", y = "PC2", color = "") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "top") }  # ITE scatter and distribution comparison. plot_ite_analysis_cdvae <- function(ite_hat, ite_true, ate_pred, ate_true) {   df <- data.frame(ite_true = ite_true, ite_hat = ite_hat)   p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(ite_true, ite_hat)) +     geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.0, color = "#534AB7") +     geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,                 linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +     geom_hline(yintercept = ate_pred, linetype = "dotted",                color = "#BA7517", linewidth = 0.7) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dotted",                color = "#0F6E56", linewidth = 0.7) +     annotate("text", x = min(ite_true) + 0.1, y = ate_pred + 0.05,              label = sprintf("Pred ATE = %.3f", ate_pred),              hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#BA7517") +     annotate("text", x = ate_true + 0.05, y = max(ite_hat) - 0.1,              label = sprintf("True ATE = %.3f", ate_true),              hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#0F6E56") +     labs(title = "Predicted vs true ITE",          x = "True ITE", y = "Predicted ITE") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11)    dfh <- dplyr::bind_rows(     data.frame(value = ite_true, type = "True ITE"),     data.frame(value = ite_hat,  type = "Predicted ITE")   )   p2 <- ggplot(dfh, aes(value, fill = type)) +     geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.5, bins = 40) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dashed",                color = "#0F6E56", linewidth = 0.7) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_pred, linetype = "dashed",                color = "#993C1D", linewidth = 0.7) +     scale_fill_manual(values = c("True ITE" = "#185FA5",                                  "Predicted ITE" = "#993C1D")) +     labs(title = "ITE distribution",          x = "ITE", y = "Count", fill = "") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "top")    list(scatter = p1, hist = p2) } # Logistic regression propensity model on raw covariates ps_df <- as.data.frame(X_train) ps_df$treatment <- treatment_train ps_model <- glm(treatment ~ ., data = ps_df, family = binomial()) ps_train <- fitted(ps_model)  df_ps <- data.frame(   ps        = ps_train,   treatment = factor(treatment_train, levels = c(0, 1),                      labels = c("Control", "Treated")) )  ggplot(df_ps, aes(ps, fill = treatment, color = treatment)) +   geom_density(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_rug(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +   scale_fill_manual(values  = c("Control" = "#185FA5", "Treated" = "#993C1D")) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#185FA5", "Treated" = "#993C1D")) +   labs(     title = "Propensity score overlap (train set)",     subtitle = "Substantial overlap is required for causal identification",     x = "Estimated propensity score P(T=1 | X)",     y = "Density", fill = "", color = ""   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(legend.position = "top") proc          <- preprocess_features(X_train, X_val) X_train_scaled <- proc$train_x X_val_scaled   <- proc$test_x  sub_train <- build_training_arrays(   x         = X_train_scaled,   t         = treatment_train,   y         = y_train,   subsample = if (run_fast) 5000L else nrow(X_train_scaled),   seed      = 42L ) sub_val <- build_training_arrays(   x         = X_val_scaled,   t         = treatment_val,   y         = y_val,   subsample = if (run_fast) 2000L else nrow(X_val_scaled),   seed      = 42L )  X_train_cd       <- sub_train$x treatment_train_cd <- sub_train$t y_train_cd       <- sub_train$y X_val_cd         <- sub_val$x  cat("Train matrix:", paste(dim(X_train_cd), collapse = " × "), "
