base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uber/causalml/master/docs/examples/data" cols <- c("treatment", "y_factual", "y_cfactual", "mu0", "mu1", paste0("X", 0:24)) df <- NULL for (i in 1:9) {   url <- sprintf("%s/ihdp_npci_%d.csv", base_url, i)   tmp <- tryCatch(read.csv(url, header = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)   if (!is.null(tmp) && nrow(tmp) > 0) {     colnames(tmp) <- cols[seq_len(ncol(tmp))]     df <- if (is.null(df)) tmp else rbind(df, tmp)   } }  if (!is.null(df) && nrow(df) > 0) {   replications <- if (run_fast) 2L else 10L   df <- do.call(rbind, replicate(replications, df, simplify = FALSE))   message("IHDP loaded (", replications, " replications): ",           nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) } else {   df <- NULL }  if (is.null(df) || nrow(df) == 0) {   d <- tryCatch(     synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 5000, p = 25, sigma = 1.0, adj = 0),     error = function(e) synthetic_data(mode = 1, n = 5000, p = 25, sigma = 1.0)   )   df <- as.data.frame(d$X)   colnames(df) <- paste0("X", 0:(ncol(df) - 1))   df$treatment  <- d$w   df$y_factual  <- d$y   df$y_cfactual <- ifelse(d$w == 1, d$b - 0.5 * d$tau, d$b + 0.5 * d$tau)   df$mu0 <- d$b - 0.5 * d$tau   df$mu1 <- d$b + 0.5 * d$tau   message("Synthetic fallback: ", nrow(df), " × ", ncol(df)) }  # Feature ordering: binary first (cols 7–25), continuous second (cols 1–6) # — matches the Python tutorial's feature permutation xcols    <- paste0("X", 0:24) perm     <- c(7:25, 1:6) X        <- as.matrix(df[, xcols][, perm]) treatment <- as.integer(df$treatment) y         <- as.numeric(df$y_factual) y_cf      <- as.numeric(df$y_cfactual) mu0       <- as.numeric(df$mu0) mu1       <- as.numeric(df$mu1) tau       <- ifelse(df$treatment == 1,                     df$y_factual - df$y_cfactual,                     df$y_cfactual - df$y_factual)  # 80/20 train–validation split (seed 1 matches the Python tutorial) n <- nrow(X) set.seed(1) ite <- sample(n, size = round(0.2 * n)) itr <- setdiff(seq_len(n), ite)  X_train         <- X[itr, ];  X_val         <- X[ite, ] treatment_train <- treatment[itr]; treatment_val <- treatment[ite] y_train         <- y[itr];   y_val         <- y[ite] tau_train       <- tau[itr]; tau_val       <- tau[ite] mu_0_train      <- mu0[itr]; mu_0_val      <- mu0[ite] mu_1_train      <- mu1[itr]; mu_1_val      <- mu1[ite]  cat("Train:", length(itr), "| Val:", length(ite), "\n") Train: 10757 | Val: 2689 cat("Treatment prevalence — train:",     round(mean(treatment_train), 3),     "| val:", round(mean(treatment_val), 3), "\n") Treatment prevalence — train: 0.184 | val: 0.196

# Standardize continuous covariates (cols 20–25 in the permuted matrix, # corresponding to the original continuous features X0–X5). # Binary covariates (cols 1–19) are left unchanged. preprocess_features <- function(train_x, test_x) {   scaled_train <- train_x   scaled_test  <- test_x   cont_cols    <- 20:25   means <- colMeans(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE])   sds   <- apply(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)   sds[sds == 0] <- 1   scaled_train[, cont_cols] <- scale(train_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE],                                      center = means, scale = sds)   scaled_test[, cont_cols]  <- scale(test_x[, cont_cols, drop = FALSE],                                      center = means, scale = sds)   list(train_x = scaled_train, test_x = scaled_test, means = means, sds = sds) }  # Random subsampling with reproducible seed — keeps training times manageable # while preserving the treatment ratio approximately. build_training_arrays <- function(x, t, y, subsample = 5000L, seed = 42L) {   set.seed(seed)   idx <- sample.int(nrow(x), size = min(subsample, nrow(x)), replace = FALSE)   list(x = x[idx, , drop = FALSE],        t = as.numeric(t[idx]),        y = as.numeric(y[idx]),        idx = idx) }  # ATE and ITE evaluation against known potential outcomes. # Returns ATE bias, absolute ATE error, and sqrt(PEHE) — # the three metrics most commonly reported in the IHDP literature. estimate_ate_cdvae <- function(model, x_eval, mu0_true, mu1_true) {   y0_hat   <- predict(model, x_eval, type = "mu0")   y1_hat   <- predict(model, x_eval, type = "mu1")   ite_hat  <- y1_hat - y0_hat   ite_true <- mu1_true - mu0_true   ate_pred <- mean(ite_hat)   ate_true <- mean(ite_true)   list(     ite_hat   = ite_hat,     ite_true  = ite_true,     ate_pred  = ate_pred,     ate_true  = ate_true,     ate_bias  = ate_pred - ate_true,     ate_error = abs(ate_true - ate_pred),     pehe      = sqrt(mean((ite_hat - ite_true)^2))   ) }  # Plot all four loss components over training epochs on a log scale. # A healthy run sees reconstruction and KL decline steadily while MMD # converges toward zero, confirming causal alignment is improving. plot_training_history_cdvae <- function(history) {   h <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(history$train), function(i) {     as.data.frame(history$train[[i]]) |> dplyr::mutate(epoch = i)   }))   h_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(h, cols = c(total, kl, mmd),                                 names_to = "component", values_to = "value")   ggplot(h_long, aes(epoch, value, color = component)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +     scale_y_log10() +     facet_wrap(~component, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +     labs(title = "CD-VAE: training loss components (log scale)",          x = "Epoch", y = "Loss") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "none") }  # MMD-only convergence plot — separating this out makes it easy to see # whether causal alignment has stabilized before reconstruction has. plot_mmd_convergence_cdvae <- function(history) {   h <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(history$train), function(i) {     as.data.frame(history$train[[i]]) |> dplyr::mutate(epoch = i)   }))   ggplot(h, aes(epoch, mmd)) +     geom_line(color = "#993556", linewidth = 0.9) +     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",                color = "gray60", linewidth = 0.5) +     labs(title = "MMD causal alignment convergence",          x = "Epoch", y = "MMD") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) }  # Latent space PCA: color by treatment group. # In a well-trained CD-VAE the two groups should overlap substantially — # the MMD penalty has removed the statistical separation that raw covariates show. plot_latent_space_cdvae <- function(model, x_data, t_data,                                     title = "Latent space (PCA)") {   z_mu <- predict(model, x_data, type = "latent")   pc   <- prcomp(z_mu, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)   z2   <- pc$x[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]   dfz  <- data.frame(     PC1       = z2[, 1],     PC2       = z2[, 2],     treatment = factor(t_data, levels = c(0, 1),                        labels = c("Control", "Treated"))   )   ggplot(dfz, aes(PC1, PC2, color = treatment)) +     geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) +     scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#185FA5", "Treated" = "#993C1D")) +     labs(title = title, x = "PC1", y = "PC2", color = "") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "top") }  # ITE scatter and distribution comparison. plot_ite_analysis_cdvae <- function(ite_hat, ite_true, ate_pred, ate_true) {   df <- data.frame(ite_true = ite_true, ite_hat = ite_hat)   p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(ite_true, ite_hat)) +     geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.0, color = "#534AB7") +     geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,                 linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +     geom_hline(yintercept = ate_pred, linetype = "dotted",                color = "#BA7517", linewidth = 0.7) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dotted",                color = "#0F6E56", linewidth = 0.7) +     annotate("text", x = min(ite_true) + 0.1, y = ate_pred + 0.05,              label = sprintf("Pred ATE = %.3f", ate_pred),              hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#BA7517") +     annotate("text", x = ate_true + 0.05, y = max(ite_hat) - 0.1,              label = sprintf("True ATE = %.3f", ate_true),              hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#0F6E56") +     labs(title = "Predicted vs true ITE",          x = "True ITE", y = "Predicted ITE") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11)    dfh <- dplyr::bind_rows(     data.frame(value = ite_true, type = "True ITE"),     data.frame(value = ite_hat,  type = "Predicted ITE")   )   p2 <- ggplot(dfh, aes(value, fill = type)) +     geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.5, bins = 40) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_true, linetype = "dashed",                color = "#0F6E56", linewidth = 0.7) +     geom_vline(xintercept = ate_pred, linetype = "dashed",                color = "#993C1D", linewidth = 0.7) +     scale_fill_manual(values = c("True ITE" = "#185FA5",                                  "Predicted ITE" = "#993C1D")) +     labs(title = "ITE distribution",          x = "ITE", y = "Count", fill = "") +     theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +     theme(legend.position = "top")    list(scatter = p1, hist = p2) }

Causal Generative Network (CausalGAN) causal-aware extension classic GAN framework, introduced Kocaoglu et al. (2018) paper CausalGAN: Learning Causal Implicit Generative Models Adversarial Training. lets train generative model respects user-specified causal DAG still producing high-quality, realistic samples joint distribution. key advantage model can answer causal queries—interventions (\(\mathrm{}(\cdot)\)) counterfactuals—without retraining additional data, something vanilla GAN . normal GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014) learns implicit generator \(G\) maps noise \(Z \sim p_Z\) samples \(\hat{\mathbf{v}} = G(Z)\) joint distribution \(p(\hat{X}, \hat{T}, \hat{Y})\) matches data distribution \(p(X, T, Y)\). However, generator black-box neural network, notion causal mechanisms. ask : - Interventional query: “\(Y\) forced \(T = 1\) everyone?” (\(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathrm{}(T=1)]\)). - Counterfactual query: “Given patient \(T=0\) outcome \(Y=0\), \(Y\) received treatment \(T=1\)?” CausalGAN fixes turning generator Structural Causal Model (SCM) whose functional form exactly causal graph provide. Architecturally, CausalGAN decomposes generator separate modules mirror structure causal DAG. simple DAG \(X \T \Y\) \(X \Y\), generator structured follows:  Instead one monolithic generator, CausalGAN decomposes generator according topological order DAG. Every node \(V_i\) gets sub-generator \(G_i\): \[ \begin{align*} \hat{X} &= G_X(Z_X) \\ \hat{T} &= G_T(\hat{X}, Z_T) \\ \hat{Y} &= G_Y(\hat{X}, \hat{T}, Z_Y) \end{align*} \] \(Z_X, Z_T, Z_Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, )\) independent exogenous noise vectors (“unobserved confounders” SCM). generated values causal parents (already sampled upstream), private noise. Data flow strictly causal: child never “sees” descendants. exactly implements structural equations causal DAG: \[ V_i := f_i(\text{Pa}(V_i), U_i), \quad U_i \perp\!\!\!\perp \text{noises} \] architecture hard-wires graph, generator automatically satisfies Markov factorization joint distribution induced DAG. perform intervention \(\mathrm{}(T = t)\): Skip \(G_T\) entirely. Set \(\hat{T} \leftarrow t\) (constant). Feed clamped \(\hat{T}\) downstream generators (\(G_Y\) example). \[ \hat{Y}_{\mathrm{}(T=1)} = G_Y(\hat{X}, \hat{T}=1, Z_Y) \] weights changed. exactly Pearl’s \(\mathrm{}\)-operator realized inside generator. can now compute interventional quantities sampling many trajectories averaging (e.g., average treatment effect, conditional interventions, etc.). Standard GANs one global discriminator \(D\) tries distinguish real \((X,T,Y)\) fake \((\hat{X},\hat{T},\hat{Y})\). CausalGAN adds one small “labeller” (local discriminator/classifier) per node. Global discriminator \(D_{\text{joint}}\): ensures entire joint looks realistic. Node-specific labellers \(D_i\): \(D_i\) trained distinguish marginal/conditional distribution node \(\) given parents real generated data. total adversarial loss becomes: \[ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{joint}} + \sum_i \lambda_i \mathcal{L}_{\text{label},} \] extra supervision forces structural equation \(G_i\) match correct conditional \(p(V_i \mid \text{Pa}(V_i))\) implied data. Without labellers, plain GAN learn joint statistically close violates causal conditionals. Counterfactuals require three steps (abduction → action → prediction), exactly Pearl’s SCM framework: Abduction: Given real observation \((x, t, y)\), find noise realization \(\mathbf{u}^* = (u_X^*, u_T^*, u_Y^*)\) best explains : \[    \mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} \;\; \bigl\| G(\mathbf{u}) - (x,t,y) \bigr\|_2^2 + \text{regularizers}   \] solved gradient descent noise vectors (dozen steps inference time; retraining). Action: Apply intervention clamping desired variable (e.g., set \(\hat{T} = 1\)). Prediction: Re-run generator noise \(\mathbf{u}^*\) new intervention: \[     y_{\text{CF}} = G_Y(x, \hat{T}=1, u_Y^*)   \] noises held fixed, answering “exact individual experienced counterfactual treatment?”—purest form individual-level causal reasoning. Zero extra training cost causal queries: trained, intervention counterfactual simple forward pass (short abduction optimization). Works differentiable generator (MLPs, CNNs, transformers, etc.). Scalable: number extra labellers linear number nodes, tiny. Applications: medical imaging (-different treatments?), fairness (counterfactual fairness auditing), causal data augmentation, policy evaluation, etc. short, CausalGAN first practical way turn black-box generative model white-box Structural Causal Model obeys statistical realism causal graph care . combination structural-equation generators, per-node labellers, explicit noise abduction gives full -calculus counterfactual power inside adversarial training loop. use {RCuasalML}s causalGAN implementation (torch-based available, else placeholder) fit model IHDP semi-synthetic dataset. Following R packages required run notebook. packages installed, can install using code : tidyverse, plyr, RCausalML, causaldata, torch, dagitty, ggdag, igraph IHDP small per replication (~6.7k rows merging nine NPCI CSVs). Setting replications=100 stacks 100 copies Monte Carlo–style benchmarks needs large RAM can stress machine; tutorial defaults replications=1. next cell defines Z_train, Z_test (needed Z_test_t training), Z_test_eval (float64 copy metrics), cols.  tutorial demonstrated implement evaluate Causal Generative Adversarial Network (CausalGAN) R using {RCausalML} package. covered: - Building structural equation generators respect user-specified causal graph. - Performing interventional analysis clamping treatment variables. - Conducting counterfactual inference abduction-action-prediction. - Evaluating model performance using metrics like FID-proxy, SEM R², CATE PEHE. However, generator black-box neural network, notion causal mechanisms. ask : - Interventional query: “\(Y\) forced \(T = 1\) everyone?” (\(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathrm{}(T=1)]\)). - Counterfactual query: “Given patient \(T=0\) outcome \(Y=0\), \(Y\) received treatment \(T=1\)?” CausalGAN fixes turning generator Structural Causal Model (SCM) whose functional form exactly causal graph provide.

Architecturally, CausalGAN decomposes generator separate modules mirror structure causal DAG. simple DAG \(X \T \Y\) \(X \Y\), generator structured follows:  Instead one monolithic generator, CausalGAN decomposes generator according topological order DAG. Every node \(V_i\) gets sub-generator \(G_i\): \[ \begin{align*} \hat{X} &= G_X(Z_X) \\ \hat{T} &= G_T(\hat{X}, Z_T) \\ \hat{Y} &= G_Y(\hat{X}, \hat{T}, Z_Y) \end{align*} \] \(Z_X, Z_T, Z_Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, )\) independent exogenous noise vectors (“unobserved confounders” SCM). generated values causal parents (already sampled upstream), private noise. Data flow strictly causal: child never “sees” descendants. exactly implements structural equations causal DAG: \[ V_i := f_i(\text{Pa}(V_i), U_i), \quad U_i \perp\!\!\!\perp \text{noises} \] architecture hard-wires graph, generator automatically satisfies Markov factorization joint distribution induced DAG. perform intervention \(\mathrm{}(T = t)\): Skip \(G_T\) entirely. Set \(\hat{T} \leftarrow t\) (constant). Feed clamped \(\hat{T}\) downstream generators (\(G_Y\) example). \[ \hat{Y}_{\mathrm{}(T=1)} = G_Y(\hat{X}, \hat{T}=1, Z_Y) \] weights changed. exactly Pearl’s \(\mathrm{}\)-operator realized inside generator. can now compute interventional quantities sampling many trajectories averaging (e.g., average treatment effect, conditional interventions, etc.). Standard GANs one global discriminator \(D\) tries distinguish real \((X,T,Y)\) fake \((\hat{X},\hat{T},\hat{Y})\). CausalGAN adds one small “labeller” (local discriminator/classifier) per node. Global discriminator \(D_{\text{joint}}\): ensures entire joint looks realistic. Node-specific labellers \(D_i\): \(D_i\) trained distinguish marginal/conditional distribution node \(\) given parents real generated data. total adversarial loss becomes: \[ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{joint}} + \sum_i \lambda_i \mathcal{L}_{\text{label},} \] extra supervision forces structural equation \(G_i\) match correct conditional \(p(V_i \mid \text{Pa}(V_i))\) implied data. Without labellers, plain GAN learn joint statistically close violates causal conditionals. Counterfactuals require three steps (abduction → action → prediction), exactly Pearl’s SCM framework: Abduction: Given real observation \((x, t, y)\), find noise realization \(\mathbf{u}^* = (u_X^*, u_T^*, u_Y^*)\) best explains : \[    \mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} \;\; \bigl\| G(\mathbf{u}) - (x,t,y) \bigr\|_2^2 + \text{regularizers}   \] solved gradient descent noise vectors (dozen steps inference time; retraining). Action: Apply intervention clamping desired variable (e.g., set \(\hat{T} = 1\)). Prediction: Re-run generator noise \(\mathbf{u}^*\) new intervention: \[     y_{\text{CF}} = G_Y(x, \hat{T}=1, u_Y^*)   \] noises held fixed, answering “exact individual experienced counterfactual treatment?”—purest form individual-level causal reasoning.

Deep Structural Causal Models (DSCMs) fuse rigorous causal semantics Judea Pearl’s Structural Causal Models (SCMs) representational flexibility deep generative networks. classical SCM uses hand-crafted parametric structural equations, DSCM replaces mechanism deep network — normalizing flow, variational autoencoder, GAN, diffusion model — capable capturing nonlinear, non-Gaussian, high-dimensional dependencies classical methods handle. DSCMs popularized Pawlowski et al. (2020), “Deep Structural Causal Models Tractable Counterfactual Inference”, systematically reviewed Poinsot et al. (2024). key contribution making Pearl’s three-step counterfactual inference procedure — Abduction, Action, Prediction (AAP) — tractable complex structured data medical images, gene expression profiles, natural language. notebook series introduced model progressively richer causal semantics: defining difference DSCMs implement Pearl’s -calculus observation level, just latent space. Every endogenous variable gets deep generative mechanism, counterfactuals produced running full SCM twice: factual inputs abduct exogenous noise, intervention applied holding noise fixed. standard SCM \(\mathcal{M} = (\mathcal{F}, P(\mathbf{U}))\) defined : \[X_i := f_i\!\bigl(\mathrm{PA}(X_i),\, U_i\bigr) \quad \text{} = 1, \dots, d\] \(\mathrm{PA}(X_i)\) parents \(X_i\) known DAG \(\mathcal{G}\), \(U_i\) exogenous noise variables (assumed independent Markovian case), functions \(f_i\) encode causal mechanisms. Given \(\mathcal{G}\) factual data, SCM supports three levels inference — Pearl’s ladder causation: Level 1 (Observation): \(P(\mathbf{X})\) — observe sampling ancestrally along \(\mathcal{G}\). Level 2 (Intervention): \(P(\mathbf{X} \mid (X_k = v))\) — distribution surgically setting \(X_k\). Level 3 (Counterfactual): \(P(X_j(v) \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\) — \(X_j\) specific individual \(\mathbf{x}\) \(X_k\) set \(v\). Classical SCMs restrict \(f_i\) simple parametric forms (linear, additive). DSCMs lift restriction entirely. DSCM, \(f_i\) replaced deep generative module. observational distribution \(P(\mathbf{X})\) still generated ancestral sampling along \(\mathcal{G}\), now deep parameterizations. DAG structure constrains architecture: module receives parents conditioning input, preserving causal ordering. DSCMs classified two axes (Poinsot et al., 2024): SCM class (identifiability): Bijective Generation Mechanisms (BGM): Mechanisms invertible diffeomorphisms, e.g., normalizing flows. Neural Causal Models (NCM): Feedforward networks non-invertible mechanisms; identifiability tied specific structural assumptions true SCM. deep generative model class (abduction tractability): Invertible explicit (conditional normalizing flows): exact, deterministic inversion \(U_i\) data. Amortized explicit (VAE-style encoder-decoder): encoder approximates \(P(U_i \mid x_i, \mathrm{pa}_i)\); tractable approximate. Amortized implicit (GANs): requires rejection sampling approximations abduction. RCausalML::dscm() implementation used follows amortized explicit paradigm — VAE-style encoder-decoder mechanism, deterministic low-level inversion step. AAP procedure separates DSCMs models series. produces individual-level counterfactuals respect factual data — rather population-level interventional distributions average data. individual \(\mathbf{x}\): Step 1 — Abduction: Infer personalized exogenous noise generated \(\mathbf{x}\). amortized explicit case: \[z_k^{(s)} \sim Q\!\bigl(z_k \mid e_k(x_k;\, \mathrm{pa}_k)\bigr), \qquad u_k^{(s)} = h_k^{-1}\!\bigl(x_k;\, g_k(z_k^{(s)};\, \mathrm{pa}_k),\, \mathrm{pa}_k\bigr)\] encoder \(e_k\) produces summary \((x_k, \mathrm{pa}_k)\); \(Q\) variational posterior high-level latent \(z_k\); \(h_k^{-1}\) deterministically recovers low-level noise \(u_k\) given \(z_k\) parents. step “personalizes” model — identifies latent factors explain particular individual’s outcomes. Every endogenous variable gets deep generative mechanism, counterfactuals produced running full SCM twice: factual inputs abduct exogenous noise, intervention applied holding noise fixed.

standard SCM \(\mathcal{M} = (\mathcal{F}, P(\mathbf{U}))\) defined : \[X_i := f_i\!\bigl(\mathrm{PA}(X_i),\, U_i\bigr) \quad \text{} = 1, \dots, d\] \(\mathrm{PA}(X_i)\) parents \(X_i\) known DAG \(\mathcal{G}\), \(U_i\) exogenous noise variables (assumed independent Markovian case), functions \(f_i\) encode causal mechanisms. Given \(\mathcal{G}\) factual data, SCM supports three levels inference — Pearl’s ladder causation: Level 1 (Observation): \(P(\mathbf{X})\) — observe sampling ancestrally along \(\mathcal{G}\). Level 2 (Intervention): \(P(\mathbf{X} \mid (X_k = v))\) — distribution surgically setting \(X_k\). Level 3 (Counterfactual): \(P(X_j(v) \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\) — \(X_j\) specific individual \(\mathbf{x}\) \(X_k\) set \(v\). Classical SCMs restrict \(f_i\) simple parametric forms (linear, additive). DSCMs lift restriction entirely. DSCM, \(f_i\) replaced deep generative module. observational distribution \(P(\mathbf{X})\) still generated ancestral sampling along \(\mathcal{G}\), now deep parameterizations. DAG structure constrains architecture: module receives parents conditioning input, preserving causal ordering. DSCMs classified two axes (Poinsot et al., 2024): SCM class (identifiability): Bijective Generation Mechanisms (BGM): Mechanisms invertible diffeomorphisms, e.g., normalizing flows. Supports strongest identifiability guarantees counterfactuals (\(\mathcal{L}_3\)). Neural Causal Models (NCM): Feedforward networks non-invertible mechanisms; identifiability tied specific structural assumptions true SCM. deep generative model class (abduction tractability): Invertible explicit (conditional normalizing flows): exact, deterministic inversion \(U_i\) data. Amortized explicit (VAE-style encoder-decoder): encoder approximates \(P(U_i \mid x_i, \mathrm{pa}_i)\); tractable approximate. Amortized implicit (GANs): requires rejection sampling approximations abduction. RCausalML::dscm() implementation used follows amortized explicit paradigm — VAE-style encoder-decoder mechanism, deterministic low-level inversion step.

original notebook used moderate hyperparameters work reliably. version improves four targeted changes: Larger hidden dimension (256 → 256, kept; treatment head 128 → 256): matching network capacities prevents treatment encoder becoming bottleneck. Longer KL warmup relative total epochs (80/120 → 100/300): gives reconstruction longer stabilize KL term competes, reducing posterior collapse. Stronger oracle supervision (lambda_oracle 0.35 → 0.5): semi-synthetic IHDP benchmark oracle labels reliable; stronger supervision materially reduces PEHE. Lower learning rate cosine decay (2e-4 → 1e-4): allows finer convergence later epochs without overshooting. Three-way split (train / val / test) rather two-way: validation set now drives early stopping exclusively, test set used final reporting, preventing information leakage.

text: load nine IHDP replication files CausalML repository. IHDP (Infant Health Development Program) dataset pairs real covariate data randomized trial simulated potential outcomes, providing known ground-truth \(\mu_0, \mu_1\) model evaluation. makes standard benchmark causal effect estimation methods, oracle loss exploits known \(\mu_0, \mu_1\) soft supervision signals training. data split three parts: 70% training, 15% validation (driving early stopping), 15% final evaluation. Binary features (columns 7–25 permutation) left original 0/1 scale; continuous features (columns 1–6) standardized using training-set statistics. fitting DSCM — causal model — verify treatment control groups share sufficient covariate support. Extreme propensity scores (near 0 1) indicate units counterfactual difficult estimate reliably regardless model complexity.

",             nrow(X_dr), ncol(X_dr))) Dose-response dataset: 2000 obs, 13 covariates cat(sprintf("Treatment range: [%.2f, %.2f]
", min(T_cont), max(T_cont))) Treatment range: [-5.85, 6.14] dr_fit <- tryCatch({   causal_egm(     X                  = X_dr_s,     treatment          = T_cont,     y                  = Y_dr,     dim_c              = if (run_fast) 3L else 6L,     dim_t              = if (run_fast) 2L else 4L,     dim_y              = if (run_fast) 2L else 4L,     hidden_dim         = if (run_fast) 64L else 128L,     num_epochs         = if (run_fast) 40L else 120L,     batch_size         = BATCH_SIZE,     learning_rate      = LR,     learning_rate_disc = LR_DISC,     weight_decay       = WEIGHT_DECAY,     lambda_recon       = LAMBDA_RECON,     lambda_treat       = LAMBDA_TREAT,     lambda_outcome     = LAMBDA_OUTCOME,     lambda_disent      = LAMBDA_DISENT,     max_grad_norm      = MAX_GRAD_NORM,     verbose            = FALSE,     device             = device_use   ) }, error = function(e) {   message("Dose-response fit failed: ", conditionMessage(e))   NULL }) if (!is.null(dr_fit)) {   dr_vals <- vapply(t_grid, function(t) {     tryCatch({       preds <- predict(dr_fit, X_dr_s[1:min(200L, nrow(X_dr_s)), , drop=FALSE],                        type="dose_response", treatment_value=t)       mean(as.numeric(preds))     }, error = function(e) NA_real_)   }, numeric(1))    if (any(!is.na(dr_vals))) {     df_dr <- data.frame(       t        = t_grid,       pred     = dr_vals,       true_avg = true_dr_mean     )     ggplot(df_dr, aes(t)) +       geom_line(aes(y=true_avg, color="True E[Y(t)]"),                 linewidth=1.0, linetype="dashed") +       geom_line(aes(y=pred, color="CausalEGM estimate"),                 linewidth=0.9) +       geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=pred - 0.15, ymax=pred + 0.15),                   alpha=0.15, fill="#534AB7") +       scale_color_manual(values=c("True E[Y(t)]"="#0F6E56",                                   "CausalEGM estimate"="#534AB7")) +       labs(title="Dose-response curve: E[Y(t)] vs continuous treatment t",            subtitle="Dashed = true marginal curve; shaded = ±0.15 uncertainty band",            x="Treatment value t", y="E[Y(t)]", color="") +       theme_minimal(base_size=11) +       theme(legend.position="top")   } else {     cat("Dose-response predictions unavailable for plotting.

text: begin linear Gaussian SEM: variables generated model \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{Z}\), \(\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, )\). ground-truth DAG known, can measure recovery accuracy precisely. setting native domain linear NOTEARS — best-case scenario nonlinear variants later compared. algorithm minimizes augmented Lagrangian \[\mathcal{L}_\rho(W, \alpha) = \frac{1}{2n}\|X - XW\|_F^2 + \lambda_1\|W\|_1 + \alpha\, h(W) + \frac{\rho}{2}h(W)^2,\] iterating () L-BFGS-B step \(W\) (ii) dual-ascent update \(\alpha \leftarrow \alpha + \rho\, h(W)\) \(h(W) < \epsilon\). Hyperparameter guidance. two impactful choices : () sparsity penalty \(\lambda_1 \[0.01, 0.5]\) — higher values prune edges, trading TPR FDR; (ii) edge-threshold \(w_{\mathrm{threshold}} \[0.1, 0.5]\) applied optimization. Cross-validate SHD held-ground-truth graph available. large \(d\), prefer notears_nonlinear() MLP model. NOTEARS recovers graph structure, causal effects directly. DAG hand, downstream causal inference proceeds two steps: () read valid adjustment set graph using backdoor criterion, (ii) estimate Average Treatment Effect (ATE) Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) regression set. example treats variable 1 treatment \(T\) variable 20 outcome \(Y\). ground-truth DAG known, five complementary metrics quantify structural recovery accuracy. FDR (False Discovery Rate) — fraction predicted edges spurious: \(\text{FDR} = \text{FP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FP})\). Lower better. TPR (True Positive Rate / Recall) — fraction true edges recovered: \(\text{TPR} = \text{TP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FN})\). Higher better. FPR (False Positive Rate) — fraction true non-edges incorrectly predicted edges: \(\text{FPR} = \text{FP} / (\text{FP} + \text{TN})\). Lower better. SHD (Structural Hamming Distance) — total number edge insertions, deletions, reversals needed convert estimated graph true graph. Lower better; SHD = 0 means perfect recovery. primary summary statistic reported causal discovery benchmarks. nnz (Non-Zero entries) — number edges estimated graph. Compare true edge count: large discrepancy indicates - -sparsification. SHD 5–10 considered excellent 20-variable graph; TPR 0.8 FDR 0.2 indicates strong recovery. estimated matrix \(W \\mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) encodes topology (entries non-zero) strength (magnitude sign) directed edge. Entry \(W[, j]\) estimated effect cause \(j\) effect \(\): positive values indicate excitatory relationships, negative values inhibitory ones. column zeros means variable detected children; row zeros means detected parents (root node).  binary thresholded version \(W\) rendered directed graph. Nodes represent variables; edges indicate estimated direct causal relationships. Compare structure visually heatmap .

text: algorithm minimizes augmented Lagrangian \[\mathcal{L}_\rho(W, \alpha) = \frac{1}{2n}\|X - XW\|_F^2 + \lambda_1\|W\|_1 + \alpha\, h(W) + \frac{\rho}{2}h(W)^2,\] iterating () L-BFGS-B step \(W\) (ii) dual-ascent update \(\alpha \leftarrow \alpha + \rho\, h(W)\) \(h(W) < \epsilon\). Hyperparameter guidance. two impactful choices : () sparsity penalty \(\lambda_1 \[0.01, 0.5]\) — higher values prune edges, trading TPR FDR; (ii) edge-threshold \(w_{\mathrm{threshold}} \[0.1, 0.5]\) applied optimization. Cross-validate SHD held-ground-truth graph available. large \(d\), prefer notears_nonlinear() MLP model.

text: ground-truth DAG known, five complementary metrics quantify structural recovery accuracy. FDR (False Discovery Rate) — fraction predicted edges spurious: \(\text{FDR} = \text{FP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FP})\). Lower better. TPR (True Positive Rate / Recall) — fraction true edges recovered: \(\text{TPR} = \text{TP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FN})\). Higher better. FPR (False Positive Rate) — fraction true non-edges incorrectly predicted edges: \(\text{FPR} = \text{FP} / (\text{FP} + \text{TN})\). Lower better. SHD (Structural Hamming Distance) — total number edge insertions, deletions, reversals needed convert estimated graph true graph. Lower better; SHD = 0 means perfect recovery. primary summary statistic reported causal discovery benchmarks. nnz (Non-Zero entries) — number edges estimated graph. Compare true edge count: large discrepancy indicates - -sparsification. SHD 5–10 considered excellent 20-variable graph; TPR 0.8 FDR 0.2 indicates strong recovery.

# ── Nonlinear SEM simulator ─────────────────────────────────────────────────── # Convention: W[i, j] = weight of directed edge j → i #             (row = destination / effect, column = source / cause) # # sem_type: #   "mlp"  – tanh(z)       smooth, bounded nonlinearity #   "mim"  – z * sin(z)    multiplicative interaction (non-monotone) #   "gp"   – sin(z)        periodic / Gaussian-process-like # simulate_nonlinear_sem_custom <- function(W, n, sem_type = "mlp", noise_sd = 0.5) {   d <- ncol(W)    # igraph adjacency convention: A[a, b] != 0 => edge a -> b   # Since W[i, j] != 0 <=> j -> i, we need A = t(W)   g   <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix((t(W) != 0) * 1L, mode = "directed")   ord <- as.integer(igraph::topo_sort(g))   # parents before children    X <- matrix(0.0, nrow = n, ncol = d)    for (i in ord) {     pa <- which(W[i, ] != 0)               # parents of node i      if (length(pa) == 0L) {       X[, i] <- rnorm(n)                   # root node: Gaussian noise     } else {       z <- as.vector(X[, pa, drop = FALSE] %*% W[i, pa])  # weighted parent sum       X[, i] <- switch(sem_type,         mlp = tanh(z)    + rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd),         mim = z * sin(z) + rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd),         gp  = sin(z)     + rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd),                  z       + rnorm(n)          # fallback: linear       )     }   }   X } # ── Dataset 2: Nonlinear SEM (d = 10) ───────────────────────────────────────── # d = 10 keeps NotearsMLP / Sobolev runtimes tractable in a notebook set_random_seed(42) n_nlin <- 2000; d_nlin <- 10; s0_nlin <- 10 B_true_nlin <- simulate_dag(d_nlin, s0_nlin, graph_type) W_true_nlin <- simulate_parameter(B_true_nlin) X_nlin      <- simulate_nonlinear_sem_custom(W_true_nlin, n_nlin, sem_type = "mlp")  write.csv(X_nlin,      "X_nonlinear.csv",      row.names = FALSE) write.csv(W_true_nlin, "W_true_nonlinear.csv", row.names = FALSE)  X_nlin <- scale(X_nlin, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)  set.seed(42) tr2  <- sample(1:n_nlin, floor(0.70 * n_nlin)) tmp2 <- setdiff(1:n_nlin, tr2) va2  <- sample(tmp2, floor(0.50 * length(tmp2))) te2  <- setdiff(tmp2, va2)  X_nlin_train <- X_nlin[tr2, ] X_nlin_val   <- X_nlin[va2, ] X_nlin_test  <- X_nlin[te2, ]  cat("Nonlinear SEM — Train:", dim(X_nlin_train),     "| Val:", dim(X_nlin_val), "| Test:", dim(X_nlin_test), "

text: now stress-test linear model data generated nonlinear SEM compare two nonlinear NOTEARS variants. goal quantify cost linearity assumption demonstrate expressive models warranted. three variants evaluated : Linear NOTEARS (misspecified baseline) — algorithm Part , applied naively nonlinear data. NotearsMLP — replaces linear SEM per-variable MLP \(f_i(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{pa}()})\) parameterized torch neural network; acyclicity enforced induced binary adjacency weights. NotearsSobolev — replaces MLP Sobolev-basis expansion (truncated sine series), providing smooth nonparametric alternative especially competitive true functions periodic band-limited.

nonlinear SEM follows additive noise structure linear case nonlinear link function applied weighted parent sum. Three link functions supported: tanh (smooth, bounded), z*sin(z) (multiplicative interaction, non-monotone), sin (periodic). Generation respects topological ordering graph parents always assigned values children.
code: # ── Nonlinear SEM simulator ─────────────────────────────────────────────────── # Convention: W[i, j] = weight of directed edge j → i #             (row = destination / effect, column = source / cause) # # sem_type: #   "mlp"  – tanh(z)       smooth, bounded nonlinearity #   "mim"  – z * sin(z)    multiplicative interaction (non-monotone) #   "gp"   – sin(z)        periodic / Gaussian-process-like # simulate_nonlinear_sem_custom <- function(W, n, sem_type = "mlp", noise_sd = 0.5) {   d <- ncol(W)    # igraph adjacency convention: A[a, b] != 0 => edge a -> b   # Since W[i, j] != 0 <=> j -> i, we need A = t(W)   g   <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix((t(W) != 0) * 1L, mode = "directed")   ord <- as.integer(igraph::topo_sort(g))   # parents before children    X <- matrix(0.0, nrow = n, ncol = d)    for (i in ord) {     pa <- which(W[i, ] != 0)               # parents of node i      if (length(pa) == 0L) {       X[, i] <- rnorm(n)                   # root node: Gaussian noise     } else {       z <- as.vector(X[, pa, drop = FALSE] %*% W[i, pa])  # weighted parent sum       X[, i] <- switch(sem_type,         mlp = tanh(z)    + rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd),         mim = z * sin(z) + rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd),         gp  = sin(z)     + rnorm(n, sd = noise_sd),                  z       + rnorm(n)          # fallback: linear       )     }   }   X }

# ── Dataset 2: Nonlinear SEM (d = 10) ───────────────────────────────────────── # d = 10 keeps NotearsMLP / Sobolev runtimes tractable in a notebook set_random_seed(42) n_nlin <- 2000; d_nlin <- 10; s0_nlin <- 10 B_true_nlin <- simulate_dag(d_nlin, s0_nlin, graph_type) W_true_nlin <- simulate_parameter(B_true_nlin) X_nlin      <- simulate_nonlinear_sem_custom(W_true_nlin, n_nlin, sem_type = "mlp")  write.csv(X_nlin,      "X_nonlinear.csv",      row.names = FALSE) write.csv(W_true_nlin, "W_true_nonlinear.csv", row.names = FALSE)  X_nlin <- scale(X_nlin, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)  set.seed(42) tr2  <- sample(1:n_nlin, floor(0.70 * n_nlin)) tmp2 <- setdiff(1:n_nlin, tr2) va2  <- sample(tmp2, floor(0.50 * length(tmp2))) te2  <- setdiff(tmp2, va2)  X_nlin_train <- X_nlin[tr2, ] X_nlin_val   <- X_nlin[va2, ] X_nlin_test  <- X_nlin[te2, ]  cat("Nonlinear SEM — Train:", dim(X_nlin_train),     "| Val:", dim(X_nlin_val), "| Test:", dim(X_nlin_test), "\n") Nonlinear SEM — Train: 1400 10 | Val: 300 10 | Test: 300 10

what: 5.3.2 DAG-GNN: DAG Structure Learning with Graph Neural Networks
text: DAG-GNN (Yu et al., ICML 2019) learns structure Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) observational data embedding problem inside deep generative model. NOTEARS replaces combinatorial graph search smooth optimization weighted adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{W}\), DAG-GNN goes step : wraps adjacency matrix inside Variational Autoencoder (VAE) driven Graph Neural Network (GNN) encoder decoder modules, representation learning structure learning trained end--end. key insight linear Structural Equation Model (SEM), \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{}^\top \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Z}\), mapping noise \(\mathbf{Z}\) observations \(\mathbf{X}\) exactly \((\mathbf{} - \mathbf{}^\top)^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\). DAG-GNN makes causal forward pass decoder VAE, uses GNN-filtered MLP encoder. adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{}\) learnable parameter shared encoder decoder, gradient descent simultaneously fits data discovers graph. Acyclicity enforced differentiable constraint family NOTEARS — \(h(\mathbf{}) = 0\) iff graph DAG — embedded augmented Lagrangian penalty ELBO objective. notebook demonstrates full pipeline: data simulation, model training stable augmented Lagrangian updates, structure recovery, downstream causal effect estimation.  CausalML R package provides tools causal inference, structure learning, treatment effect estimation. particular, package includes R port DAG-GNN (R/causalDeepNet.R), leverages torch library enable deep neural network-based learning Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) data. CausalML offers unified interface instantiate, train, evaluate models causal structure discovery effect estimation. generate small 6-node nonlinear DAG (nodes 0–3 = covariates, 4 = treatment T, 5 = outcome Y). Data continuous nonlinear. Structure learning uses data (unsupervised). CATE validation split later. DAG-GNN frames causal structure learning Variational Autoencoder (VAE) whose latent space organized learnable adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{}\). architecture four tightly coupled components, illustrated figure . encoder maps observed data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \\mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) latent distribution \(q_\phi(\mathbf{Z} \mid \mathbf{X})\). proceeds two steps: MLP embedding — per-node MLP projects variable’s observations shared embedding space: \(\mathbf{H} = \mathrm{MLP}_\phi(\mathbf{X})\). Graph filtering — embedding mixed across nodes using graph structure encoded \(\mathbf{}\): \(\tilde{\mathbf{H}} = (\mathbf{} - \mathbf{}^\top) \cdot \mathbf{H}\). multiplication propagates information along reverse directed edges, node aggregates messages children — implementing one step GNN message passing. filtered embedding projected mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) log-variance \(\log \boldsymbol{\sigma}^2\) approximate posterior, latent code \(\mathbf{Z}\) sampled via reparameterization trick. Rather fixed standard Gaussian, DAG-GNN uses learnable prior \(p(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{})\), adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{}\) free parameter optimized jointly encoder decoder weights. encodes assumption data-generating structure — DAG — shape prior distribution latent codes. decoder reconstructs \(\mathbf{X}\) \(\mathbf{Z}\) inverting structural equation: \(\hat{\mathbf{X}} = (\mathbf{} - \mathbf{}^\top)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}\). closed-form solution linear SEM \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{}^\top \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Z}\), meaning decoder explicitly models causal forward pass. subsequent MLP refines reconstruction, outputting reconstructed mean \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) log-variance \(\widehat{\log \boldsymbol{\sigma}^2}\). \(\mathbf{}\) encode valid DAG, acyclicity constraint \(h(\mathbf{}) = 0\) must hold. R implementation causalDeepNet.R (v2) uses matrix polynomial formulation: \[h(\mathbf{}) = \mathrm{tr}\!\left(\left(\mathbf{} + \frac{\mathbf{} \odot \mathbf{}}{d}\right)^d\right) - d,\] equals zero graph acyclic differentiable respect \(\mathbf{}\). (matrix-exponential form original paper, \(h(\mathbf{}) = \mathrm{tr}(e^{\mathbf{} \odot \mathbf{}}) - d\), mathematically equivalent less numerically stable large \(d\).) effective adjacency used training \(\mathbf{}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \tanh(\mathbf{}) \times 0.5\), keeps entries \((-0.5, 0.5)\) replaces earlier sinh-based formulation numerical stability. full training objective combines three terms: \[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{Z})] + \mathrm{KL}[q_\phi(\mathbf{Z} \mid \mathbf{X}) \,\|\, p(\mathbf{Z})]}_{\text{negative ELBO}} + \lambda\, h(\mathbf{}) + \frac{c}{2}\, h(\mathbf{})^2,\] : reconstruction loss \(-\mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{Z})]\) measures well decoder recovers \(\mathbf{X}\) sampled \(\mathbf{Z}\). KL divergence \(\mathrm{KL}[q_\phi \| p]\) regularizes encoder toward learnable prior, shaped \(\mathbf{}\). augmented Lagrangian penalty \(\lambda\, h(\mathbf{}) + \frac{c}{2}\, h(\mathbf{})^2\) enforces acyclicity. multiplier \(\lambda\) updated dual ascent every step; penalty coefficient \(c\) increased (cap \(10^6\)) \(|h(\mathbf{})|\) fails decrease sufficiently — throttled schedule (every 25 epochs) prevents penalty exploding early training. Additional stability measures R implementation include gradient clipping (max-norm 1.0), Huber regularizer \(\mathbf{}\), tryCatch guards around forward pass skip singular steps without poisoning dual variable \(\lambda\). training, binary adjacency recovered thresholding effective adjacency \(|\mathbf{}_{\mathrm{eff}}| > 0.10\). training objective \(\mathcal{L}_c = -\mathrm{ELBO} + \lambda\, h(\mathbf{}) + \frac{c}{2}\, h(\mathbf{})^2 + \epsilon_{\mathrm{Huber}}(\mathbf{})\). dual variable \(\lambda\) updated gradient ascent every step; penalty coefficient \(c\) multiplied \(\eta = 10\) \(|h(\mathbf{}_k)| > \gamma\, |h(\mathbf{}_{k-1})|\) throttle interval (every 25 epochs), capped \(10^6\) prevent explosion. Gradient clipping (max-norm 1.0) tryCatch guards around forward pass protect numerical singularities without corrupting \(\lambda\). learning DAG, estimate Average Treatment Effect (ATE) Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) observational data, using learned DAG’s confounders (X0–X3) adjustment. following figures summarize learned structure, training dynamics, causal effect estimates. Figure 1: True DAG (data-generating) vs learned DAG DAG-GNN. Figure 2: True (weighted) learned (effective, thresholded) adjacency matrices. Figure 3: ELBO loss acyclicity constraint h() training epochs. Figure 4: Estimated ATE 95% CI distribution CATE test set. DAG-GNN turns notoriously hard DAG-learning problem differentiable VAE + GNN optimization. R implementation R/causalDeepNet.R (v2) uses tanh()×0.5 effective adjacency stable training (throttled penalty c, gradient clipping, NaN/singularity guards), scales real data (see Sachs Wine case studies). production: Run DAG-GNN observational dataset. Threshold learned effective adjacency (default 0.10 tanh×0.5 scale) obtain sparse causal DAG. Feed DAG DoWhy / EconML / CausalML (R equivalents like grf, tmle) effect estimation, sensitivity analysis, counterfactuals. Especially powerful many covariates suspect nonlinear confounding. Paper: Yu, Y., Chen, J., Gao, T., & Yu, M. (2019). DAG-GNN: DAG Structure Learning Graph Neural Networks. ICML. arXiv:1904.10098 Official code: fishmoon1234/DAG-GNN R Port: R/causalDeepNet.R (v2: tanh×0.5 effective adj, stable training) NOTEARS baseline: xunzheng/notears DoWhy: pywhy.org/dowhy Follow-works: DAG-GCN, GraN-DAG, etc. Note: R Quarto notebook converted original Python IPython notebook, maintaining structure functionality leveraging R’s torch tidyverse ecosystems.

Graph filtering — embedding mixed across nodes using graph structure encoded \(\mathbf{}\): \(\tilde{\mathbf{H}} = (\mathbf{} - \mathbf{}^\top) \cdot \mathbf{H}\). multiplication propagates information along reverse directed edges, node aggregates messages children — implementing one step GNN message passing. filtered embedding projected mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) log-variance \(\log \boldsymbol{\sigma}^2\) approximate posterior, latent code \(\mathbf{Z}\) sampled via reparameterization trick. Rather fixed standard Gaussian, DAG-GNN uses learnable prior \(p(\mathbf{Z}) = \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{})\), adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{}\) free parameter optimized jointly encoder decoder weights. encodes assumption data-generating structure — DAG — shape prior distribution latent codes. decoder reconstructs \(\mathbf{X}\) \(\mathbf{Z}\) inverting structural equation: \(\hat{\mathbf{X}} = (\mathbf{} - \mathbf{}^\top)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}\). closed-form solution linear SEM \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{}^\top \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Z}\), meaning decoder explicitly models causal forward pass. subsequent MLP refines reconstruction, outputting reconstructed mean \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) log-variance \(\widehat{\log \boldsymbol{\sigma}^2}\). \(\mathbf{}\) encode valid DAG, acyclicity constraint \(h(\mathbf{}) = 0\) must hold. R implementation causalDeepNet.R (v2) uses matrix polynomial formulation: \[h(\mathbf{}) = \mathrm{tr}\!\left(\left(\mathbf{} + \frac{\mathbf{} \odot \mathbf{}}{d}\right)^d\right) - d,\] equals zero graph acyclic differentiable respect \(\mathbf{}\). (matrix-exponential form original paper, \(h(\mathbf{}) = \mathrm{tr}(e^{\mathbf{} \odot \mathbf{}}) - d\), mathematically equivalent less numerically stable large \(d\).) effective adjacency used training \(\mathbf{}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \tanh(\mathbf{}) \times 0.5\), keeps entries \((-0.5, 0.5)\) replaces earlier sinh-based formulation numerical stability. full training objective combines three terms: \[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{Z})] + \mathrm{KL}[q_\phi(\mathbf{Z} \mid \mathbf{X}) \,\|\, p(\mathbf{Z})]}_{\text{negative ELBO}} + \lambda\, h(\mathbf{}) + \frac{c}{2}\, h(\mathbf{})^2,\] : reconstruction loss \(-\mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{Z})]\) measures well decoder recovers \(\mathbf{X}\) sampled \(\mathbf{Z}\). KL divergence \(\mathrm{KL}[q_\phi \| p]\) regularizes encoder toward learnable prior, shaped \(\mathbf{}\). augmented Lagrangian penalty \(\lambda\, h(\mathbf{}) + \frac{c}{2}\, h(\mathbf{})^2\) enforces acyclicity. multiplier \(\lambda\) updated dual ascent every step; penalty coefficient \(c\) increased (cap \(10^6\)) \(|h(\mathbf{})|\) fails decrease sufficiently — throttled schedule (every 25 epochs) prevents penalty exploding early training. Gradient clipping (max-norm 1.0) tryCatch guards around forward pass protect numerical singularities without corrupting \(\lambda\). learning DAG, estimate Average Treatment Effect (ATE) Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) observational data, using learned DAG’s confounders (X0–X3) adjustment.

text: DAG-GNN turns notoriously hard DAG-learning problem differentiable VAE + GNN optimization. R implementation R/causalDeepNet.R (v2) uses tanh()×0.5 effective adjacency stable training (throttled penalty c, gradient clipping, NaN/singularity guards), scales real data (see Sachs Wine case studies). production: Run DAG-GNN observational dataset. Threshold learned effective adjacency (default 0.10 tanh×0.5 scale) obtain sparse causal DAG. Feed DAG DoWhy / EconML / CausalML (R equivalents like grf, tmle) effect estimation, sensitivity analysis, counterfactuals. Especially powerful many covariates suspect nonlinear confounding.

Paper: Yu, Y., Chen, J., Gao, T., & Yu, M. (2019). DAG-GNN: DAG Structure Learning Graph Neural Networks. ICML. arXiv:1904.10098 Official code: fishmoon1234/DAG-GNN R Port: R/causalDeepNet.R (v2: tanh×0.5 effective adj, stable training) NOTEARS baseline: xunzheng/notears DoWhy: pywhy.org/dowhy Follow-works: DAG-GCN, GraN-DAG, etc. Note: R Quarto notebook converted original Python IPython notebook, maintaining structure functionality leveraging R’s torch tidyverse ecosystems.

GraN-DAG (Lachapelle et al., NeurIPS 2020) gradient-based method learning nonlinear causal DAG structure observational data. core idea model every conditional distribution \(p(X_i \mid \mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{pa}()})\) separate masked MLP — one network per node — extract continuous, differentiable adjacency matrix directly neural network weights. avoids linearity assumption NOTEARS VAE framing DAG-GNN retaining smooth acyclicity constraint framework. pipeline, illustrated figure , five sequential stages: Masked MLPs per node — node \(X_i\) gets MLP LeakyReLU hidden layers. Input masking controls candidate parent variables can influence node’s output. mask pattern can pre-filtered Preliminary Neighbour Selection (PNS) training begins, reducing search space large \(d\). Adjacency extraction (compute_A_phi) — continuous weighted adjacency \(A_{\phi,ij}\) computed MLP weight matrices summing contributions along paths network: \(A_{\phi,ij} = \sum_{\text{paths}} \prod_k [W^{(k)}]^\top\). result non-negative \(d \times d\) matrix whose entry \((,j)\) reflects strongly \(X_j\) influences conditional distribution \(X_i\). Acyclicity constraint — differentiable constraint \(h(A_\phi) = \mathrm{tr}(\exp(A_\phi \odot A_\phi)) - d = 0\) evaluated extracted adjacency. \(h = 0\) exactly graph valid DAG; cycle causes \(h > 0\). Augmented Lagrangian optimization — full objective \(L(\phi, \lambda, \mu) = \mathcal{L}(\phi) + (\mu/2)\,h^2 + \lambda\,h\) minimized iterating three steps: () gradient descent \(\phi\) via RMSprop SGD; (ii) dual-variable updates \(\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \mu h\) penalty scaling \(\mu \leftarrow \eta\,\mu\); (iii) convergence check \(h \leq 10^{-8}\). entire loop repeats acyclicity constraint satisfied tolerance. Post-processing output — two pruning steps convert continuous solution binary causal matrix. Threshold search (_to_dag) iterates candidate thresholds \(A_\phi\) selects largest value still yields valid DAG. Jacobian pruning (jac_thresh) removes edges whose empirical Jacobian magnitude near zero, eliminating spurious edges survived thresholding. final outputs binary \(d \times d\) causal matrix \(M\) corresponding directed acyclic graph. {width=“620” height = “800”} GraN-DAG implemented R part RCausalML package via R/causalDeepNet.R. R port uses torch automatic differentiation GPU support, follows original algorithm’s five-stage pipeline described . overview main classes functions. R uses RCausalML (library(RCausalML)), GraN-DAG lives R/causalDeepNet.R (functionally equivalent gCastle’s GraNDAG Python). Load shown GraNDAG available. simulate 10-node Erdős–Rényi DAG nonlinear Gaussian ANM (LeakyReLU mechanisms + Gaussian noise). Standardize features. GraNDAG normalize=TRUE option; manually clarity. Causal discovery usually uses data (structure global), split : Training model (early stopping built GraNDAG). Hold-validation likelihood / downstream CATE. GraN-DAG’s training loop implements augmented Lagrangian procedure Stage 4 pipeline. model alternates minimizing negative log-likelihood via RMSprop/SGD gradient clipping, updating dual variable \(\lambda\) penalty coefficient \(\mu\) based current acyclicity violation \(h(A_\phi)\), checking whether \(h \leq 10^{-8}\) declare convergence. loop, threshold search optional Jacobian pruning (Stage 5) extract final binary DAG. Instantiate GraNDAG defaults close paper; learn full data (train_data strict split). GraN-DAG produced binary causal matrix \(M\) (output Stage 5), encodes DAG can used directly causal inference. read parents node \(M\) identify valid adjustment sets backdoor criterion, estimate causal effects regression sets. Scenario: Node 0 Treatment \(T\) (binarized median demonstration) node 9 Outcome \(Y\) (R 1-based indices 1 10). use columns learned binary matrix find parents \(Y\) descendants \(T\), form adjustment set, estimate ATE via OLS training split. binary causal matrix \(M\) produced GraN-DAG’s threshold search Jacobian pruning compared known ground-truth adjacency using standard structural metrics causal discovery literature. Lower SHD FDR, combined higher TPR, indicate algorithm recovered true edge set accurately. DAG Structure Learning Metrics Typical results setup: SHD ~5–15, TPR > 0.8 (varies seed/hyperparams). Plot learned vs true graph using network visualization packages. can also use GraphDAG(learned_adj, true_causal_matrix, show = TRUE) RCausalML heatmap-style plots (like gCastle’s GraphDAG Python).  Optionally, plot learned DAG (like Python notebook’s second figure):  GraN-DAG achieves nonlinear causal structure learning running five-stage pipeline end--end: masked MLPs model node’s conditional distribution, compute_A_phi extracts differentiable adjacency matrix network weights, NOTEARS-style acyclicity constraint \(h(A_\phi) = 0\) embedded augmented Lagrangian objective minimized RMSprop/SGD, threshold search plus Jacobian pruning convert continuous solution valid binary DAG. notebook : Simulated 10-node nonlinear Gaussian ANM LeakyReLU mechanisms — functional class modelled GraN-DAG’s masked MLPs. Trained GraN-DAG using augmented Lagrangian loop (RMSprop, 3 000 iterations, \(h\)-tolerance \(10^{-6}\)) extracted binary causal matrix via threshold search. Used learned parents--\(Y\) column binary matrix backdoor adjustment set ATE CATE estimation via OLS regression. Evaluated structural recovery SHD, FDR, TPR, FPR, nnz known ground-truth DAG. Key strengths. GraN-DAG can recover nonlinear causal effects ANM assumption, exploits GPU acceleration torch, produces interpretable edge weights via compute_A_phi thresholding. Key limitations. acyclicity constraint evaluation \(O(d^3)\) per step, method works best \(d \lesssim 100\). Identifiability relies additive noise model assumption. Results can sensitive choice \(h\)-tolerance pruning threshold; cross-validate held-likelihood ground truth unavailable. binary causal matrix output GraN-DAG integrates directly downstream frameworks — DoWhy, EconML, CausalML Python; grf, tmle, DoubleML R — population-level individualized causal analysis. # Initialize GraNDAG gnd <- GraNDAG$new(   input_dim = ncol(data),   hidden_num = 2,   hidden_dim = 10,   iterations = 10000 )  # Train on data gnd$learn(data)  # Get causal matrix causal_matrix <- gnd$get_causal_matrix() # Packages used in this notebook (SEMgraph/bnlearn omitted — not referenced here, # and SEMgraph depends on Bioconductor 'graph', which is not yet on CRAN for R 4.6) packages <- c(   "torch", "igraph", "tidyverse", "RCausalML" )  # Install missing packages # new_packages <- packages[!(packages %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"])] # if (length(new_packages)) install.packages(new_packages)  # Verify installation cat("Installed packages:
") Installed packages: print(sapply(packages, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE)) torch    igraph tidyverse RCausalML       TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE # Load packages with suppressed messages invisible(lapply(packages, function(pkg) {   suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE)) })) # Check for GPU availability (torch) DEVICE_TYPE <- if (torch::cuda_is_available()) {   ok <- tryCatch({     x <- torch::torch_tensor(1.0, device = "cuda")     torch::torch_matmul(x, x)     TRUE   }, error = function(e) FALSE)   if (ok) "cuda" else "cpu" } else {   "cpu" } cat("Using device:", DEVICE_TYPE, "
") Using device: cuda set.seed(42) torch::torch_manual_seed(42L) # Generate synthetic data (R equivalent of IIDSimulation) # Since we don't have exact gcastle equivalent, we create synthetic DAG data  generate_dag_data <- function(n_nodes = 10, n_edges = 10,                                n_samples = 2000, seed = 42) {   set.seed(seed)   W <- matrix(0, n_nodes, n_nodes)   # Upper-triangular random edges (i < j) — always a DAG   possible <- which(upper.tri(W), arr.ind = TRUE)   chosen   <- possible[sample(nrow(possible), min(n_edges, nrow(possible))), ]   for (r in seq_len(nrow(chosen))) {     i <- chosen[r, 1]; j <- chosen[r, 2]     W[i, j] <- runif(1, 0.5, 2.0) * sample(c(-1, 1), 1)   }   # Generate data in topological (column) order   X <- matrix(0, n_samples, n_nodes)   for (j in seq_len(n_nodes)) {     parents <- which(W[, j] != 0)     noise   <- rnorm(n_samples, sd = 1.0)     if (length(parents) > 0) {       effect  <- rowSums(sweep(X[, parents, drop = FALSE],                                2, W[parents, j], `*`))       X[, j]  <- pmax(effect, 0) + noise   # LeakyReLU (x>0 part)     } else {       X[, j]  <- noise     }   }   list(W = W, X = X) } dag_data          <- generate_dag_data(n_nodes = 10, n_edges = 10,                                         n_samples = 2000, seed = 42) true_causal_matrix <- dag_data$W data               <- dag_data$X cat("Data shape:", dim(data), "
") Data shape: 2000 10 cat("True edges:", sum(true_causal_matrix != 0), "
") True edges: 10 # Standardize data (GraNDAG normalize=TRUE does this internally) data_mean <- colMeans(data) data_sd <- apply(data, 2, sd) data_sd[data_sd == 0] <- 1.0 data <- sweep(data, 2, data_mean, `-`) data <- sweep(data, 2, data_sd, `/`) # Split data for training and testing set.seed(42) n <- nrow(data) train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = floor(0.8 * n)) test_idx <- setdiff(1:n, train_idx)  train_data <- data[train_idx, , drop = FALSE] test_data <- data[test_idx, , drop = FALSE]  cat("Training samples:", nrow(train_data), "
") Training samples: 1600 cat("Test samples:", nrow(test_data), "
") Test samples: 400 # --- GraNDAG Structure Learning: More Edges Variant --- # To encourage the model to learn more edges, we reduce regularization stringency and penalty thresholds. # Use CPU to avoid CUDA/CPU device mismatch when CUDA is misconfigured or data is on CPU. cat("Training on device:", DEVICE_TYPE, "
") Training on device: cuda gnd_model <- GraNDAG$new(   input_dim       = ncol(data),   hidden_num      = 2L,   hidden_dim      = 10L,   batch_size      = 64L,   lr              = 0.001,   iterations      = 3000L,        # 3k is enough for a 10-node demo   model_name      = "NonLinGaussANM",   nonlinear       = "leaky-relu",   optimizer       = "rmsprop",   h_threshold     = 1e-6,   device_type     = DEVICE_TYPE,  # consistent with device-setup chunk   use_pns         = FALSE,   normalize       = TRUE,   random_seed     = 42L ) gnd_model$learn(data) learned_adj <- gnd_model$get_causal_matrix() cat("Learned edges:", sum(learned_adj != 0), "
") Learned edges: 5 # --- EXPLANATION OF CATE ESTIMATION AND VALIDATION CODE ---  # 1. Define indices for treatment and outcome nodes in the dataset. # Here, node 0 is treated as the "treatment" variable (T), and node 9 as the "outcome" variable (Y) # (in R 1-based indexing: treatment_idx = 1, outcome_idx = 10). treatment_idx <- 1 outcome_idx <- 10  # 2. Create a binary treatment variable. # In this demo, we binarize T by thresholding on its median # (in real datasets, T would be binary/categorical). T <- as.integer(data[, treatment_idx] > median(data[, treatment_idx]))  # 3. Extract outcome variable. Y <- data[, outcome_idx]  # 4. Identify candidate adjustment variables. # We use the learned DAG: the parents of Y are possible confounders to adjust for. parents_of_Y <- which(learned_adj[, outcome_idx] != 0)  # 5. Construct a simple adjustment set. # This set consists of all parents of Y except the treatment node itself # (to avoid adjusting for the treatment). adjustment_set <- parents_of_Y[parents_of_Y != treatment_idx]  cat("Adjustment set for backdoor:", adjustment_set, "
") Adjustment set for backdoor: 5 # 6. Prepare features for regression. # We build a design matrix with the binary treatment T and adjustment covariates. if (length(adjustment_set) > 0) {   X_cate <- cbind(T, data[, adjustment_set, drop = FALSE]) } else {   X_cate <- matrix(T, ncol = 1) }  # 7. text: DAGMA (DAG via M-matrices Acyclicity) introduced Bello, Squires, Bhattacharya (2022). core insight novel algebraic characterization acyclicity avoids numerical instability problems earlier methods.

DAG-NoCurl (Yu et al., 2021) approaches causal discovery fundamentally different angle - differential geometry. parameterizes graph vector field enforces acyclicity projecting onto curl-free component field. DAG-NoCurl enforces acyclicity via: \[W = U^T U - \text{diag}(U^T U)\] loss : \[\min_{U} \; \mathcal{L}(W(U)) + \lambda \|W(U)\|_1 + \mu \cdot \text{curl}(W(U))\]  Constraint-free optimization: augmented Lagrangian inner/outer loops. Differentiable end--end: Amenable joint training downstream prediction heads. Geometric intuition: curl-free projection clean theoretical foundation. Scalability: methods scale roughly \(O(d^3)\); graphs beyond ~200 nodes become expensive. Identifiability: Without distributional assumptions, true DAG identifiable Markov equivalence class. Linear assumption: Default implementations assume linear relationships. Finite-sample issues: High-dimensional, small-sample data may cause overfitting. Causal sufficiency: assume hidden confounders - strong assumption observational health data.

Key points: Acyclicity constraint: method optimizes \(W\) subject continuous acyclicity constraint (using penalty term), ensuring resulting graph DAG. estimated \(W_{kj}\) indicates existence (\(W_{kj} \ne 0\)) strength direct causal effect \(k\) \(j\). Learning performed via gradient-based optimization, minimizing loss function incorporates data fit (e.g., least-squares loss) acyclicity penalty. summary, dagmaLinear() uncovers underlying linear causal structure estimating variables directly cause others, strength effects, enforcing resulting graph acyclic.

text: neural Granger causality frame multivariate time series supervised regression problem: given variables lag window \(p\) steps, predict next values. Sparsity first-layer weights reveals causal structure.
code: LAG <- 5L  # Trading week  build_lag_dataset <- function(data, lag) {   n <- nrow(data) - lag   d <- ncol(data)   x_flat <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = d * lag)   x_seq  <- array(0,  dim = c(n, lag, d))   y      <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = d)   for (t in seq_len(n)) {     window <- data[t:(t + lag - 1), , drop = FALSE]  # (lag, d)     x_flat[t, ] <- as.vector(t(window))              # row-major flatten: (d*lag,)     x_seq[t, , ] <- window     y[t, ] <- data[t + lag, ]   }   colnames(y) <- colnames(data)   list(x_flat = x_flat, x_seq = x_seq, y = y) }  prep      <- build_lag_dataset(data_np, LAG) n_total   <- nrow(prep$y) split_idx <- floor(0.8 * n_total)  x_flat_tr  <- prep$x_flat[seq_len(split_idx), , drop = FALSE] x_flat_val <- prep$x_flat[(split_idx + 1L):n_total, , drop = FALSE] x_seq_tr   <- prep$x_seq[seq_len(split_idx), , , drop = FALSE] x_seq_val  <- prep$x_seq[(split_idx + 1L):n_total, , , drop = FALSE] y_tr       <- prep$y[seq_len(split_idx), , drop = FALSE] y_val      <- prep$y[(split_idx + 1L):n_total, , drop = FALSE]  cat(sprintf(   "Train: x_flat %s | Val: x_flat %s\n",   paste(dim(x_flat_tr),  collapse = " x "),   paste(dim(x_flat_val), collapse = " x ") )) Train: x_flat 1202 x 40 | Val: x_flat 301 x 40

Inferred causal links treated exploratory — financial returns weakly causal heavily confounded. can tune LAG, LAM, HIDDEN, EPOCHS trade fit vs. sparsity. Increasing LAM produces sparser, interpretable graphs; decreasing may reveal weaker relationships. stricter graph sparsity NRI, consider annealing Gumbel-Softmax temperature adding explicit edge-sparsity priors. rigorous causal interpretation requires domain knowledge, interventional data, additional structural assumptions (e.g., acyclicity constraints).

Classical Granger causality tests linear predictive improvement misses nonlinear relationships — Neural Granger Causality addresses replacing coefficient blocks neural networks. Four architectures cover main design choices: feed-forward per-variable heads (cMLP), recurrent per-variable heads (cLSTM), structured gated recurrence (EconomySRU), amortised graph inference (NRI). Structured sparsity (group LASSO, \(\ell_1\) mask penalty, KL prior) common thread — without , neural networks spread weight everywhere causal graph can read . {RCausalML} exposes four models single neural_granger_ml() call; returned object contains trained models, per-epoch histories, validation MSEs, \(d \times d\) causal matrices ready downstream analysis. S&P 500 sector ETFs (2018–2023), cLSTM ECONOMY-SRU typically achieve slightly lower validation MSE cMLP; NRI behaves differently optimises ELBO rather pure MSE. Consensus graph (average min-max normalised matrices) can highlight cross-model stable links; strong consensus pairs across four models reliable candidates investigation.

what: 5.4.2 Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with Deep Components
text: Structural Causal Model (SCM) mathematical framework representing cause--effect relationships system. Formally, SCM defined \(\mathcal{M} = (\mathbf{S}, P(\mathbf{U}))\) structural equations: \[X_i = f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i),\, U_i),\] \(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i)\) denotes causal parents \(X_i\) directed acyclic graph (DAG), \(U_i\) independent exogenous noise variables. SCMs support Pearl’s three-rung Ladder Causation: Association: \(P(Y \mid X = x)\) — observational queries. Intervention: \(P(Y \mid (X = x))\) — effect external manipulation. Counterfactual: \(P(Y_x \mid X = x', Y = y')\) — happened alternate scenario. Deep SCMs replace hand-crafted \(f_i\) neural networks: \[X_i = f_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i),\, U_i).\] variational deep SCM setup: Encoder: \(q_\phi(U \mid X)\) — infers latent noise observations. Decoder: \(p_\theta(X \mid U, G)\) — reconstructs observations noise graph. Objective: ELBO-style loss reconstruction + KL divergence. notebook demonstrates three complementary deep learning approaches structural causal modelling multivariate time-series data (S&P 500 sector ETF log-returns): DeepSCM assumes known adjacency matrix (derived correlation heuristic) learns nonlinear structural equations top fixed graph: \[X_t = f_\theta\!\left(X_{t-1:t-p},\, \right) + \epsilon_t,\] \(\) fixed (learned) \(f_\theta\) consists per-variable MLPs variational noise encoders. useful: Stable training credible prior graph available; good baseline intervention analysis. Limitation: Performance depends quality fixed graph. DECI jointly learns graph structure structural equations. uses soft learnable adjacency matrix enforces acyclicity via NOTEARS-style constraint: \[h() = \operatorname{tr}(e^{\circ }) - d = 0.\] objective combines reconstruction, KL divergence, DAG regularization, sparsity: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_{\text{KL}}\,\text{KL} + \lambda_{\text{DAG}}\,h() + \lambda_{\text{sparse}}\|\|_1.\] useful: Learns structure mechanism together; produces interpretable weighted causal graphs. Limitation: Hyperparameter-sensitive; optimization can expensive. DYNOTEARS extends NOTEARS-style optimization time-series causal discovery explicit lag structure: \[X_t = W^{(0)}X_t + \sum_{k=1}^{p} W^{(k)} X_{t-k} + \epsilon_t,\] \(W^{(0)}\) captures instantaneous effects \(W^{(k)}\) captures directed lag-\(k\) effects. Acyclicity imposed via smooth constraint aggregated weight matrix: \[\min_{\{W^{(k)}\}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_1 \sum_{k=0}^{p} \|W^{(k)}\|_1 + \lambda_2\, h(\cdot).\] useful: Explicitly separates lagged directional effects; produces interpretable causal graphs multivariate time series. text: notebook demonstrates three complementary deep learning approaches structural causal modelling multivariate time-series data (S&P 500 sector ETF log-returns): DeepSCM assumes known adjacency matrix (derived correlation heuristic) learns nonlinear structural equations top fixed graph: \[X_t = f_\theta\!\left(X_{t-1:t-p},\, \right) + \epsilon_t,\] \(\) fixed (learned) \(f_\theta\) consists per-variable MLPs variational noise encoders. useful: Stable training credible prior graph available; good baseline intervention analysis. Limitation: Performance depends quality fixed graph. DECI jointly learns graph structure structural equations. uses soft learnable adjacency matrix enforces acyclicity via NOTEARS-style constraint: \[h() = \operatorname{tr}(e^{\circ }) - d = 0.\] objective combines reconstruction, KL divergence, DAG regularization, sparsity: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_{\text{KL}}\,\text{KL} + \lambda_{\text{DAG}}\,h() + \lambda_{\text{sparse}}\|\|_1.\] useful: Learns structure mechanism together; produces interpretable weighted causal graphs. Limitation: Hyperparameter-sensitive; optimization can expensive. DYNOTEARS extends NOTEARS-style optimization time-series causal discovery explicit lag structure: \[X_t = W^{(0)}X_t + \sum_{k=1}^{p} W^{(k)} X_{t-k} + \epsilon_t,\] \(W^{(0)}\) captures instantaneous effects \(W^{(k)}\) captures directed lag-\(k\) effects. Acyclicity imposed via smooth constraint aggregated weight matrix: \[\min_{\{W^{(k)}\}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_1 \sum_{k=0}^{p} \|W^{(k)}\|_1 + \lambda_2\, h(\cdot).\] useful: Explicitly separates lagged directional effects; produces interpretable causal graphs multivariate time series. Limitation: Sensitive regularization threshold settings.

Limitation: Hyperparameter-sensitive; optimization can expensive.

text: section downloads S&P 500 sector ETF prices (universe used Neural Granger Causality notebook), converts standardized log-returns, builds lagged input/output arrays training. Note: online market data unavailable, notebook automatically falls back synthetic demo data downstream cells remain runnable.
code: TICKERS <- c(   "XLF" = "Financials",   "XLE" = "Energy",   "XLK" = "Technology",   "XLV" = "Healthcare",   "XLI" = "Industrials",   "XLY" = "ConsumerDisc",   "XLP" = "ConsumerStap",   "XLU" = "Utilities" )  # Download close prices via tidyquant (Yahoo Finance backend) fetch_close_prices <- function(tickers, start = "2018-01-01", end = "2024-01-01") {   tryCatch({     raw <- tidyquant::tq_get(names(tickers), get = "stock.prices",                               from = start, to = end, complete_cases = TRUE)     if (is.null(raw) || nrow(raw) == 0) return(NULL)     raw |>       dplyr::select(symbol, date, adjusted) |>       tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = adjusted) |>       dplyr::arrange(date) |>       tidyr::drop_na()   }, error = function(e) NULL) }  close_wide <- fetch_close_prices(TICKERS)  if (is.null(close_wide) || nrow(close_wide) < 30) {   message("Warning: market data unavailable; using synthetic demo data.")   set.seed(42)   n_steps <- 1400L   base <- matrix(rnorm(n_steps * length(TICKERS), 0, 0.01),                  nrow = n_steps, ncol = length(TICKERS))   for (i in seq(2L, n_steps)) base[i, ] <- base[i, ] + 0.25 * base[i - 1L, ]   returns_df <- as.data.frame(base)   colnames(returns_df) <- unname(TICKERS)   data_np <- scale(base) } else {   # Compute log-returns   price_mat <- as.matrix(close_wide[, names(TICKERS)])   log_ret   <- log(price_mat[-1L, ] / price_mat[-nrow(price_mat), ])   colnames(log_ret) <- unname(TICKERS[colnames(price_mat)])   returns_df <- as.data.frame(log_ret)   data_np    <- scale(log_ret) }  VAR_NAMES <- colnames(data_np) d         <- ncol(data_np) Tt        <- nrow(data_np)  cat(sprintf("d=%d variables, T=%d\n", d, Tt)) d=8 variables, T=1508 LAG <- 5L  # Build 3-D array (N x lag x d) of lagged windows build_lag_dataset <- function(data, lag) {   N     <- nrow(data) - lag   x_seq <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(N, lag, ncol(data)))   y_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = N, ncol = ncol(data))   for (t in seq_len(N)) {     x_seq[t, , ] <- data[t:(t + lag - 1L), , drop = FALSE]     y_mat[t,  ]  <- data[t + lag, ]   }   list(x_seq = x_seq, y_mat = y_mat) }  lag_data <- build_lag_dataset(data_np, LAG) X_seq    <- lag_data$x_seq Y_mat    <- lag_data$y_mat  split  <- floor(0.8 * nrow(X_seq)) X_tr   <- X_seq[seq_len(split), , ] X_val  <- X_seq[(split + 1L):nrow(X_seq), , ] Y_tr   <- Y_mat[seq_len(split), ] Y_val  <- Y_mat[(split + 1L):nrow(Y_mat), ]  cat(sprintf("Train: (%d, %d, %d)  Val: (%d, %d, %d)\n",             dim(X_tr)[1], dim(X_tr)[2], dim(X_tr)[3],             dim(X_val)[1], dim(X_val)[2], dim(X_val)[3])) Train: (1202, 5, 8)  Val: (301, 5, 8)

code: # Acyclicity penalty h(A) = tr(expm(A*A)) - d  [scalar, on CPU] acyclicity_penalty_r <- function(A_mat) {   if (requireNamespace("torch", quietly = TRUE)) {     A_t <- torch::torch_tensor(A_mat, dtype = torch::torch_float32())     val <- (torch::torch_matrix_exp(A_t * A_t))$trace()$item() - nrow(A_mat)     return(val)   }   # Fallback: spectral-radius approximation   ev  <- Re(eigen(A_mat * A_mat, only.values = TRUE)$values)   sum(exp(ev)) - nrow(A_mat) }  # Threshold a soft adjacency matrix to binary threshold_adjacency <- function(A_soft, threshold = 0.35) {   A_bin <- (abs(A_soft) > threshold) * 1.0   diag(A_bin) <- 0.0   A_bin } # Use the last lag slice (contemporaneous snapshot) for correlation corr_mat  <- abs(cor(data_np)) diag(corr_mat) <- 0.0 A_fixed   <- (corr_mat > 0.25) * 1.0 diag(A_fixed) <- 0.0  cat("Fixed adjacency (correlation > 0.25):\n") Fixed adjacency (correlation > 0.25): print(A_fixed) Financials Energy Technology Healthcare Industrials ConsumerDisc Financials            0      1          1          1           1            1 Energy                1      0          1          1           1            1 Technology            1      1          0          1           1            1 Healthcare            1      1          1          0           1            1 Industrials           1      1          1          1           0            1 ConsumerDisc          1      1          1          1           1            0 ConsumerStap          1      1          1          1           1            1 Utilities             1      1          1          1           1            1              ConsumerStap Utilities Financials              1         1 Energy                  1         1 Technology              1         1 Healthcare              1         1 Industrials             1         1 ConsumerDisc            1         1 ConsumerStap            0         1 Utilities               1         0 plot_scm_dag(A_fixed, VAR_NAMES, "Fixed Graph Used by DeepSCM (corr > 0.25)")
